concepts.statement: Diversification removes unsystematic risk, the part specific to individual securities. What remains in a well-diversified portfolio is systematic risk, which beta measures and which no amount of diversification can remove.
An option premium is intrinsic value plus time value. A put's intrinsic value is the excess of strike over spot (zero if spot is higher); whatever of the premium is not intrinsic value is time value.

concepts.subsection: Foreign Exchange Exposure and Risk Management
concepts.statement: Under interest rate parity, the currency with the higher interest rate trades at a forward discount and the lower-rate currency at a forward premium, by the interest differential — otherwise borrowing in one currency and depositing in the other would be a free profit.

citation.ref: Ch. Foreign Exchange Exposure and Risk Management

concepts.statement: Duration measures a bond's price sensitivity to interest rate changes. It rises with maturity and falls with coupon; a zero-coupon bond's duration equals its maturity, the maximum for any bond of that term.

To hedge a stock portfolio with index futures, the number of contracts is the portfolio's value multiplied by its beta, divided by the value of one futures contract. Ignoring beta hedges a different portfolio than the one held.

concepts.subsection: Foreign Exchange Exposure and Risk Management
concepts.statement: An importer with a foreign currency payable loses when that currency rises, so the hedge is to buy it forward or buy a call option on it. A forward locks the rate both ways; the option caps the cost while keeping the gain if the currency falls, at the price of the premium.

citation.ref: Ch. Foreign Exchange Exposure and Risk Management

concepts.statement: When mutually exclusive projects rank differently under NPV and IRR, NPV decides. IRR assumes reinvestment at the IRR itself and can prefer a small project with a high rate over a large one that adds more value; NPV measures the wealth actually added at the real cost of capital.

Net asset value per unit is the market value of the fund's investments plus other assets, minus liabilities and accrued expenses, divided by units outstanding. Entry and exit prices derive from NAV, and the expense ratio quietly drags it every day.

Under constant dividend growth, equity value per share is next year's expected dividend divided by the excess of the required return over the growth rate. The model runs on the coming dividend, not the one just paid, and dies where growth meets or beats the required return.

A forward rate agreement fixes today the interest rate for a future borrowing or deposit period — a 6x9 FRA covers a three-month period starting six months out. The buyer gains when rates rise above the agreed rate and is compensated by a discounted settlement at the period's start; no principal ever moves.

For European options on the same share, strike and expiry, the call price minus the put price equals the share price minus the present value of the strike. When market prices break that chain, a riskless arbitrage exists — buy the cheap side, sell the dear one, and lock the difference.

Sharpe divides excess return by total risk (standard deviation); Treynor divides the same excess return by systematic risk (beta). For a fully diversified portfolio the two rank alike, because diversification has squeezed out the unsystematic part. Where they disagree, the fund is carrying diversifiable risk the market does not pay for.

concepts.subsection: CAPM and the security market line
concepts.statement: CAPM's required return is the risk-free rate plus beta times the market risk premium. A security whose expected return sits above that line has positive alpha — it is underpriced, and the decision rule says buy; below the line, overpriced, sell. Alpha measures mispricing against systematic risk only.

The fair futures price is the spot price grown at the carrying cost — financing, storage, minus any yield the asset throws off. A traded futures price above fair value invites cash-and-carry arbitrage (buy spot, sell futures); below fair value, reverse cash-and-carry (sell spot, buy futures). The arbitrage, not opinion, is what pins the price to the formula.

In a share-for-share merger, the acquirer's EPS rises when the price paid values the target at a lower price-earnings multiple than the acquirer's own, and falls when the target is bought at a higher multiple. The exchange ratio decides how the combined earnings spread over the combined shares; accretion is arithmetic, not evidence of a good deal.

citation.ref: Ch. Mergers, Acquisitions and Corporate Restructuring

concepts.statement: A money market hedge manufactures a forward rate from the two interest rates: an exporter awaiting foreign currency borrows that currency today against the receivable, converts at spot, and invests at home; the foreign loan is repaid by the receivable itself. If interest rate parity holds exactly, the locked-in rate equals the forward rate and the choice is a matter of transaction cost and access, not principle.

citation.ref: Ch. Foreign Exchange Exposure and Risk Management

concepts.statement: Value at Risk states the largest loss expected over a stated horizon at a stated confidence — a one-day 99 per cent VaR of ₹10 lakh means one trading day in a hundred should lose more than ₹10 lakh. It says nothing about how much worse that hundredth day gets, which is the measure's famous blind spot.

concepts.subsection: Capital market line and security market line
concepts.statement: The capital market line prices total risk (standard deviation) and holds only efficient portfolios — combinations of the risk-free asset and the market portfolio. The security market line prices systematic risk (beta) and holds every fairly priced asset, efficient or not. A single stock full of diversifiable risk plots on the SML yet below the CML.

Modigliani and Miller hold that in a perfect market — no taxes, no transaction costs, no information gaps — dividend policy cannot change shareholder wealth: paying a dividend drops the ex-dividend price by the same amount, and a shareholder wanting cash can manufacture a dividend by selling shares. Real-world relevance arguments live exactly in the frictions the proof assumes away — taxes, signalling, clientele effects.

In a plain vanilla interest rate swap one party pays fixed and receives floating on a notional principal that is never exchanged; only net interest differences change hands each period. A borrower with floating-rate debt who pays fixed on a swap has synthetically fixed its cost; the swap's value at inception is zero and moves as rates move.

concepts.subsection: Foreign exchange — cross rates and triangular arbitrage
concepts.statement: Three currencies imply each cross rate from the other two; when a quoted cross rate strays from the implied rate, riding the three legs in the right circle returns more of the starting currency than was put in, risk-free. The direction matters — one way round the triangle profits, the other way loses — and the trade itself pushes the quotes back into line.

citation.ref: Ch. Foreign Exchange Exposure and Risk Management

concepts.statement: Free cash flow to the firm belongs to all capital providers and discounts at the weighted average cost of capital to give enterprise value; free cash flow to equity — FCFF less after-tax interest and net debt repayments — belongs to shareholders alone and discounts at the cost of equity to give equity value directly. Mixing a flow with the other side's discount rate is the classic valuation error.

concepts.subsection: Risk in capital budgeting — certainty equivalents
concepts.statement: The certainty equivalent approach shrinks each risky cash flow to the certain amount the decision-maker would accept instead, then discounts at the risk-free rate; the risk-adjusted discount rate approach keeps the expected flows and loads the risk into a higher rate. The rate route compounds the risk penalty with time even when risk does not grow; certainty equivalents price each year's risk on its own.

A term loan turns non-performing when interest or principal stays overdue for more than ninety days; a cash credit when the account stays out of order. Once non-performing, the asset walks a ladder — substandard for its first twelve months as an NPA, doubtful once it stays substandard beyond twelve months, loss when identified as such — and income on it is recognised only on realisation, not accrual.

citation.ref: Prudential norms on Income Recognition, Asset Classification and Provisioning

concepts.statement: Section 141(3)(d) with Rule 10 draws money lines around the auditor's independence: a relative may hold securities of the company up to one lakh rupees face value; indebtedness to the company beyond five lakh rupees disqualifies; a guarantee for a third party's debt to the company beyond one lakh rupees disqualifies. The disqualification reaches the member, the firm and its partners, and one incurred during the term vacates the office.

CARO's fraud clause asks three things: whether any fraud by the company or on the company was noticed or reported during the year, with nature and amount; whether any section 143(12) report was filed in Form ADT-4; and whether the auditor considered whistle-blower complaints received by the company. The clause covers fraud on the company by anyone, not only by its officers and employees.

SQC 1 requires an engagement quality control review — an objective evaluation of the significant judgments and the conclusions reached — for audits of financial statements of listed entities, completed before the report is dated. The reviewer stands outside the engagement team, and the report cannot be signed past an unresolved difference with the reviewer.

An audit expresses an opinion on financial statements against a framework; due diligence is a purchaser-side examination of a target's whole position — financial, legal, operational — to price a deal and surface hidden liabilities; an investigation is a deep, targeted probe into a suspected specific matter, going wherever the suspicion leads. Scope, purpose and the reporting audience differ across all three; assurance levels are not interchangeable.

citation.ref: Ch. Due Diligence, Investigation and Forensic Accounting

concepts.statement: Propriety audit asks questions regularity audit cannot: not only was the expenditure sanctioned and lawful, but was it wise, economical, and free of personal advantage — would a person of ordinary prudence have spent his own money so? The C&AG's audit of public undertakings runs on both rails, and a transaction can pass every rule yet fail propriety.

citation.ref: Ch. Audit of Public Sector Undertakings

concepts.statement: Peer review examines a practice unit's systems — whether its quality controls, documentation and compliance with technical standards for attestation services are adequate and were followed — through sample engagements. The reviewer evaluates the unit, not the clients: a review is not a second audit of any auditee, and its report speaks to the unit's systems, leading to a peer review certificate.

A company's first auditor (other than a government company) is appointed by the board within thirty days of registration; if the board fails, the members appoint within ninety days at an extraordinary general meeting. The first auditor holds office until the conclusion of the first annual general meeting — and needs no ratification meanwhile.

concepts.subsection: Section 54 — Capital gains on residential property
concepts.statement: Section 54 exempts long-term capital gains on the transfer of a residential house only when the gain is reinvested in a residential house in India — purchased within one year before or two years after the transfer, or constructed within three years. Reinvestment in commercial property earns no exemption.

Tax audit applies to a business at turnover above ₹1 crore, but the limit rises to ₹10 crore where cash receipts and cash payments each stay within 5 per cent of the respective totals. For a profession the limit is gross receipts above ₹50 lakh.

A domestic company that opts for section 115BAA pays tax at the concessional rate, must give up the specified deductions and incentives, and is outside MAT entirely — book profit tax does not apply to it at all.

A company files its return by 31 October of the assessment year. Where it must furnish a transfer pricing report under section 92E, the due date extends to 30 November. The 31 July date belongs to persons with no audit requirement.

Long-term capital gains on listed equity shares where STT is paid are taxed under section 112A above an annual exemption threshold, without indexation. The rate and threshold are Finance Act figures and move; the structure — exemption slab, no indexation, STT condition — is the stable part.

An eligible resident individual, HUF or firm with business turnover within the limit may declare profit at 8 per cent of turnover — 6 per cent for amounts received through banking channels — and skip books and tax audit. Companies and LLPs are outside the scheme, as are commission, agency and section 44AE transport businesses.

concepts.subsection: Sections 72 and 80 — Carry forward of losses
concepts.statement: A business loss carries forward for eight assessment years, but only if the return of the loss year was filed by its due date — section 80 makes the timely return the price of the carry forward. Unabsorbed depreciation lives under section 32(2) instead, needs no timely return, and has no eight-year limit.

Money received without consideration is taxable as other-sources income if the aggregate from all persons in the year exceeds fifty thousand rupees — and then the whole amount is taxed, not the excess. Gifts from relatives as defined, and on the occasion of the individual's marriage, stay outside regardless of size.

A resident individual or firm in a specified profession with gross receipts within the limit may declare 50 per cent of receipts as income. The enhanced limit applies where cash receipts stay within 5 per cent. Declaring less than 50 per cent while over the basic exemption brings books and audit.

concepts.subsection: Section 194-IA — TDS on purchase of property
concepts.statement: A buyer of immovable property, other than rural agricultural land, deducts tax at 1 per cent of the consideration where consideration or stamp duty value is fifty lakh rupees or more — and then on the whole amount, not the excess. The buyer needs no TAN; the deduction rides on the buyer's PAN.

An individual is resident if present in India for 182 days in the year, or 60 days in the year plus 365 across the four preceding years. The 60-day limb stretches to 182 for a citizen leaving for employment or as crew, and to 120 for a visiting citizen or person of Indian origin whose Indian income exceeds fifteen lakh rupees.

A minor child's income is clubbed with the income of the parent whose total income is higher, with an exemption of fifteen hundred rupees per child. Income from the minor's own manual work or from activity involving the minor's skill and talent stays with the minor.

Loss under house property can be set off against other heads only up to two lakh rupees in a year; the balance carries forward for eight years, and then only against house property income. The interest deduction itself may be larger — the cap bites at set-off, not at computation.

concepts.subsection: Section 43B(h) — Payments to micro and small enterprises
concepts.statement: Sums payable to micro and small enterprises are deductible only in the year of actual payment when paid beyond the time section 15 of the MSMED Act allows — and the usual escape of paying before the return's due date does not apply to this clause. Medium enterprises are outside it.

concepts.subsection: Section 50C — Stamp duty value on transfer of land or building
concepts.statement: Where land or a building sells below its stamp duty value, the stamp value is deemed the consideration for capital gains — but only when it exceeds one hundred and ten per cent of the actual consideration; within that tolerance the actual price stands. The seller can also ask for a valuation officer's reference where the stamp value is contested.

Where tax deductible on a payment to a resident is not deducted, or not deposited by the return's due date, thirty per cent of the expense is disallowed — not the whole of it — and the thirty per cent comes back as a deduction in the year the tax is finally paid.

The 54EC exemption is only for long-term capital gains from land or a building or both, only up to fifty lakh rupees in a financial year, and only where the specified bonds are bought within six months of transfer. The bonds lock in for five years, and taking a loan against them counts as cashing out.

concepts.subsection: Section 79 — Carry forward on change in shareholding
concepts.statement: A closely held company loses its carried-forward losses if, on the last day of the year the loss is set off, shares carrying at least fifty-one per cent of voting power are not held by the persons who held them on the last day of the loss year. Eligible start-ups get a softer test — continuity of all original shareholders, or the seven-year window. Unabsorbed depreciation is outside section 79 entirely.

concepts.subsection: Section 90(4) — Treaty relief and the TRC
concepts.statement: A non-resident claiming treaty benefit must hold a tax residency certificate from its home government; without it the treaty door does not open. The Act also lets the taxpayer choose whichever is more beneficial — treaty or domestic law — provision by provision, and a treaty can never be used to make the position worse than the Act.

An unexplained credit in the books is taxed as income unless the taxpayer explains its nature and source to the officer's satisfaction; for share capital in a closely held company, the source of the source — the resident investor's own funds — must be explained too. Income taxed this way falls under section 115BBE: a sixty per cent rate plus surcharge, with no deductions, allowances, or set-off of losses against it.

concepts.subsection: Section 64(1)(iv) — Income from assets transferred to spouse
concepts.statement: Income from an asset transferred to a spouse without adequate consideration is clubbed with the transferor's income. The clubbing follows the transferred asset's income, not income earned on that income — reinvested earnings belong to the spouse. A transfer before the marriage, or for adequate consideration, or under an agreement to live apart, escapes.

An assessee owning not more than ten goods carriages at any time in the year may declare presumptive income: for a heavy goods vehicle (over 12MT gross weight), one thousand rupees per ton of gross vehicle weight per month or part; for others, seven thousand five hundred per vehicle per month or part. Ownership months count, idle or running; declaring lower than the presumption invites books and audit.

GAAR strikes an arrangement whose main purpose is a tax benefit and which carries a tainted element — non-arm's-length dealings, misuse of the Act, lack of commercial substance, or means not ordinarily employed for bona fide purposes. Both limbs must be satisfied; a tax benefit alone is legitimate planning. The rules spare arrangements whose aggregate tax benefit is within three crore rupees.

concepts.subsection: Transfer pricing — Arm's length price methods
concepts.statement: The arm's length price of an international transaction between associated enterprises is determined by the most appropriate of the prescribed methods — comparable uncontrolled price, resale price, cost plus, profit split, transactional net margin, or other prescribed method. No hierarchy ranks them; suitability to the transaction, functions and available data picks the method, and CUP prevails only when true comparables exist.

A company not under the concessional regimes pays the higher of tax on total income and fifteen per cent of book profit — the audited profit adjusted by the section's own list of additions and deletions. Excess MAT paid becomes credit, carried forward to set against regular tax for up to fifteen years. Companies opting into section 115BAA leave MAT, and MAT credit, behind.

Under-reported income draws a penalty of fifty per cent of the tax on it; where the under-reporting flows from misreporting — misrepresentation of facts, false entries, unrecorded investments, claims without evidence — the penalty is two hundred per cent. A bona fide explanation with disclosed material facts takes an addition out of under-reporting altogether; immunity under section 270AA needs tax and interest paid and no appeal, and never covers misreporting.

concepts.subsection: Section 263 — Revision of orders prejudicial to revenue
concepts.statement: The Commissioner may revise an assessment only where it is both erroneous and prejudicial to the revenue's interests — two conditions, cumulative. An officer's view that is a possible view after real enquiry is not erroneous merely because the Commissioner prefers another; no enquiry where enquiry was called for is the classic error. The window is two years from the end of the financial year of the order.

Interest paid to a non-resident associated enterprise beyond one crore rupees is deductible only up to thirty per cent of EBITDA; the excess carries forward up to eight years. The section reaches loans guaranteed by the associated enterprise too, and spares banks and insurers. It caps deduction, not the interest's character — TDS and the lender's taxation run unaffected.

concepts.subsection: Section 9 — Business connection and significant economic presence
concepts.statement: A non-resident's income is deemed to accrue in India through a business connection — which since 2018 includes an agent habitually playing the principal role in concluding contracts, and since the SEP amendment, a significant economic presence built on transactions or user engagement in India without any physical presence. Treaty definitions of permanent establishment still override for treaty residents, which keeps SEP's bite mainly on non-treaty cases.

Accepting an audit previously held by another chartered accountant without first communicating with him in writing is professional misconduct. The duty is to communicate — the outgoing auditor's permission or no-objection is not required, and the purpose is to learn whether the change hides something the incoming auditor should weigh.

Disclosing information acquired in the course of a professional engagement to anyone other than the client, without the client's consent, is professional misconduct — unless law requires the disclosure. Legal compulsion and client consent are the only two doors out of the duty.

Expressing an opinion on the financial statements of any business in which the member, his firm, or a partner in his firm has a substantial interest is professional misconduct. The clause reaches the firm and the partners, not only the signing member, and no disclosure cures it — the opinion itself is barred.

Failing to exercise due diligence, or being grossly negligent in the conduct of professional duties, is professional misconduct. The clause needs no dishonesty and no client loss — signing what was never examined is the classic case.

A chartered accountant in practice may not engage in any business or occupation other than the profession unless the Council permits it. The clause's own proviso allows a directorship simpliciter — an ordinary board seat without managing or whole-time office — unless the member or a partner is interested in the company as its auditor. General and specific permissions of the Council carve the remaining space.

Failing to keep a client's moneys — other than fees or money meant to be spent — in a separate banking account, or failing to use such moneys for their intended purpose within a reasonable time, is professional misconduct. The office account is for the firm's money; the client account is for the client's, and mixing them is the offence regardless of eventual repayment.

concepts.subsection: Ind AS 115 — Revenue from Contracts with Customers
concepts.statement: Revenue is recognised when (or as) a performance obligation is satisfied by transferring control of the promised good or service to the customer. Transfer of control, not transfer of risks and rewards, is the recognition trigger.
Inventories of items that are not ordinarily interchangeable are costed by specific identification. For the rest, FIFO or weighted average is used. LIFO is not permitted.

An investor controls an investee only when it has all three elements together — power over the investee, exposure or rights to variable returns, and the ability to use its power to affect those returns. Control does not require a majority shareholding.

Loss allowances are measured on an expected credit loss basis, recognised from initial recognition without waiting for a default. For trade receivables the simplified approach applies, and the allowance is always lifetime expected credit losses.

Under the Indian carve-out, a gain on a bargain purchase is recognised in other comprehensive income and accumulated in capital reserve, not in profit or loss — unlike IFRS 3, which takes it to profit or loss.

concepts.subsection: Ind AS 115 — Revenue from Contracts with Customers
concepts.statement: A performance obligation is satisfied over time only when one of three criteria is met — the customer consumes the benefit as the entity performs, the customer controls the asset as it is created, or the asset has no alternative use and the entity has an enforceable right to payment for performance to date. Otherwise control passes at a point in time.

concepts.subsection: Ind AS 37 — Provisions, Contingent Liabilities and Contingent Assets
concepts.statement: A provision is recognised only when all three conditions hold — a present obligation, legal or constructive, from a past event; a probable outflow of resources; and a reliable estimate. For a restructuring, the obligating event is announcing the plan to those affected or beginning to implement it, never the board decision alone.

concepts.subsection: Ind AS 16 — Property, Plant and Equipment
concepts.statement: The cost of a major inspection or overhaul that is a condition of continuing to operate an asset is capitalised into the asset's carrying amount when incurred, and any remaining carrying amount of the previous inspection is derecognised — even if the previous inspection's cost was never separately identified.

concepts.subsection: Ind AS 21 — The Effects of Changes in Foreign Exchange Rates
concepts.statement: At each reporting date, foreign currency monetary items are translated at the closing rate, with exchange differences to profit or loss. Non-monetary items carried at historical cost stay at the transaction-date rate. Whether an item is money fixes which rate it gets.

Internally generated goodwill is never recognised as an asset, and internally generated brands, mastheads, customer lists and similar items are barred with it. Development costs are the exception, capitalised only from the day all six conditions are demonstrated; research is always expensed.

An operating segment is separately reportable if it crosses ten per cent of combined revenue (internal plus external), of the greater of combined profits or combined losses, or of combined assets — and reportable segments must together cover seventy-five per cent of external revenue, adding segments until they do.

concepts.subsection: Ind AS 1 — Presentation of Financial Statements
concepts.statement: A liability is current when the entity lacks, at the reporting date, the right to defer settlement for at least twelve months. A covenant breached by the year end makes the loan payable on demand and therefore current — unless the lender agreed, on or before the reporting date, not to demand payment; a waiver arriving after the year end comes too late to change the classification.

concepts.subsection: Ind AS 7 — Statement of Cash Flows
concepts.statement: Under the Indian carve-out, an entity other than a financial institution classifies interest paid as a financing cash flow and interest and dividends received as investing — the options IFRS offers are removed. A bank classifies all of them as operating, because lending is its business.

A lessee recognises a right-of-use asset and a lease liability for every lease, with two elections out — leases of twelve months or less with no purchase option, and leases of low-value assets. The exemptions are elections about recognition, not about whether the contract is a lease.

An asset is impaired when its carrying amount exceeds its recoverable amount, and recoverable amount is the higher of fair value less costs of disposal and value in use. Higher — the entity keeps the better of selling and using, so either measure alone can clear the asset of impairment.

concepts.subsection: Ind AS 10 — Events after the Reporting Period
concepts.statement: An event after the reporting period adjusts the financial statements only when it evidences a condition that existed at the reporting date; a condition that arose afterwards is disclosed, not adjusted. Dividends declared after the reporting period are the standard's own worked example — no liability at the reporting date, however certain the declaration.

concepts.subsection: Ind AS 105 — Non-current Assets Held for Sale
concepts.statement: Held-for-sale classification needs the asset available for immediate sale in its present condition and the sale highly probable — management committed to a plan, an active programme to find a buyer, active marketing at a reasonable price, and completion expected within a year. Once classified, the asset is measured at the lower of carrying amount and fair value less costs to sell, and depreciation stops.

concepts.subsection: Ind AS 8 — Policies, Estimates and Errors
concepts.statement: A change in accounting policy is applied retrospectively, restating comparatives as if the new policy had always applied; a change in accounting estimate is recognised prospectively, in the period of change and the future. Where the two are hard to tell apart, the standard itself says treat the change as an estimate. Depreciation method and useful life are estimates; measurement basis is policy.

Borrowing costs directly attributable to acquiring, constructing or producing a qualifying asset — one that necessarily takes a substantial period to get ready for its intended use or sale — are capitalised as part of the asset's cost; all other borrowing costs are expensed. Capitalisation is suspended during extended periods when active development pauses, and ends when the asset is substantially ready.

Ind AS 40 permits only the cost model for investment property — the Indian carve-out removed IAS 40's fair value model. Fair value is still measured and disclosed in the notes, but the balance sheet carries cost less depreciation and impairment. Property held to earn rentals or for capital appreciation, not for use in production or administration, is what the standard covers.

citation.ref: measurement after recognition (cost model; fair value model not permitted)

concepts.statement: The fair value hierarchy ranks inputs, not techniques: Level 1 is unadjusted quoted prices in active markets for identical items; Level 2 is other observable inputs — quoted prices for similar items, or corroborated market data; Level 3 is unobservable inputs. A measurement sits at the lowest level of any input significant to it, and Level 1 prices are used unadjusted where available.

For equity-settled awards to employees, the expense is measured at the fair value of the equity instruments at grant date — and that value is never remeasured, however the share price moves. What does move is the number of awards expected to vest under service and non-market conditions, trued up each period until vesting. Market conditions are priced into grant-date value once and never trued up.

Defined benefit cost splits three ways: service cost and net interest go to profit or loss; remeasurements — actuarial gains and losses, and the return on plan assets beyond the amount already in net interest — go to other comprehensive income, and once there they are never reclassified to profit or loss. The split keeps the operating result clear of actuarial volatility without hiding it.

Twenty per cent or more of voting power presumes significant influence — the power to participate in financial and operating policy decisions — and less than twenty presumes its absence; both presumptions yield to clear demonstration otherwise. Board representation, policy participation, material transactions, interchange of personnel or essential technical dependence can evidence influence below the line. An associate is equity accounted, not consolidated.

A deferred tax asset on unused tax losses is recognised only to the extent future taxable profit is probable — and a history of recent losses is itself evidence against that. A loss-making entity records the asset only to the extent of taxable temporary differences or convincing other evidence of future profit, such as a firm order book from a cause that has demonstrably ended.

concepts.subsection: Ind AS 109 — Classification of financial assets
concepts.statement: A financial asset is carried at amortised cost only when both tests pass: the business model is to hold and collect contractual cash flows, and those cash flows are solely payments of principal and interest. Held-to-collect with equity-linked returns fails the second; plain-interest bonds bought for trading fail the first. Failures land in fair value categories.

concepts.subsection: Going concern across FR and audit
concepts.statement: Material uncertainties about going concern are disclosed in the financial statements themselves — Ind AS 1 requires it of management when it is aware of them. A mention in the board's report or a covering letter is not a substitute, and the auditor's going concern section points to the note, so the note must exist.

concepts.subsection: Related party transactions under company law
concepts.statement: A contract with a related party of the kinds listed in section 188 — sale or purchase of goods, property, services, agency — needs board approval by resolution when it is not in the ordinary course of business or not at arm's length, and shareholder approval past the prescribed thresholds. An interested director does not participate.

A chartered accountant in practice cannot charge professional fees as a percentage of profits or contingent on results, outside the specific exceptions the Council has carved out — an auditor paid a share of what he certifies has bought a stake in the number.

concepts.subsection: Fraud reporting under the Companies Act
concepts.statement: An auditor who has reason to believe a fraud of one crore rupees or more is being or has been committed against the company by its officers or employees reports it to the Central Government, routed first through the board or audit committee for their reply within the prescribed time. Frauds below that threshold go to the board or audit committee, and are disclosed in the board's report.

A company crossing any one threshold — net worth ₹500 crore, turnover ₹1000 crore, or net profit ₹5 crore in the immediately preceding year — must constitute a CSR committee and spend 2 per cent of its average net profits of the three preceding years. Unspent amounts follow the ongoing-project rules or move to a specified fund; mere disclosure no longer discharges it.

concepts.subsection: Internal financial controls in the auditor's report
concepts.statement: The auditor of a company reports on whether the company has an adequate internal financial controls system with reference to financial statements and whether it operated effectively — a separate opinion under section 143(3)(i), distinct from the opinion on the statements themselves. Smaller private companies are exempted by notification.

A chartered accountant in practice may not solicit clients or professional work directly or indirectly — by circular, advertisement, personal communication or interview. Responding to tenders, applying for empanelment that has been announced, and seeking work from another chartered accountant in practice sit outside the bar.

The audit committee of a listed public company needs a minimum of three directors, with independent directors forming a majority, and a majority of members — the chairperson included — able to read and understand financial statements. It recommends auditor appointment and remuneration, reviews independence, and runs the vigil mechanism.

CARO 2020 applies to companies generally but not to banking companies, insurance companies, section 8 companies, one person companies, small companies, and private companies within all the prescribed size limits — paid-up capital and reserves up to one crore, borrowings up to one crore, and revenue up to ten crore. Cross any one limit and the order applies.

Dividend is declared out of profits after providing for depreciation, or out of free reserves under the prescribed conditions. Losses and depreciation of earlier years are set off first, and the securities premium and revaluation surplus are not distributable — a dividend needs earned, realised profit behind it.

Listed companies and the prescribed classes cannot appoint an individual auditor for more than one term of five consecutive years, or an audit firm for more than two such terms, followed in each case by a five-year cooling-off. A firm sharing common partners with the retiring firm is caught by the same bar.

Internal audit is compulsory for every listed company, and for unlisted public companies and private companies crossing the prescribed size lines — for a private company, turnover of two hundred crore rupees or outstanding borrowings of one hundred crore during the preceding year. The internal auditor may be a chartered accountant, cost accountant, or other professional the board decides, and may be an employee.

A listed public company needs at least one-third of its board as independent directors. An independent director holds office for up to five years a term, at most two consecutive terms, then a three-year cooling-off during which no association with the company is permitted. Independence is defined by negatives — no pecuniary relationship with the company beyond permitted limits, no promoter linkage, and the director must declare independence at first appointment and annually.

A company's loans, guarantees, securities and investments beyond sixty per cent of paid-up capital plus free reserves and securities premium — or one hundred per cent of free reserves plus securities premium, whichever is more — need a special resolution. Every such loan needs prior approval of all directors present at the board meeting, carries interest at no less than the prevailing government-security yield, and is barred entirely while the company is in default on public deposits.

A company may not lend to, or guarantee or secure the debts of, its directors or their partners and firms — that circle is absolute. One ring out — a private company in which a director is interested, or a body corporate under a director's control — the loan is possible, but only with a special resolution and the borrower using it for its principal business. Loans to managing or whole-time directors ride narrow exceptions such as a scheme for all employees.

An operational creditor must serve a demand notice under section 8 before filing; the corporate debtor has ten days to point to a pre-existing dispute or proof of payment, and a genuine pre-existing dispute kills the section 9 application — insolvency is not a debt recovery forum. A financial creditor under section 7 faces no such dispute defence; default alone carries the application.

Prescribed companies must have whole-time key managerial personnel — a managing director or CEO or manager (or in their absence a whole-time director), a company secretary, and a chief financial officer. A whole-time KMP holds office in only one company at a time (a subsidiary excepted), and a vacancy must be filled by the board within six months.

concepts.subsection: Oppression and mismanagement — who may apply
concepts.statement: A petition under section 241 needs standing under section 244: for a company with share capital, at least one hundred members, or one-tenth of the total members, or holders of one-tenth of the issued share capital — whichever is least — with all calls paid. The Tribunal may waive the threshold for a deserving case, and consenting members can combine to make up the numbers.

A buy-back may not exceed twenty-five per cent of paid-up capital plus free reserves, with the board alone able to approve up to ten per cent of paid-up equity plus free reserves and a special resolution needed beyond; post buy-back debt may not exceed twice the capital and free reserves; shares must be fully paid; and a year must pass between buy-backs. Funding comes from free reserves, securities premium or fresh issue proceeds of other securities.

Input tax credit needs every section 16(2) condition together — a tax invoice, receipt of the goods or services, the detail appearing in GSTR-2B, the tax actually paid to the Government by the supplier, and the return filed. Holding a valid invoice while the supplier has not paid the tax defeats the credit.

For notified supplies — legal services from an advocate to a business entity among them — the recipient, not the supplier, is liable to pay the tax, and pays it in cash rather than through input tax credit.

Registration becomes compulsory when aggregate turnover crosses ₹20 lakh for a supplier of services. The ₹40 lakh limit is for suppliers exclusively of goods in eligible States, and special category States carry lower limits.

A composition taxpayer cannot make inter-State outward supplies of goods. The scheme trades a small turnover-based levy for staying local; crossing the State line with outward supplies forfeits eligibility.

Additions to the transaction value of imported goods include selling commissions, and cost of transport and insurance to the place of importation — but buying commission, paid to the importer's own agent for representing him abroad, is not added.

concepts.subsection: Section 16(4) — Time limit for input tax credit
concepts.statement: Input tax credit for an invoice cannot be taken after the thirtieth of November following the end of the financial year the invoice belongs to, or the filing of the relevant annual return, whichever is earlier. A valid, eligible credit dies purely of lateness.

concepts.subsection: IGST Act — Place of supply of goods
concepts.statement: Where a supply involves movement of goods, the place of supply is the location where the movement terminates for delivery to the recipient. Who arranges the transport does not decide it; where the goods end up does.

An advance received for a supply of services is taxable when received. For goods, suppliers other than composition taxpayers pay tax only on issue of the invoice — advances for goods were taken out of the tax net by notification. The same rupee of advance is taxed on one side of the goods-services line and not the other.

A discount given after the supply reduces the taxable value only if it was agreed before or at the time of supply and can be linked to the specific invoices, and the recipient reverses the proportionate input tax credit. A goodwill discount invented after the event changes the price, not the tax.

Interest on delayed payment of tax runs at 18 per cent, and on the portion paid through the electronic cash ledger it is charged only on that net cash amount where the return is filed late — the credit-covered portion carries no interest. Wrongly availed and utilised credit draws its own interest.

Inputs sent for job work must return, or be supplied from the job worker's premises, within one year; capital goods within three years. Miss the window and the original despatch is deemed a supply from the day the goods went out, with tax and interest reaching back to it.

Exports and supplies to SEZ units are zero-rated, not exempt: the output carries no tax, yet input tax credit survives. The exporter either supplies under a letter of undertaking without paying tax and claims refund of unutilised credit, or pays IGST and claims refund of the tax paid.

An e-way bill is generated before movement of goods worth more than fifty thousand rupees in a consignment. The obligation attaches to the movement, not the sale — stock transfers, job work despatches and sales returns all need one, and some States set higher intra-State limits.

concepts.subsection: Section 129 — Detention of goods in transit
concepts.statement: Goods moved in contravention — typically without a valid e-way bill or invoice — are detained, and release requires a penalty of two hundred per cent of the tax payable where the owner comes forward. Detention is a transit consequence and runs independently of whether the tax on the supply itself was ever evaded.

Four transactions are supplies even without consideration — permanent transfer of business assets on which credit was taken, supplies between related or distinct persons in business, goods moved through agents who undertake to supply or receive on the principal's behalf, and imported services from a related person for business. Employer gifts to an employee stay out up to fifty thousand rupees a year.

concepts.subsection: Schedule III — Neither goods nor services
concepts.statement: Schedule III lists what GST cannot touch at all — an employee's services to the employer in the course of employment, sale of land and of completed buildings, actionable claims other than specified ones, funeral services, and duties of courts and MPs. These are not exempt supplies; they are not supplies, so they never enter aggregate turnover.

A refund claim is filed within two years from the relevant date, and the relevant date moves with the ground of the claim — export shipment dates for goods exported, the date payment lands for export of services, the judgment's date where tax was paid under a later-reversed demand. Miss the window and the money stays with the Government however good the ground was.

A supplier of services outside the restaurant category, ineligible for the ordinary composition scheme, may opt for the special scheme where aggregate turnover in the preceding year stayed within fifty lakh rupees, paying six per cent. The ordinary scheme's goods-centred gates do not decide this one.

Input tax credit on motor vehicles for transporting persons with seating capacity up to thirteen (including the driver) is blocked — unless the vehicle is used for further supply of such vehicles, transporting passengers, or driving training. Vehicles above thirteen seats and goods-transport vehicles are outside the block, and services of insurance, repair and maintenance follow the vehicle they attach to.

concepts.subsection: Section 13 — Time of supply of services
concepts.statement: For services, time of supply is the earlier of invoice and payment where the invoice issues within the thirty-day limit; where it does not, the earlier of the date the service is provided and the payment. The clock decides which tax period the liability lands in — issuing the invoice late does not push the liability later.

Section 74 refunds up to ninety-eight per cent of import duty when the imported goods themselves are re-exported within two years, identified as the same goods. Goods that were used before re-export get tapering rates by period of use. Section 75 is the other drawback — for duty on inputs consumed in manufacturing exported goods — and the two never apply to the same claim.

concepts.subsection: IGST — Place of supply for immovable property services
concepts.statement: Services directly relating to immovable property — architects, surveyors, engineers, hotel accommodation, letting, construction-linked services — are supplied where the property sits, whatever the locations of supplier and recipient. The property anchors the tax, and if it lies outside India the default recipient-location rule takes over.

concepts.subsection: Schedule II — Works contract as a service
concepts.statement: A works contract — a contract for building, construction, fabrication or similar work on immovable property involving transfer of property in goods — is deemed wholly a supply of services by Schedule II. One levy, one classification: the old VAT-plus-service-tax split of a single contract is gone, and works contract input credit has its own restrictions in section 17(5).

Customs duty is assessed on transaction value — the price actually paid or payable for the goods when sold for export to India — plus prescribed additions, at the time and place of importation. A relationship between buyer and seller displaces that price only where it influenced it; a related-party price the importer shows to be at arm's length stands.

The value of supply includes taxes other than GST itself, amounts the supplier was liable to pay but the recipient paid, incidental expenses like packing and commission charged by the supplier, interest or penalty for delayed payment of consideration, and subsidies directly linked to price from anyone other than the Government. Each inclusion widens the base beyond the bare price.

A service is exported only when all five conditions hold: supplier in India, recipient outside India, place of supply outside India, payment received in convertible foreign exchange (or INR where RBI permits), and supplier and recipient not merely two establishments of one person. Failing any one, the supply is not an export and zero-rating is lost.

A supplier who has charged too much tax — goods returned, deficient supply, price revised down — issues a credit note and reduces output liability, but only up to the thirtieth of November following the financial year of supply (or the annual return, if earlier), and only if the incidence of tax has not been passed to someone who bears it. A commercial credit note without GST can issue any time, adjusting price but not tax.

Import of goods is taxed as inter-State supply, but the IGST is levied and collected as customs duty — under the Customs Tariff Act, on the value determined under the Customs Act at the point of importation, together with basic customs duty. The importer generally takes credit of the IGST so paid; basic customs duty is never creditable.

Registrations of one entity in different States are distinct persons, and supplies between them — stock transfers, services of one office to another — are taxable supplies even without consideration, valued under the rules with full input credit typically flowing. One legal person, several taxable persons: the design keeps each State's revenue whole.

Goods pilfered after unloading but before clearance attract no duty from the importer — unless restored — and the custodian pays instead; goods lost or destroyed before clearance earn remission on the Assistant Commissioner's satisfaction, and goods relinquished before clearance drop the duty too. Pilferage is automatic by the section's operation; remission must be sought and shown.

An e-commerce operator collects tax at source on the net value of supplies made through it by others — a collection mechanism, not a levy. For the notified services — passenger transport, accommodation, restaurants, housekeeping — section 9(5) goes further: the operator is liable to pay the tax as if it were the supplier, and the actual supplier's registration position changes accordingly. TCS and 9(5) never apply to the same supply.

Four different fates: a nil-rated supply is taxable at zero in the tariff; an exempt supply is freed by notification and includes nil-rated and non-taxable supplies for definition purposes; a non-taxable supply is outside the levy itself, like alcohol for human consumption; zero-rated means exports and SEZ supplies — taxable in principle, taxed at zero, with input credit preserved. Only zero-rating keeps the credit; exemption breaks the credit chain.

concepts.subsection: SA 200 — Overall Objectives of the Independent Auditor
concepts.statement: An audit conducted under the Standards on Auditing obtains reasonable assurance, which is a high level of assurance but not absolute assurance.

concepts.subsection: SA 200 — Overall Objectives of the Independent Auditor
concepts.statement: The audit is planned and performed with professional skepticism — a questioning mind alert to conditions indicating possible misstatement, and a critical assessment of evidence. It neither assumes management dishonest nor assumes it honest; records are accepted as genuine absent reason to believe otherwise, and doubted the moment there is one.

concepts.subsection: SA 210 — Agreeing the Terms of Audit Engagements
concepts.statement: The preconditions for an audit are an acceptable financial reporting framework and management's agreement to the premise on which an audit is conducted — its responsibility for the financial statements, for internal control, and for giving the auditor access and information. Where the preconditions are not present, the auditor does not accept the engagement.

concepts.subsection: SA 210 — Agreeing the Terms of Audit Engagements
concepts.statement: Where management imposes a limitation on scope before the engagement is accepted, and the auditor expects that limitation will result in a disclaimer of opinion, the auditor does not accept the engagement unless law or regulation requires it.

concepts.subsection: SA 210 — Agreeing the Terms of Audit Engagements
concepts.statement: On recurring audits the auditor assesses whether circumstances require the engagement terms to be revised and whether the entity needs reminding of the existing terms. A fresh letter every year is not demanded; a changed situation — new management, changed ownership, a changed framework, misunderstood scope — is what calls for one.

concepts.subsection: SA 220 (Revised) — Quality Management for an Audit
concepts.statement: The engagement partner takes overall responsibility for managing and achieving quality on the engagement. Work may be delegated across the engagement team, but the responsibility for quality is not delegated with it.
The final audit file is assembled ordinarily within not more than 60 days after the date of the auditor's report.

Audit documentation must be sufficient for an experienced auditor with no previous connection to the audit to understand the procedures performed, the results and evidence obtained, and the significant matters and conclusions. The file must speak for itself; the auditor's memory is not part of the record.

concepts.subsection: SA 240 — The Auditor's Responsibilities Relating to Fraud
concepts.statement: Management override of controls is a significant risk presumed to be present in every audit, and it is not rebuttable.

concepts.subsection: SA 240 — The Auditor's Responsibilities Relating to Fraud
concepts.statement: There is a presumed risk of fraud in revenue recognition, and unlike management override that presumption may be rebutted with documented reasons.

concepts.subsection: Auditor resignation under the Companies Act
concepts.statement: An auditor who resigns files a statement in the prescribed form with the company and the Registrar within thirty days of resignation, stating the reasons and any relevant facts. For specified companies the statement also goes to the Comptroller and Auditor-General. Failure invites a penalty on the auditor personally.

concepts.subsection: SA 250 — Consideration of Laws and Regulations
concepts.statement: SA 250 splits laws into two categories, and the auditor's responsibility differs between them. For laws with a direct effect on the determination of material amounts and disclosures, the auditor obtains sufficient appropriate audit evidence about compliance. For other laws that are fundamental to the operating aspects of the business, the auditor only performs specified procedures to help identify non-compliance.

concepts.subsection: SA 260 (Revised) — Communication with Those Charged with Governance
concepts.statement: The auditor communicates the planned scope and timing of the audit to those charged with governance, not only the findings.

concepts.subsection: SA 265 — Communicating Deficiencies in Internal Control
concepts.statement: Significant deficiencies in internal control are communicated in writing to those charged with governance on a timely basis.

concepts.subsection: SA 299 (Revised) — Joint Audit of Financial Statements
concepts.statement: Each joint auditor is responsible for the work divided to that auditor, and all joint auditors are jointly and severally responsible for the work not divided.

concepts.subsection: SA 315 (Revised) — Identifying and Assessing the Risks of Material Misstatement
concepts.statement: A significant risk is one requiring special audit consideration, and for such risks the auditor must obtain an understanding of the entity's related controls.

concepts.subsection: SA 320 — Materiality in Planning and Performing an Audit
concepts.statement: Performance materiality is set below materiality for the financial statements as a whole, to reduce to an appropriately low level the probability that uncorrected and undetected misstatements aggregate above materiality.

concepts.subsection: SA 330 — The Auditor's Responses to Assessed Risks
concepts.statement: When the auditor has determined that an assessed risk of material misstatement at the assertion level is a significant risk, substantive procedures specifically responsive to that risk must be performed.

concepts.subsection: SA 330 — The Auditor's Responses to Assessed Risks
concepts.statement: Irrespective of the assessed risks, the auditor designs and performs substantive procedures for each material class of transactions, account balance and disclosure. Excellent controls reduce substantive work; they never reduce it to zero for anything material.

concepts.subsection: SA 402 — Audit Considerations Relating to an Entity Using a Service Organisation
concepts.statement: A Type 1 report describes the service organisation's system and the design of its controls at a point in time. A Type 2 report also reports on their operating effectiveness over a period. Only a Type 2 report can give evidence about operating effectiveness.

concepts.subsection: SA 450 — Evaluation of Misstatements Identified during the Audit
concepts.statement: Uncorrected misstatements are communicated to those charged with governance and the auditor evaluates whether they are material individually or in aggregate.
Sufficiency is the measure of the quantity of audit evidence; appropriateness is the measure of its quality, being its relevance and its reliability.

concepts.subsection: SA 501 — Audit Evidence: Specific Considerations for Selected Items
concepts.statement: When inventory is material to the financial statements, the auditor must attend the physical inventory counting unless it is impracticable.

Where inventory held by a third party is material, the auditor obtains evidence of its existence and condition by requesting confirmation from the custodian, or by inspection, or both — and considers whether more is needed where the custodian's integrity or independence is in doubt.

Negative confirmations may be used as the sole substantive procedure only when the assessed risk is low, the population is large and homogeneous, a very low exception rate is expected, and the auditor is not aware of circumstances that would cause recipients to disregard them.

concepts.subsection: SA 510 — Initial Audit Engagements: Opening Balances
concepts.statement: In an initial audit engagement the auditor obtains sufficient appropriate audit evidence about whether opening balances contain misstatements that materially affect the current period's financial statements, and whether accounting policies reflected in the opening balances have been consistently applied.

Analytical procedures are mandatory at two points in an audit — as risk assessment procedures during planning, and near the end of the audit to form an overall conclusion. Using them as substantive procedures is optional, a choice the auditor makes about how to respond to an assessed risk.

Misstatements found in a sample are projected to the population the sample was drawn from. The sample is a means of reaching a conclusion about the whole population, so the error found in it is evidence about the whole population, not only about the items examined.

The auditor reviews the outcome, or subsequent re-estimation, of the prior period's accounting estimates — not to second-guess last year's audit, but to learn how management estimates: where its judgments proved biased, where uncertainty was understated, and where this year's risk therefore sits. Estimates resolved far from their booked amounts are risk assessment gold, not automatic prior-period errors.

A significant related party transaction outside the entity's normal course of business gives rise to a significant risk. The auditor inspects the underlying contracts and evaluates whether the business rationale suggests the transaction was entered into to engage in fraudulent financial reporting or to conceal misappropriation of assets.
Where the report is amended for a subsequent event, dual dating confines the auditor's responsibility for events after the original date to that amendment alone.

Between the financial statements' date and the auditor's report date, the auditor actively performs procedures to catch events needing adjustment or disclosure. After the report's date the duty to search ends — but a fact coming to the auditor's knowledge before the statements are issued, which would have changed the report, must be pursued: discuss, determine amendment, and act on the outcome.

Where a material uncertainty about going concern exists and is adequately disclosed, the opinion is unmodified and a separate section headed "Material Uncertainty Related to Going Concern" is included.

Written representations are audit evidence, but they are not sufficient appropriate audit evidence on their own about any of the matters they deal with. Obtaining them does not affect the nature or extent of the other evidence the auditor obtains.

concepts.subsection: SA 600 — Using the Work of Another Auditor
concepts.statement: Where a principal auditor uses the work of another auditor for a component, the principal auditor states the division of responsibility in the audit report, indicating the extent of the financial information audited by the other auditor. The principal auditor is not responsible for the work entrusted to the other auditor, except where circumstances should have aroused suspicion about its reliability.

concepts.subsection: SA 610 (Revised) — Using the Work of Internal Auditors
concepts.statement: SA 610 (Revised) permits internal auditors to provide direct assistance under the external auditor's direction, supervision and review — but never for procedures that involve significant judgments, relate to higher assessed risks where more than limited judgment is required, or cover work the internal audit function has itself reported on. Written agreements from the entity and the internal auditors come first.

concepts.subsection: SA 620 — Using the Work of an Auditor's Expert
concepts.statement: The auditor has sole responsibility for the audit opinion, and that responsibility is not reduced by using the work of an auditor's expert. The auditor's report does not refer to the expert unless the reference is required by law or regulation, and where it is, the report must state that the reference does not reduce the auditor's responsibility.

concepts.subsection: SA 700 (Revised) — Forming an Opinion and Reporting
concepts.statement: The auditor's report presents the Opinion as its first section, and the Basis for Opinion comes directly after it. The conclusion is stated before the reasons for it, so a reader who stops after the first paragraph has still read the opinion.
Key audit matters are required for audits of complete sets of general purpose financial statements of listed entities, and where otherwise required by law or voluntarily undertaken.
A material misstatement that is not pervasive gives a qualified opinion; a material misstatement that is pervasive gives an adverse opinion.

concepts.subsection: SA 706 (Revised) — Emphasis of Matter and Other Matter Paragraphs
concepts.statement: An Emphasis of Matter paragraph refers to a matter presented or disclosed in the financial statements; an Other Matter paragraph refers to a matter not so disclosed but relevant to users' understanding of the audit, the auditor's responsibilities or the report.

concepts.subsection: SA 710 — Comparative Information: Corresponding Figures and Comparative Financial Statements
concepts.statement: Where comparatives are presented as corresponding figures, the auditor's opinion refers to the current period only and does not refer to the corresponding figures. Where they are presented as comparative financial statements, the opinion refers to each period for which financial statements are presented.

concepts.subsection: SA 720 — The Auditor's Responsibilities Relating to Other Information
concepts.statement: The auditor reads the other information in the annual report and considers whether it is materially inconsistent with the financial statements or with the auditor's knowledge obtained in the audit. The auditor does not audit the other information and expresses no opinion or conclusion on it.

items.stem: Which risk is the portfolio still carrying?

options.text: Liquidity risk, since twelve industries cannot all be sold at once
options.misconception: substitutes a trading concern for the pricing question asked
options.why: Liquidity affects the cost of exiting, not why the valuation tracked the index. The co-movement with the market is systematic risk by definition.

options.text: Unsystematic risk, because thirty stocks are too few
options.misconception: believes firm-specific risk lingers until the portfolio holds the whole market
options.why: The gain from diversification flattens quickly — most firm-specific risk is gone well before thirty stocks. The 9 per cent fall tracking a 10 per cent market fall is market behaviour, not stock-picking noise.

options.text: None — a fall proves the portfolio was badly constructed
options.misconception: reads any loss as evidence of avoidable risk
options.why: A diversified portfolio is supposed to move with the market; that is what remains after the removable risk is removed. A loss in a falling market is the priced risk showing up.

options.text: Systematic risk, which diversification cannot remove
options.why: Thirty stocks across twelve industries has diversified away nearly all firm-specific risk. What moves the portfolio now is the market itself — interest rates, the cycle, policy — and that risk is common to every security, so holding more of them does not dilute it.

items.scenario: An investor holds a portfolio of 30 stocks spread across twelve industries and asks why its value still fell 9 per cent in a month when the market index fell 10 per cent.

items.stem: What are the put's intrinsic value and time value?

options.text: Intrinsic value nil, time value ₹11
options.misconception: applies the call test to a put and reads spot below strike as out of the money
options.why: For a call this spot would mean no intrinsic value, and that is the reflex being tested. A put gains when the share falls, so spot below strike is in the money.

options.text: Intrinsic value ₹11, time value nil
options.misconception: equates the whole premium with intrinsic value
options.why: The premium is the price of the option, not its exercise value. Intrinsic value comes from strike against spot alone, and here that is ₹8.

options.text: Intrinsic value ₹8, time value ₹3
options.why: The put lets its holder sell at ₹100 what the market prices at ₹92, so exercising now is worth ₹8 — the intrinsic value. The premium's remaining ₹3 is time value, paid for the chance the share falls further before expiry.

options.text: Intrinsic value ₹3, time value ₹8
options.misconception: swaps the two components
options.why: The split runs the other way. Exercise value first — strike ₹100 less spot ₹92 — and only the remainder of the premium is time value.

items.scenario: A put option on a share has a strike price of ₹100. The share trades at ₹92 and the put's premium is ₹11.

items.stem: Where must the one-year forward rate sit, relative to spot?

options.text: Above ₹84 — the dollar at a forward premium, the rupee at a discount
options.why: A depositor could otherwise convert to rupees, earn 7 per cent against 3, and convert back with nothing lost. The forward rate removes that free profit by making future dollars dearer — roughly by the 4 per cent differential, near ₹87.2.

options.text: Below ₹84 — the rupee at a forward premium because its interest rate is higher
options.misconception: gives the forward premium to the high-rate currency
options.why: This is parity read backwards. The higher rate is compensation for the currency expected to weaken; if the rupee also strengthened forward, holding rupees would win twice and arbitrage would close the gap at once.

options.text: It depends only on expected inflation in the two countries
options.misconception: answers with purchasing power parity when the question fixes interest rates
options.why: Inflation drives the long-run story through PPP, but the covered forward rate is pinned by interest rate parity — the rates given are the whole calculation.

options.text: Exactly ₹84, because forward rates track spot when markets are efficient
options.misconception: treats efficiency as making the interest differential irrelevant
options.why: Efficiency is what forces the gap open, not shut. A forward equal to spot with a 4 per cent rate differential is a money machine, and efficient markets price it away.

citation.ref: Ch. Foreign Exchange Exposure and Risk Management

items.scenario: One-year interest rates are 7 per cent in India and 3 per cent in the United States. The spot rate is ₹84 per dollar. Markets are free of arbitrage.

items.stem: A fund expects interest rates to fall and wants the largest price gain. Which bond should it hold?

options.text: A floating-rate bond resetting every six months
options.misconception: reaches for the bond that adjusts to rates rather than the one that gains from them
options.why: A floater's coupon resets to the market, so its price barely moves — near-zero duration. It is the instrument for avoiding the bet, not winning it.

options.text: A ten-year bond with a 12 per cent coupon
options.misconception: picks the highest coupon as the biggest gainer
options.why: Large coupons return money early, which shortens duration and dampens the price move. Same maturity, less sensitivity than the zero.

options.text: A ten-year zero-coupon bond
options.why: Price sensitivity follows duration, and a zero-coupon bond's duration equals its full maturity because every rupee arrives at the end. Ten years of duration is the most leverage to a rate fall among these choices.

options.text: A two-year zero-coupon bond
options.misconception: remembers zeros are sensitive but forgets maturity drives it
options.why: Being a zero helps only as far as the maturity allows. Two years of duration moves far less than ten when rates shift.

items.stem: How many futures contracts should the fund sell?

options.misconception: applies beta twice
options.why: ₹12.6 crore already carries the beta adjustment. Multiplying by 1.4 again hedges an exposure the fund does not have, and the excess contracts are a speculative short.

options.misconception: hedges the portfolio's value while ignoring its beta
options.why: ₹9 crore ÷ ₹10.5 lakh gives about 86, which hedges a beta-one portfolio. This portfolio swings 40 per cent harder than the market, and 86 contracts leave that excess exposed.

options.text: 120 contracts bought, not sold
options.misconception: gets the size right and the direction backwards
options.why: Long futures gain when the market rises — added to a long portfolio, that doubles the bet. A hedge against a fall needs the futures to pay when the market drops, which means selling.
The exposure to hedge is value times beta — ₹9 crore × 1.4 = ₹12.6 crore, because the portfolio moves 1.4 times the market. Divided by ₹10.5 lakh per contract, that is 120 contracts sold.

items.scenario: A fund holds a ₹9 crore equity portfolio with a beta of 1.4 against the index. Index futures trade at 21,000 with a lot size of 50, making one contract worth ₹10.5 lakh. The fund wants a full hedge against a market fall.

items.stem: Which hedge fits that requirement?

options.text: Sell a put option on the dollar
options.misconception: confuses writing options with buying protection
options.why: Selling a put collects a premium and takes on obligation — if the dollar falls, the importer is put dollars at the strike. It provides no protection at all against a rise.

options.text: Do nothing, since a payable in dollars gains when the dollar weakens
options.misconception: keeps the exposure because one side of it is pleasant
options.why: The open position gains on a fall and loses on a rise; the loss side is the risk to be managed. Doing nothing is a bet, not a hedge.

options.text: Buy a call option on the dollar
options.why: A dollar call caps the buying rate at the strike if the dollar rises, and lapses if the dollar falls, letting the importer buy cheaper in the market. That asymmetry is exactly what was asked for, and the premium is its price.

options.text: Buy dollars forward
options.misconception: reaches for the standard hedge and gives away the benefit that was wanted
options.why: A forward locks the rate in both directions. It removes the risk of a rise but equally removes the gain from a fall, which the finance head specifically wanted to keep.

citation.ref: Ch. Foreign Exchange Exposure and Risk Management

items.scenario: An importer must pay $500,000 in three months. The rupee has been volatile, and the finance head wants protection if the dollar rises but would like the benefit if it falls.

items.stem: Which project should be accepted, and why?

options.text: A — the smaller outlay carries less risk for the same decision
options.misconception: substitutes an outlay-size intuition for a discounting answer
options.why: Risk is already priced into the 12 per cent discount rate. Introducing outlay size as a separate criterion double-counts caution.

options.text: B — with mutually exclusive projects, the higher NPV measures the wealth added
options.why: Only one can be taken, and B adds ₹52 lakh of value against A's ₹28 lakh at the firm's actual cost of capital. IRR's higher rate on A is a rate on a much smaller base, and its reinvestment assumption at 24 per cent is not available to the firm.

options.text: A — its IRR of 24 per cent beats B's 17 per cent
options.misconception: ranks mutually exclusive projects by rate of return
options.why: A high rate on ₹1 crore can add less wealth than a modest rate on ₹4 crore. Ranking by IRR answers which project is more efficient per rupee, not which makes the firm richer.

options.text: Both, since each has a positive NPV and an IRR above the cost of capital
options.misconception: forgets that mutual exclusivity means choosing
options.why: Independent projects with positive NPV are all accepted. These are mutually exclusive — taking one forecloses the other, which is the whole reason the ranking conflict matters.

items.scenario: Two mutually exclusive projects at a 12 per cent cost of capital. Project A needs ₹1 crore and has NPV ₹28 lakh with IRR 24 per cent. Project B needs ₹4 crore and has NPV ₹52 lakh with IRR 17 per cent.

items.stem: What is the NAV per unit?

options.misconception: drops the accrued income and the liabilities together
options.why: ₹840 over 40 crore units alone is a portfolio-only shortcut. NAV is the whole balance sheet in one number — everything owned less everything owed.
NAV works on market value, not cost — ₹840 plus ₹12 minus ₹22 gives net assets of ₹830 crore, and over 40 crore units that is ₹20.75. The unrealised gain over cost is already inside it.

options.misconception: values the portfolio at cost instead of market
options.why: ₹700 plus ₹12 minus ₹22 over 40 crore units gives ₹17.25, a number that hides ₹140 crore of gains from every unitholder transacting today. Cost is history; NAV is a price.

options.misconception: forgets the liabilities and expenses
options.why: ₹840 plus ₹12 over 40 crore units ignores ₹22 crore that unitholders owe. Gross assets per unit overstate what a redeeming investor actually gets.

items.scenario: A fund holds investments with market value ₹840 crore and cost ₹700 crore, accrued income of ₹12 crore, and liabilities plus accrued expenses of ₹22 crore, with 40 crore units outstanding.

items.stem: What is the value of the share under the dividend growth model?

options.why: The model discounts the coming dividend — ₹6 grown one year at 8 per cent is ₹6.48 — divided by the 6 per cent spread between the 14 per cent required return and the growth rate. ₹6.48 over 0.06 is ₹108.

options.misconception: uses the dividend just paid instead of the next one
options.why: ₹6 over 0.06 forgets that the valuation stands at the start of a growth year. The formula runs on the expected dividend, and the ₹8 difference is exactly the missed growth step.

options.misconception: divides by the required return alone, ignoring growth
options.why: ₹6.48 over 0.14 values a dividend frozen forever. Perpetual growth is the model's whole engine, and it lives in the denominator's subtraction.

options.misconception: swaps the growth and required-return roles
options.why: ₹6.48 over 0.08 discounts at the growth rate — a rate at which the investor requires nothing and the model means nothing. The spread, not either rate alone, prices the share.

items.scenario: A company has just paid a dividend of ₹6 per share. Dividends are expected to grow at 8 per cent for the foreseeable future, and equity investors require a 14 per cent return.

items.stem: What does the FRA deliver?

options.text: The counterparty compensates the company for the 1.5 per cent difference, settled at the start of the borrowing period at its discounted value
options.why: The buyer of an FRA is protected against rates rising past the agreed 8 per cent. The settlement pays the rate difference on the notional for three months, discounted because it arrives at the period's start while borrowing costs bite at its end.

options.text: The company pays the counterparty, since it locked 8 per cent and rates moved to 9.5
options.misconception: reverses who wins when rates rise
options.why: Paying away when rates rise would make the hedge a double loss. The buyer fixed a borrowing cost; the market moving above it is precisely the event the buyer is paid for.

options.text: Nothing — the FRA lapsed because it was not exercised within six months
options.misconception: treats a binding forward as an option needing exercise
