options.why: An FRA is a firm contract, not an option. Settlement happens automatically on the fixing date, whichever way rates went.

options.text: The company borrows the ₹50 crore from the FRA counterparty at 8 per cent
options.misconception: expects the FRA to deliver the loan itself
options.why: An FRA is a contract on a rate, not a source of funds. The company borrows wherever it chooses at 9.5 per cent, and the settlement brings the effective cost back to 8.

items.scenario: A company will need to borrow ₹50 crore for three months, starting six months from now. Its treasurer buys a 6x9 FRA at 8 per cent. Six months later the three-month reference rate sets at 9.5 per cent.

items.stem: Is there an arbitrage, and on which side?

options.text: No — the call costing more than the put is the natural order of things
options.misconception: eyeballs the two premiums instead of testing the parity equation
options.why: Which option costs more is not the question; the equation is. The gap between ₹7 and ₹18.50 is the mispricing, whatever the premiums' order.

options.text: Yes — sell both options and pocket ₹83 of premium
options.misconception: mistakes premium income for arbitrage
options.why: A short straddle collects ₹83 and stands naked to every large move in the share. Arbitrage means a locked, riskless difference; this is a bet wearing its costume.

options.text: Yes — the call is cheap relative to parity; buy the call, sell the put, short the share, invest the strike's present value
options.why: Parity wants call minus put equal to share minus present value of strike: ₹18.50. The market offers ₹45 minus ₹38, only ₹7. The left side is underpriced, so buy it — long call, short put — against a short share and lending, locking ₹11.50 without risk.

options.text: Cannot be determined without knowing the share's expected volatility
options.misconception: drags valuation inputs into a no-arbitrage identity
options.why: Volatility prices each option; parity binds their difference regardless. The identity holds for any volatility, which is what makes its breach a free lunch.

items.scenario: A share trades at ₹500. A one-year European call at strike ₹520 costs ₹45, and the matching put costs ₹38. The one-year risk-free rate makes the present value of the strike ₹481.50.

items.stem: What explains the disagreement, and which measure fits an investor holding only this fund?

options.text: X carries diversifiable risk that Treynor ignores; a sole-fund investor should trust Sharpe
options.why: Treynor prices only systematic risk, so X's extra, diversifiable volatility vanishes from its denominator and the funds tie. An investor whose whole wealth rides on one fund bears total risk, and Sharpe is the measure that charges for all of it.

options.text: The measures conflict, so the data must contain an arithmetic error
options.misconception: expects consistent rankings from measures built on different denominators
options.why: The disagreement is the information. Identical Treynor with worse Sharpe is the signature of an underdiversified portfolio, not of a miscalculation.

options.text: Treynor, because beta is the more scientific risk measure
options.misconception: picks the measure by prestige instead of by what the investor bears
options.why: Beta is the right charge for a fund inside a diversified portfolio. Held alone, the fund's diversifiable risk is not diversified away by anyone, and a measure that ignores it flatters X.

options.text: Sharpe always, since total risk always exceeds systematic risk
options.misconception: right choice here, universalised for the wrong reason
options.why: For a fund that is one sleeve of a larger portfolio, Treynor is the better lens — the holder's other sleeves absorb the unsystematic part. The choice follows the investor's position, not a fixed hierarchy.

items.scenario: Fund X and Fund Y both earned 14 per cent against a risk-free rate of 6 per cent. X has standard deviation 20 per cent and beta 1.6; Y has standard deviation 10 per cent and beta 1.0. On Sharpe, Y wins (0.8 against 0.4); on Treynor, X and Y tie at 8. An investor asks which measure to trust.

items.stem: What does CAPM say about this stock?

options.text: Required return is 15 per cent; the stock offers 16, so it is underpriced — buy
options.why: CAPM charges 6 + 1.5 × (12 − 6) = 15 per cent for this stock's systematic risk. An expected 16 per cent sits one point above the security market line — positive alpha. The market price is too low for the return on offer, which is the definition of a buy.

options.text: Required return is 15 per cent; expecting more means the stock is overpriced — sell
options.misconception: inverts the alpha rule
options.why: Overpricing shows up as expected return below the line — paying too much shrinks the return. Extra return above the charge for risk is the reward being too big, not the price.

options.text: CAPM cannot judge the stock without its standard deviation
options.misconception: imports total risk into a model that prices only systematic risk
options.why: CAPM's whole claim is that diversifiable risk earns nothing, so beta is the only risk input the line needs. Standard deviation belongs to Sharpe's world, not the SML's.

options.text: Required return is 18 per cent, so the stock falls short — sell
options.misconception: multiplies beta into the whole market return instead of the premium
options.why: Beta scales the market risk premium of 6, not the market return of 12. The risk-free 6 per cent is earned without any beta at all.

items.scenario: Risk-free rate 6 per cent, expected market return 12 per cent. A stock with beta 1.5 is expected by analysts to return 16 per cent. An investor concludes the stock should be sold, since 16 per cent is a higher return and higher return means higher risk.

items.stem: What does an arbitrageur do?

options.text: Sell the stock (or short it), invest the proceeds, and buy the cheap futures
options.why: The futures trade ₹7 below fair value, so the reverse cash-and-carry runs: shorting the stock raises ₹500 that earns interest to about ₹515, while the futures lock repurchase at ₹508. The ₹7 is collected whichever way the stock itself moves.

options.text: Buy the futures and wait for the stock to rise above ₹508
options.misconception: replaces arbitrage with a directional bet
options.why: Needing the stock to rise means carrying market risk. The arbitrage earns the gap with both legs locked, indifferent to direction — that indifference is what makes it arbitrage.

options.text: Buy the stock with borrowed money and sell the futures against it
options.misconception: runs the cash-and-carry in the wrong direction
options.why: That trade profits when futures are rich. Here it locks in buying at ₹500 plus ₹15 of interest to deliver at ₹508 — a guaranteed loss of the same ₹7.

options.text: Nothing — ₹508 for a ₹500 stock already includes a fair carrying charge
options.misconception: eyeballs the premium instead of computing it
options.why: The question is never whether futures exceed spot but whether the gap equals the carry. Three months of 12 per cent on ₹500 is about ₹15; a ₹8 premium is ₹7 short.

items.scenario: A stock trades at ₹500 and pays no dividend. Money costs 12 per cent a year. The three-month futures contract on the stock trades at ₹508, while the cost-of-carry fair value works out to about ₹515.

items.stem: What does the EPS rise actually prove?

options.text: Only that T's earnings were bought at a lower multiple than A's — the market may still mark the deal down
options.why: Shares worth ₹400 crore at A's price bought ₹25 crore of earnings — a multiple of 16 against A's own 20, so the arithmetic guarantees accretion. Whether value was created depends on what T's earnings deserve; if their quality merits only a low multiple, the higher EPS can price at a lower P/E and shareholders gain nothing.

options.text: That A overpaid, since issuing 2 crore shares diluted control
options.misconception: confuses ownership dilution with earnings dilution
options.why: Existing holders do own a smaller fraction of a bigger company — that is every share-funded deal. Overpayment is measured against T's value, and a 16-times price for earnings A's own market rates at 20 is not overpayment on its face.

options.text: That the merger created value for A's shareholders
options.misconception: reads bootstrap arithmetic as wealth creation
options.why: EPS accretion follows mechanically from buying low-multiple earnings with high-multiple paper. Value creation needs synergies or underpricing — neither is shown by the ₹0.42.

options.text: Nothing — EPS should fall whenever new shares are issued
options.misconception: sees only the denominator of the fraction
options.why: The new shares arrive carrying T's ₹25 crore of earnings. Whether EPS rises or falls is the race between the two, settled by the relative multiples.

citation.ref: Ch. Mergers, Acquisitions and Corporate Restructuring

items.scenario: Acquirer A earns ₹100 crore on 10 crore shares (EPS ₹10) and trades at a P/E of 20. Target T earns ₹25 crore and A buys it by issuing 2 crore new shares. The CFO announces the merger is a success because combined EPS rises to about ₹10.42.

items.stem: How does the money market hedge run, and roughly what does it lock in?

options.text: The hedge fails because rupee interest is higher than dollar interest
options.misconception: reads the rate differential as a barrier instead of the price
options.why: The differential is exactly what sets the locked rate above spot. Higher home interest is why the exporter's manufactured forward is favourable, not why the hedge breaks.

options.text: Borrow about $0.98 million now, convert at ₹84, invest in rupees — locking roughly ₹85.6 per dollar
options.why: Borrowing $1m ÷ 1.02 today means the $1 million receivable exactly repays the loan in six months. The ₹82.35 crore-odd raised at spot grows at 4 per cent for the half year, and the effective rate works out near 84 × 1.04/1.02 ≈ ₹85.6 — the same figure interest rate parity would quote as the forward.

options.text: Borrow rupees now, convert to dollars, and invest the dollars for six months
options.misconception: runs the importer's hedge on an exporter's exposure
options.why: That trade builds a dollar asset — useful when dollars must be paid later. The exporter already has dollars coming; the hedge must create the offsetting dollar liability.

options.text: Invest $1 million abroad now and convert whatever it grows to at the spot rate then
options.misconception: hedges nothing and postpones the conversion risk
options.why: The exporter has no dollars today to invest — they arrive in six months — and converting at an unknown future spot is the exposure itself, prolonged rather than removed.

citation.ref: Ch. Foreign Exchange Exposure and Risk Management

items.scenario: An exporter will receive $1 million in six months. Dollar interest is 4 per cent a year, rupee interest 8 per cent, spot ₹84. The exporter wants the rupee amount fixed today without using the forward market.

items.stem: What has the board misunderstood?

options.text: Nothing — a 99 per cent VaR is designed to state the maximum loss
options.misconception: reads a quantile as a bound
options.why: A quantile marks where the worst 1 per cent begins, not where losses end. Maximum loss on a leveraged book may have no finite bound at all.

options.text: The error is the horizon — one-day VaR must be annualised before boards may read it
options.misconception: converts a comprehension problem into a units problem
options.why: The horizon was stated and matched the daily question. Stretching it changes the number, not the board's mistake of treating any VaR as a worst case.

options.text: The board should double the VaR to be safe, making the true ceiling ₹1 crore
options.misconception: patches a conceptual gap with an arbitrary multiplier
options.why: Scaling a quantile still yields a quantile. What the board wants is a tail measure — expected shortfall reports the average loss on the breaching days — not a bigger copy of the same blind spot.

options.text: VaR is a threshold crossed about one day in a hundred, and is silent about how bad those days get
options.why: Ninety-nine per cent confidence means roughly two or three trading days a year should breach the number in the ordinary course. Beyond the threshold, VaR offers no ceiling — the ₹2 crore day lives precisely in the tail the measure does not describe.

items.scenario: A treasury reports a one-day 99 per cent VaR of ₹50 lakh. The board takes comfort that the worst possible loss on any day is ₹50 lakh, and that a ₹2 crore loss is therefore impossible.

items.stem: What does the stock's position actually show?

options.text: Overpricing — a correctly priced asset must plot on both lines
options.misconception: treats the two lines as one test administered twice
options.why: Only perfectly diversified holdings can sit on the CML. Demanding it of a single stock condemns every individual security in the market as overpriced at once.

options.text: The analyst mixed up the axes, since both lines chart the same risk
options.misconception: misses that the lines are drawn against different risk measures
options.why: The CML's horizontal axis is standard deviation; the SML's is beta. The stock's two positions differ precisely because its total risk exceeds its systematic risk.

options.text: A buying opportunity — below a line means cheap
options.misconception: applies the SML's alpha reading to the CML
options.why: Above or below has that meaning on the SML, where the line is the fair price of beta. Distance below the CML measures inefficiency of diversification, not a bargain.

options.text: Normal pricing — single stocks carry diversifiable risk, so they sit on the SML and below the CML
options.why: The SML is the pricing line for all assets: on it means fairly priced for beta. The CML is reserved for efficient portfolios, whose only risk is market risk. A lone stock's extra, diversifiable volatility pushes it rightward off the CML without any mispricing — both lines are saying exactly what they should.

items.scenario: An analyst finds that a single pharmaceutical stock, correctly priced by CAPM, plots exactly on the security market line but well below the capital market line. He concludes the stock must be overpriced, since it fails one of the two lines.

items.stem: Who is misusing the theorem?

options.text: Neither — they are debating taste, on which finance is silent
options.misconception: files a structured disagreement under preference
options.why: Both positions make testable claims about wealth effects. The frictions that separate them — taxes, signalling, clienteles — are the syllabus of dividend policy, not matters of taste.

options.text: Only the director — market reactions are noise around a proven identity
options.misconception: defends the proof by dismissing the evidence
options.why: The reaction is real and repeatable; it documents signalling. A theorem holding under assumptions is not a description of markets that breach them.

options.text: Only the CFO — MM was refuted the day dividends started moving prices
options.misconception: reads a conditional proof as an empirical claim
options.why: MM never predicted real prices would ignore dividends; it proved they would under stated conditions. The interesting question is which condition fails, and here it is symmetric information.

options.text: Both — MM's irrelevance assumes perfect markets, and the price fall shows a signalling friction, not a refuted proof
options.why: The CFO transplants a frictionless-market result into a world of taxes and information gaps — in that world a cut can carry a message. The director errs the mirror way: the 4 per cent fall is investors reading the cut as bad news about earnings, which is a violated assumption, not a disproof. The theorem's value is telling you exactly where to look — at the frictions.

items.scenario: A CFO cites MM to the board: "dividend policy is irrelevant, so scrapping our dividend to fund the new plant changes nothing for shareholders." A director counters that the share price fell 4 per cent the last time a dividend was cut, so MM must simply be wrong.

items.stem: What changes hands, and what does the debt now cost?

options.text: Net differences only, but the cost floats at MIBOR + 2 as before, plus 7 fixed
options.misconception: adds the legs without netting the received one
options.why: The received MIBOR leg exists precisely to cancel the loan's MIBOR. Adding all three without the cancellation double-counts the floating rate.

options.text: Nothing until maturity, when one lump sum settles the whole swap
options.misconception: confuses a running swap with a single forward settlement
options.why: A vanilla swap is a strip of periodic settlements aligned to the loan's interest dates. Deferring everything to maturity would leave the interim cash flows unhedged.

options.text: Only periodic net interest differences; the all-in cost is fixed at 9 per cent
options.why: Notional principal is a measuring rod, never a payment. Each period the company pays 7 fixed, receives MIBOR, and pays MIBOR + 2 on the loan — the MIBOR legs cancel, leaving 7 + 2 = 9 per cent whatever rates do. That cancellation is the synthetic fixing.

options.text: The ₹100 crore principals are exchanged at the start and returned at the end
options.misconception: imports currency-swap mechanics into an interest rate swap
options.why: Exchanging identical rupee principals would be handing money to yourself through a counterparty. Same-currency swaps settle interest differences only.

items.scenario: A company has ₹100 crore of floating-rate debt at MIBOR + 2 per cent and fears rates will rise. It enters a swap on ₹100 crore notional: pay 7 per cent fixed, receive MIBOR. The treasurer's junior worries the company must now find ₹100 crore to hand over, and cannot say what the debt effectively costs.

items.stem: Which circle makes the riskless profit, and roughly how much?

options.text: Rupees to euros at ₹90, euros to dollars at 1.10, dollars to rupees at 84 — about ₹2.2 lakh on ₹84 lakh
options.why: The euro is cheap in the cross market, so buy it there: ₹84,00,000 ÷ 90 ≈ €93,333, which becomes about $102,667, which becomes about ₹86.24 lakh — a gain near ₹2.24 lakh with no open position at any moment. Buy where the quote is below the implied rate, and the circle does the rest.

options.text: No profit exists — ₹90 against ₹92.40 is within normal quoting variation
options.misconception: waves away a 2.6 per cent gap as noise
options.why: Transaction costs in liquid currency markets are hundredths of a per cent. A gap this size funds the round trip many times over, which is exactly why real quotes are never left this far apart.

options.text: Hold euros and wait for the quoted rate to rise to ₹92.40
options.misconception: converts an arbitrage into a directional bet
options.why: Waiting bears currency risk the arbitrage does not. The three simultaneous legs collect the discrepancy whatever rates do next — that simultaneity is the whole trick.

options.text: Rupees to dollars, dollars to euros, euros to rupees at ₹90 — the same profit the other way
options.misconception: assumes any direction around a mispriced triangle pays
options.why: Run that way, ₹84 lakh becomes $1,00,000, then about €90,909, then ₹81.8 lakh — a loss of the same order. The mispricing has one profitable direction; the reverse circle pays the market instead.

citation.ref: Ch. Foreign Exchange Exposure and Risk Management

items.scenario: Quotes: one dollar buys ₹84; one euro buys $1.10; one euro is quoted at ₹90 in the cross market. A dealer holds ₹84 lakh and spots that the implied euro-rupee rate is 84 × 1.10 = ₹92.40, above the quoted ₹90.

items.stem: What two errors sit in this valuation?

options.text: Nothing — a higher discount rate is conservative, and conservative valuations protect users
options.misconception: confuses bias with prudence
options.why: A valuation is useful when unbiased; deliberate understatement misleads a seller as surely as overstatement misleads a buyer. Conservatism is not a licence to mismatch flows and rates.

options.text: Only the discount rate — FCFF valuations do produce equity value directly
options.misconception: forgets whose cash the firm-level flow is
options.why: FCFF includes the cash that services debt. Handing its full present value to shareholders values the lenders' claim at zero — the bondholders would object.

options.text: Only the missing debt deduction — any defensible discount rate is acceptable
options.misconception: treats rate selection as taste rather than matching
options.why: The rate must price the risk of the specific flow being discounted. WACC and cost of equity differ by five points here; the mismatch alone misstates value materially.

options.text: FCFF discounted at the equity rate, and enterprise value passed off as equity value without deducting net debt
options.why: FCFF pairs with WACC because the flow belongs to debt and equity together; discounting it at 16 per cent punishes lenders' cash flows with shareholders' risk premium and calls the resulting understatement caution. And whatever the rate, an FCFF valuation yields enterprise value — the shares are worth that less net debt, a subtraction the analyst skipped.

items.scenario: An analyst projects a company's free cash flow to the firm, discounts it at the cost of equity of 16 per cent "to be conservative" (WACC is 11 per cent), and presents the result as the value of the company's shares without further adjustment.

items.stem: What does the constant risk-adjusted rate do to the year-eight flow?

options.text: It understates risk, since 18 per cent is too low for an eight-year horizon
options.misconception: doubles down on the compounding in the wrong direction
options.why: The complaint runs the other way: the year-eight flow is over-penalised. Raising the rate further would widen the very distortion at issue.

options.text: It compounds an eleven-point risk premium for eight years, punishing a flow whose risk did not grow with time
options.why: A constant premium in the discount rate charges for risk exponentially with distance, so the year-eight flow is treated as vastly riskier than year one's despite bearing the identical uncertainty. Certainty equivalents — ₹9 crore in each year, discounted at 7 per cent — price the risk once, where it actually lives.

options.text: Nothing wrong — later cash flows are always riskier, and compounding reflects that
options.misconception: assumes risk always accumulates with time
options.why: Often true, not here: the scenario's risk resolves at year one. When risk's time profile is flat or front-loaded, the compounding premium misprices by construction.

options.text: The two methods always agree, so nothing turns on the choice
options.misconception: assumes equivalence that holds only under a specific risk pattern
options.why: They coincide only when certainty equivalent factors decay geometrically to match the compounding premium. Any other risk profile — like this one-time risk — splits their answers.

items.scenario: A project's ₹10 crore expected inflow in year one is judged worth ₹9 crore for certain; the identical ₹10 crore expected in year eight is also judged worth ₹9 crore for certain — the risk in both years is the same one-time regulatory approval, already resolved by year one. An analyst instead applies a constant 18 per cent risk-adjusted rate (risk-free is 7 per cent) to both flows.

items.stem: How should the account stand in the year-end financial statements?

options.text: Standard, because the post-year-end instalment cured the overdue position
options.misconception: uses a later receipt to rewrite the balance sheet date
options.why: Classification is tested as at the reporting date. The week-later payment is next year's recovery — evidence for upgrade in due course, not an eraser for the year-end position.

options.text: Doubtful, since any default this size shows the loan is unlikely to be repaid
options.misconception: skips the ladder's first rung
options.why: Doubtful status is earned by remaining substandard for twelve months, not by the auditor's pessimism on day one. Over-classifying misstates provisions exactly as under-classifying does.

options.text: Standard — the security cover means the bank will lose nothing
options.misconception: lets collateral answer a question asked about repayment
options.why: Security affects how much is provided, not whether the asset performs. An account can be fully secured and fully non-performing at once; the ninety-day clock reads payments, not valuations.

options.text: Substandard NPA, with the accrued interest reversed — record of recovery decides, not security or reputation
options.why: Past ninety days overdue at the balance sheet date, the classification is automatic and borrower-wise reputation, group standing and security value have no vote — the norms look at the record of recovery alone. A fresh NPA starts as substandard, and unrealised interest on it comes out of income.

citation.ref: Prudential norms on Income Recognition, Asset Classification and Provisioning

items.scenario: As branch auditor you find a term loan whose last instalment was received 100 days before year-end, shown as standard with interest accrued to income. The branch manager explains the borrower is a reputed group, the security comfortably covers the loan, and one further instalment arrived a week after year-end.

items.stem: Which facts block the appointment?

options.text: All three — any financial connection with an audit client disqualifies
options.misconception: replaces the statutory thresholds with a zero-tolerance rule
options.why: Parliament drew money lines precisely so trivial connections would not bar appointment. Reading them as zero makes the limits in the rule meaningless.

options.text: B's loan and C's guarantee — only the relative's shareholding is tolerated
options.misconception: forgets the guarantee has its own threshold
options.why: The guarantee disqualifies only beyond one lakh rupees. At ₹90,000 it is inside the line; the only fact past its ceiling is the ₹6 lakh debt.

options.text: None — the interests belong to a spouse, a borrower on market terms, and a guarantor, not the auditors themselves
options.misconception: shrinks the provision to the signing partner's own name
options.why: The section speaks of the person, the relative and the partner, and the rule prices each connection. B's own debt crosses its line regardless of the loan's fairness.

options.text: Only B's loan — the spouse's holding and C's guarantee sit within their limits
options.why: A relative's securities are permitted up to one lakh rupees face value, so ₹80,000 passes. The guarantee limit is one lakh, so ₹90,000 passes. Indebtedness has a five-lakh ceiling and B's ₹6 lakh crosses it — market terms do not matter — and one disqualified partner disqualifies the firm.

items.scenario: A firm is proposed as auditor of a company. Partner A's spouse holds shares of the company of face value ₹80,000. Partner B owes the company ₹6 lakh on a car loan taken on market terms. Partner C has guaranteed his friend's ₹90,000 dues to the company.

items.stem: What does clause 3(xi) actually require here?

options.text: Report both frauds with nature and amount — the clause covers any fraud on the company, noticed or reported, whoever committed it
options.why: CARO 2020 widened the clause to any fraud by the company or on the company noticed or reported during the year. The outsider's ₹1.2 crore is a fraud on the company, and its being reported to the police is exactly what makes it "reported". Nature and amount go into the report for each.

options.text: Report both, but omit amounts to avoid prejudicing the pending investigations
options.misconception: lets litigation caution trim a prescribed disclosure
options.why: The clause asks for nature and amount in terms. The auditor reports what was noticed; investigations run on their own track and are not compromised by a statutory report stating the figure involved.

options.text: Report only the stores officer — outsider frauds are police matters, not audit matters
options.misconception: carries the old officers-and-employees limit into the 2020 order
options.why: The 2016 order's wording was narrower; the 2020 clause dropped the limitation. An auditor answering the old question in the new report under-reports by ₹1.2 crore.

options.text: Report neither, since clause 3(xi) is triggered only by frauds the auditor discovers himself
options.misconception: reads "noticed or reported" as "noticed by the auditor"
options.why: Noticed or reported during the year — by anyone. Frauds surfacing through management, police complaints or whistle-blowers are squarely inside the words.

items.scenario: During the year, a company's stores officer was caught inflating supplier invoices for ₹40 lakh, and an outside gang defrauded the company of ₹1.2 crore through a fake vendor registration. Writing the CARO report, the audit senior drafts clause 3(xi) to cover only the stores officer, reasoning that CARO concerns frauds by the company's own people, and the vendor fraud was reported to the police, not to the auditor.

items.stem: Can the report be signed today?

options.text: No — for a listed entity the quality review must be completed before the report is dated
options.why: SQC 1 makes the engagement quality control review a gate, not a debrief: an objective look at the significant judgments and conclusions, finished before the report's date. A review conducted after signing can no longer change the one thing it exists to test.

options.text: Yes — the review is the firm's internal process and the report is the engagement's
options.misconception: files a signing condition under housekeeping
options.why: The review is internal in who performs it, not in what it protects. Its position before the report date is what gives the reviewer's objections any force.

options.text: Yes, provided the reviewer belongs to the engagement team and already knows the file
options.misconception: staffs the review with the people it is meant to check
options.why: The reviewer's value is distance — someone outside the team evaluating the team's judgments. A team member reviewing his own conclusions is the engagement grading itself.

options.text: No, unless the engagement partner documents that he considered the open issues himself
options.misconception: substitutes self-review for the second pair of eyes
options.why: The partner's own consideration is the thing under review. His memo cannot stand in for the objective evaluation SQC 1 assigns to another qualified person.

items.scenario: The audit of a listed company is nearly done. The engagement partner, under deadline pressure, proposes signing the report today and having the firm's quality control reviewer go through the significant judgments next week, arguing the review is an internal formality that does not concern the client.

items.stem: Is the clean audit a substitute for due diligence?

options.text: Yes for the financials, with diligence confined to legal and operational matters
options.misconception: carves financial diligence out on the audit's authority
options.why: Financial due diligence reads the same numbers with a buyer's eyes — quality of earnings, sustainability, normalisation. The audit did none of that, and a deal is priced on exactly that.

options.text: No, because audits performed by the target's own auditor are inherently unreliable
options.misconception: wins the right conclusion by slandering the wrong party
options.why: The reputed firm's work needs no doubting for the lawyer to be right. Even a flawless audit is a different exercise; the argument is scope, not competence.

options.text: Yes — a true and fair view certified by auditors is the highest assurance available
options.misconception: ranks assurance levels instead of matching scope to purpose
options.why: The opinion's assurance is high on the question it answered. A buyer's losses come overwhelmingly from matters outside that question — commitments, dependencies, liabilities that are disclosed correctly yet deadly.

options.text: No — the audit answered a different question for a different audience, and the rumour needs an investigation alongside the diligence, not instead of it
options.why: The audit opined that the statements fairly present the past under a framework — it never priced the business, tested contract terms, tax exposures or customer concentration, and it owed its opinion to shareholders, not to a buyer. Due diligence asks the buyer's questions. The promoter rumour is a specific suspicion — an investigation's job — and it runs beside the diligence with its own depth.

citation.ref: Ch. Due Diligence, Investigation and Forensic Accounting

items.scenario: A client acquiring a rival says: "The target's accounts carry a clean audit opinion from a reputed firm, so due diligence would duplicate work already done. If anything, just investigate the promoter's rumoured side-dealings." His lawyer insists a full due diligence is still needed.

items.stem: What does propriety audit make of an unimpeachable file?

options.text: Nothing, unless a rule specifically caps renovation rates
options.misconception: demands a broken rule before any audit comment
options.why: Propriety supplies the standard where rules run out — that is its function. Waiting for a rate cap turns the auditor into a rule-checker for a class of loss rules cannot foresee.

options.text: The transaction fails — sanctioned extravagance in a relative's favour is exactly what propriety audit exists to catch
options.why: Regularity audit reads the file and finds every rule followed; propriety audit reads the bargain and asks whether a prudent person would pay triple his own money to a relative of the decision-maker. The standards of prudence, economy and no personal advantage condemn it however complete the sanctions.

options.text: The auditor may only report the relationship, not question the price
options.misconception: shrinks propriety to conflict disclosure
options.why: Economy is a propriety canon in its own right. Triple market rate fails it with or without the relative; the relationship adds the personal-advantage failure on top.

options.text: The transaction passes — audit tests compliance, and compliance is total
options.misconception: stops at the regularity rail
options.why: If sanction ended the enquiry, the surest waste would be waste with the best paperwork. Government audit added propriety precisely because public money can be lost lawfully.

citation.ref: Ch. Audit of Public Sector Undertakings

items.scenario: A public sector company buys office renovation services at triple the market rate from a vendor who is the purchasing director's relative. Every step carried proper sanction: budget approval, tender committee sign-off, board ratification. Management tells the government auditor the file is unimpeachable.

items.stem: Do the objections hold?

options.text: Neither — the review tests the firm's systems on sample files, not the client's accounts, and access to attestation working papers is inherent in the framework
options.why: Nothing about the client reopens: the reviewer asks whether the firm's quality controls, documentation and standards compliance operated on that engagement. The confidentiality objection fails because the peer review framework itself provides for the reviewer's access with confidentiality obligations of his own — a member cannot plead the client against the profession's oversight of the member.

options.text: The confidentiality objection holds — client consent is needed for each file shown
options.misconception: puts a consent gate where the framework put an obligation
options.why: The reviewer stands under his own duty of confidentiality within the review's structure. Engagement-by-engagement client vetoes would let firms curate their own review.

options.text: Both — completed audits are closed files in every sense
options.misconception: confuses reviewing the auditor with reopening the audit
options.why: Closed for the client is not closed for the firm's own quality trail. The completed file is precisely the evidence of how the firm's systems behaved when it mattered.

options.text: Both fail, but only because peer review reports are never made public
options.misconception: right result hung on secrecy instead of scope
options.why: The objections fail on what review is — systems examination of the practice unit — not on who reads the outcome. Publicity is beside the point.

items.scenario: A peer reviewer examining an audit firm selects a completed statutory audit as a sample. The firm's managing partner objects on two grounds: the client's financial statements were approved long ago and cannot be reopened, and client confidentiality bars an outsider from the working papers.

items.stem: Who appoints the first auditor now?

options.text: The Registrar of Companies, on the company's application
options.misconception: imports a government-company style default into an ordinary company
options.why: The C&AG-then-Comptroller cascade belongs to government companies. For others the statute keeps the appointment inside the company — board, then members.

options.text: The board — statutory timelines for internal appointments are directory, not mandatory
options.misconception: keeps a lapsed power alive by calling the deadline soft
options.why: The section's structure is a handover: board first, members on the board's failure. Reading the deadline away erases the members' role the provision creates.

options.text: The members, in an extraordinary general meeting within ninety days
options.why: The board's thirty-day window from registration closed on 30 April; section 139(6) hands the power to the members, who appoint at an EGM within ninety days. The appointee serves until the first AGM concludes — the same tenure the board's appointee would have had.

options.text: No one — the company must wait for the first annual general meeting
options.misconception: leaves the company auditor-less for up to a year
options.why: The first auditor's whole purpose is covering the stretch before the first AGM. The ninety-day EGM route exists so the office never waits that long.

items.scenario: A private company incorporated on 1 April has a board that never appoints a first auditor. On 20 May the promoters realise the lapse. One director suggests the board can still appoint, being only a few days late; another says the power is gone and the Registrar now appoints; a third says the members must do it.

items.stem: Is he entitled to the section 54 exemption?

options.text: No, but he can claim it under section 54F instead
options.misconception: swaps in the section that runs in the opposite direction
options.why: Section 54F exempts gains on assets other than a residential house when the proceeds buy a residential house. Here the sale was residential and the purchase was not — the wrong way round for both sections.

options.text: Yes, because the amount invested exceeds the capital gain
options.misconception: reads the quantum condition and skips the nature-of-asset condition
options.why: The amount decides how much of the gain is exempt once the conditions are met. It cannot substitute for the condition that the new asset be a residential house.

options.text: Yes, if the shop is let out for residential use by the tenant
options.misconception: lets the tenant's use recharacterise the property
options.why: The character of the asset purchased is what it is — commercial premises. What a tenant does inside it does not turn a shop into a residential house for section 54.

options.text: No — the reinvestment must be in a residential house in India
options.why: Section 54 is an exemption for keeping capital in residential housing. Both ends of the transaction must be residential: the asset sold and the asset bought. A shop fails the second condition however large the investment.

items.scenario: An individual sells a residential house in June 2025, earning a long-term capital gain of ₹65 lakh. Within a year he invests ₹70 lakh in a commercial shop, arguing the whole gain is exempt because the reinvestment exceeds the gain.

items.stem: Is a tax audit under section 44AB required?

options.text: Yes, because turnover exceeds ₹1 crore
options.misconception: applies the base limit without testing for the digital-transactions proviso
options.why: ₹1 crore is the starting rule, and the proviso is the examinable part: heavy banking- channel usage lifts the limit tenfold precisely to spare businesses like this one.

options.text: Yes, because the limit for firms is ₹50 lakh
options.misconception: applies the professional gross-receipts limit to a business
options.why: ₹50 lakh is the threshold for a profession's gross receipts. A trading firm is a business and takes the business limits.

options.text: No, because audit under section 44AB applies only to companies
options.misconception: confuses tax audit with statutory audit under the Companies Act
options.why: Section 44AB turns on turnover, not on the form of the entity. Individuals, firms and companies are all within it; companies separately face statutory audit regardless.

options.text: No — the enhanced ₹10 crore limit applies because cash stays within 5 per cent
options.why: Where both cash receipts and cash payments are within 5 per cent of their totals, the audit threshold is ₹10 crore, not ₹1 crore. At ₹8 crore of largely digital turnover, no audit is required.

items.scenario: A trading firm has turnover of ₹8 crore for the year. Its cash receipts are 3 per cent of total receipts and cash payments are 2 per cent of total payments; everything else moves through banking channels.

items.stem: What is the MAT position of this company?

options.text: MAT applies at the standard rate on book profit, payable if higher
options.misconception: runs the MAT comparison out of habit for every company
options.why: The compare-and-pay-higher routine belongs to companies under the normal regime. For a 115BAA company there is nothing to compare — the computation itself is switched off.

options.text: MAT does not apply to it at all
options.why: Opting into 115BAA takes the company outside MAT entirely — section 115JB(5A) says the book profit provisions do not apply. The bargain is a lower flat rate in exchange for the incentives, and MAT has no role because there are no incentives left to claw back.

options.text: MAT applies, but unused MAT credit can be set off against it
options.misconception: keeps MAT credit alive inside a regime that has no MAT
options.why: Old MAT credit lapses on opting in — one of the real costs of the choice. There is no future MAT liability for the credit to meet.

options.text: MAT applies only if book profit exceeds taxable income by 20 per cent
options.misconception: invents a threshold test for when MAT switches on
options.why: No such trigger exists anywhere in the Act. Under the normal regime MAT is always computed; under 115BAA it never is.

items.scenario: A domestic company opted for section 115BAA two years ago. This year its book profit is high while its taxable income is modest, and the tax team begins computing MAT on book profit as a comparison.

items.stem: What is the due date?

options.text: 30 November 2026
options.misconception: extends the transfer pricing date to every company
options.why: 30 November applies only where a report under section 92E is required — international or specified domestic transactions. This company has none.

options.text: 30 September 2026
options.misconception: recalls the pre-amendment audit due date
options.why: 30 September was the audit-case date years ago and survives in old material. The current date is 31 October.

options.text: 31 July 2026
options.misconception: applies the no-audit individual due date to a company
options.why: 31 July belongs to taxpayers with no audit requirement. A company never files by this date.

options.text: 31 October 2026
options.why: A company is an audit case by definition for this purpose, and the due date for audit cases is 31 October of the assessment year.

items.scenario: A private limited company with no international or specified domestic transactions asks for the last date to file its income-tax return for assessment year 2026-27.

items.stem: Which statement describes the section 112A treatment?

options.text: Taxed with indexation benefit at the general long-term rate
options.misconception: applies the section 112 computation that 112A displaces
options.why: Indexation is the general regime's feature. Section 112A trades it away for the lower rate and the annual exempt slab.

options.text: Taxed above an annual exemption threshold at the special rate, without indexation
options.why: Section 112A carves listed STT-paid equity out of the general LTCG regime: a slab of gain each year is exempt, the excess is taxed at the concessional rate, and no indexation is available against it.

options.text: Taxed at normal slab rates like any other income
options.misconception: ignores the special regime entirely
options.why: Listed equity LTCG never meets slab rates while 112A stands; the section exists to give it its own rate and threshold.

options.text: Fully exempt, because STT was paid at both purchase and sale
options.misconception: remembers the pre-2018 section 10(38) exemption as still alive
options.why: The blanket exemption ended when 112A arrived. STT payment is now the condition for the concessional regime, not for exemption.

items.scenario: An investor sells listed equity shares after two years, through the exchange with STT paid, realising a long-term gain. She asks how the gain is taxed.

items.stem: Who can use section 44AD here?

options.text: The LLP can, because presumptive schemes exist for entities without detailed books
options.misconception: reasons from the scheme's purpose instead of its words
options.why: Whatever the purpose suggests, the definition decides — and it names the LLP only to shut it out.

options.text: The firm can; the LLP cannot
options.why: Section 44AD is open to a resident individual, HUF or firm — and the definition expressly excludes a limited liability partnership. The firm declares 6 per cent on its banked turnover; the LLP keeps books and computes profit normally.

options.text: Neither, because turnover above ₹1 crore requires audited books
options.misconception: applies the 44AB audit limit to a presumptive filer
options.why: Declaring under 44AD is precisely what makes the audit requirement fall away within the scheme's turnover limit. The two sections are alternatives, not a ladder.

options.text: Both, since their turnover and business are identical
options.misconception: tests eligibility by size and trade rather than by the person
options.why: The scheme's gate is the kind of person, not the kind of business. Identical turnover does not bring an excluded entity inside.

items.scenario: A resident partnership firm runs a retail business with turnover of ₹1.8 crore, received almost entirely through UPI and bank transfer. An LLP in the same market, with the same turnover, asks to declare profit the same presumptive way.

items.stem: What survives to be carried forward?

options.text: Only the ₹80 lakh unabsorbed depreciation
options.why: Section 80 forfeits the carry forward of a business loss claimed in a late return, so ₹2.2 crore is gone. Unabsorbed depreciation is carried under section 32(2), which stands outside that condition — it survives the late filing, and with no eight-year limit either.

options.text: The whole ₹3 crore, since the return was filed with a valid explanation
options.misconception: believes an explained delay preserves the loss
options.why: Section 80 has no explanation clause. The due date is the condition, and missing it is the consequence, however good the reason.

options.text: The whole ₹3 crore, but for four years instead of eight
options.misconception: invents a penalty of a shortened period rather than a forfeiture
options.why: Section 80 does not shorten the window; it shuts the door. The loss either carries for its full period or, filed late, does not carry at all.

options.text: Nothing at all, because the return was late
options.misconception: extends the section 80 forfeiture to depreciation it does not touch
options.why: The forfeiture reaches what is carried under sections 72 and its siblings. Depreciation travels under section 32(2), a different vehicle the late return does not stop.

items.scenario: A company incurs a business loss of ₹3 crore, of which ₹80 lakh is unabsorbed depreciation. It files the loss year's return four months after the due date.

items.stem: How much is taxable under section 56(2)(x)?

options.text: ₹25,000 — the amount by which the friends' gifts exceed fifty thousand
options.misconception: taxes the excess over the threshold instead of the whole
options.why: Fifty thousand is a trigger, not an exemption slab. One rupee past it and the entire aggregate is income — the cliff is the examinable feature.

options.text: ₹3,75,000 — all gifts, since the aggregate crossed the threshold
options.misconception: pulls relatives' gifts into the aggregate once the threshold breaks
options.why: Relatives' gifts are excluded from the section altogether, not merely from the trigger. The uncle's money neither counts toward the fifty thousand nor becomes taxable when the line is crossed.

options.text: Nothing, because each individual gift is below fifty thousand
options.misconception: applies the threshold gift by gift instead of in aggregate
options.why: The section aggregates all such receipts in the year. Splitting a sum across givers or occasions does not defeat it — ₹40,000 plus ₹35,000 is ₹75,000 against one limit.

options.text: ₹75,000 — the friends' gifts in full; the uncle's gift is exempt as from a relative
options.why: The friends' gifts aggregate to ₹75,000, past the fifty-thousand line, and the section then taxes the whole aggregate, not the excess. The mother's brother is within the definition of relative, so his ₹3 lakh never enters the computation.

items.scenario: During the year an individual receives ₹40,000 from one friend and ₹35,000 from another, both as birthday gifts, and ₹3 lakh from his mother's brother for no particular occasion.

items.stem: What does section 44ADA actually permit?

options.text: She must declare the actual ₹42 lakh, since presumptive income cannot be below truth
options.misconception: reads the presumption as a minimum-of-actual rule
options.why: The presumption replaces the actual computation; that is its point. The words "or a higher amount claimed" give her the option of more, never the obligation.

options.text: She may declare ₹30 lakh only if she also maintains full books as a safeguard
options.misconception: attaches the books requirement to the scheme instead of to leaving it
options.why: Books and audit are the price of declaring BELOW the presumptive rate, not of using it. Inside the scheme, freedom from books is the principal benefit.

options.text: Declaring 50 per cent of receipts — ₹30 lakh — is permitted as her deemed income, even if the true profit is higher
options.why: The section deems 50 per cent or such higher sum as the assessee claims; declaring the floor is the scheme working as designed. The bargain runs the other way too — with true profit above the deemed figure, the law still accepts the 50 per cent declaration.

options.text: Nothing — architecture is not a specified profession for this section
options.misconception: shrinks the section 44AA list that 44ADA borrows
options.why: The section covers the legal, medical, engineering, architectural, accountancy, technical consultancy and interior decoration professions. Architecture is named in it.

items.scenario: A practising architect has gross receipts of ₹60 lakh, received almost entirely by bank transfer. Her actual expenses are low and true profit is around ₹42 lakh. She asks whether she can declare ₹30 lakh under section 44ADA and keep the difference untaxed.

items.stem: What did section 194-IA require?

options.text: Deduction of ₹18,000 — 1 per cent of the amount above ₹50 lakh
options.misconception: taxes the excess over the threshold instead of the whole
options.why: Fifty lakh is a trigger, not a slab. Once crossed, the deduction runs on the full consideration from the first rupee.

options.text: Nothing, because the buyer is an individual not liable to tax audit
options.misconception: imports the audit-linked exemption from other TDS sections into this one
options.why: Sections like 194C spare small individual payers; 194-IA deliberately does not. Property purchases were pulled in precisely because ordinary buyers are the payers.

options.text: Nothing, because TDS on property applies only when the seller is a non-resident
options.misconception: swaps in section 195 and discards the resident-seller section
options.why: A non-resident seller invokes section 195 at different rates. Resident sellers are the very case 194-IA exists for.

options.text: Deduction of ₹68,000 — 1 per cent of the whole consideration — with no TAN needed
options.why: The section binds any buyer, business or not, once consideration or stamp duty value reaches ₹50 lakh, and it charges 1 per cent on the entire amount. It was built for exactly this buyer: the form works on PAN alone, no TAN required.

items.scenario: An individual buys a flat for ₹68 lakh from a resident seller. At registration the buyer pays the full amount without deducting anything, saying he has no TAN and is not in business, so TDS provisions cannot apply to him.

items.stem: Is he resident for the year?

options.text: Yes — 123 days this year and 365 in the preceding four satisfies the second condition
options.misconception: applies the ordinary 60-plus-365 limb to a departing employee
options.why: That limb is exactly what the explanation switches off for this taxpayer. Applying it taxes a departing worker's global income for the very year he left — the outcome the carve-out exists to prevent.

options.text: No, because employment abroad automatically makes anyone non-resident from the date of departure
options.misconception: turns a day-count adjustment into an automatic exemption
options.why: The carve-out changes the threshold, not the method. Leave in February after 200 days and the same employee is resident, employment abroad notwithstanding.

options.text: No — for a citizen leaving for employment, only the 182-day test applies, and 123 fails it
options.why: The explanation to section 6(1) replaces the 60-day limb with 182 for a citizen leaving India for employment abroad. His four-year history becomes irrelevant; 123 days against a 182-day test makes him non-resident.

options.text: Yes, because an Indian citizen is always resident unless he stays out a full year
options.misconception: attaches residence to citizenship rather than days
options.why: Residence under the Act is arithmetic on days, not passport. Citizenship enters only to select which day-count applies.

items.scenario: An Indian citizen left India on 1 August 2025 to take up employment in Dubai, after being in India for 123 days of the year. Over the four preceding years he was in India throughout. His accountant applies the 60-plus-365 test and calls him resident.

items.stem: How is the minor's income taxed?

options.text: Both incomes club with the father, as the natural guardian
options.misconception: picks the parent by guardianship instead of income
options.why: The section names the parent whose total income is greater. Guardianship has no role in the choice.

options.text: Both incomes club with the mother, as she earns more
options.misconception: clubs talent income along with passive income
options.why: The skill-and-talent exclusion exists because that income is genuinely the child's earning, not a parental arrangement wearing the child's name. The chess money is assessed in the minor's own hands.

options.text: Neither clubs, since the source money came from grandparents, not parents
options.misconception: tests clubbing by who gave the capital
options.why: Section 64(1A) clubs a minor's income regardless of where the underlying funds came from. The giver matters under other provisions; here only the child's age does.

options.text: Interest of ₹2,38,500 clubs with the mother; the chess winnings stay the minor's own
options.why: Passive income clubs with the higher-earning parent — the mother — after the ₹1,500 exemption. Chess prize money is income from the minor's skill and talent, which section 64(1A) leaves out of clubbing altogether.

items.scenario: A fourteen-year-old earns ₹2.4 lakh in bank interest on money gifted by grandparents, and ₹3 lakh in prize money from national-level chess tournaments. The father's income is ₹30 lakh and the mother's ₹42 lakh.

items.stem: How much of the loss reduces his other income this year?

options.text: The full ₹5.6 lakh, since let-out property interest has no ceiling
options.misconception: confuses the uncapped interest deduction with uncapped set-off
options.why: Both statements are true separately and the trap is joining them. Interest is fully deductible in computing the property loss; the loss then hits the two-lakh gate on its way to the salary.

options.text: ₹2 lakh now; ₹3.6 lakh carries forward against house property income for eight years
options.why: Section 71(3A) caps the inter-head set-off at two lakh however large the computed loss. The remainder is not lost — it carries forward — but it waits for house property income, which for many taxpayers means it waits a long time.

options.text: Nothing, because losses from let-out property cannot touch salary at all
options.misconception: overreads the cap into a prohibition
options.why: The set-off exists — section 71 permits it — and the 2017 amendment only capped it. Two lakh of this loss reduces the salary income this year.

options.text: ₹2 lakh now, with the balance carrying forward against any head of income
options.misconception: carries the loss forward with wider set-off rights than it left with
options.why: Carried-forward house property loss narrows, not widens — in later years it meets only house property income. The inter-head window exists in year one alone, capped.

items.scenario: An individual's let-out property produces a loss of ₹5.6 lakh this year, driven by home loan interest. His salary income is ₹28 lakh, and he expects the whole loss to reduce his salary tax this year.

items.stem: In which year is the ₹22 lakh deductible?

options.text: Next year — the due-date escape does not apply to MSME dues, so payment year governs
options.why: Clause (h) was built without the proviso that rescues other 43B items. The February bill on 30-day terms was payable beyond the MSMED window at the year end, so the deduction waits for the year of actual payment, the return's due date notwithstanding.

options.text: This year, since payment preceded the due date of filing the return
options.misconception: applies the general 43B proviso to the one clause carved out of it
options.why: The proviso's absence for clause (h) is the whole design — Parliament wanted MSMEs paid in days, not by October. The familiar rule is the trap laid for the well-prepared.

options.text: This year, because the liability was incurred when the goods were supplied
options.misconception: answers from the mercantile system that 43B overrides
options.why: Accrual is exactly what section 43B suspends for its listed sums. Incurring the liability starts the story; only payment finishes it.

options.text: Never, as delayed MSME payments are disallowed permanently as a penalty
options.misconception: converts a timing provision into a permanent disallowance
options.why: Section 43B defers, it does not confiscate. The deduction arrives with the payment year — the cost of delay is timing and the MSMED interest, not the deduction itself.

items.scenario: At 31 March a trader owes ₹22 lakh to a registered micro enterprise for goods supplied in February on 30-day terms. He pays on 25 July, well before filing his return on 31 October, and claims the deduction this year, citing the familiar rule that payment before the return's due date preserves it.

items.stem: What consideration does section 50C adopt for each sale?

options.text: ₹100 lakh and ₹96 lakh — the stamp value always prevails when higher
options.misconception: applies the deeming without the tolerance band
options.why: The 110 per cent tolerance exists exactly for genuine small gaps like the first sale. Deeming there taxes a difference Parliament chose to ignore.

options.text: ₹92 lakh and ₹88 lakh — the second sale is deemed at exactly 110 per cent
options.misconception: caps the deeming at the tolerance line instead of the stamp value
options.why: The tolerance is a gate, not a ceiling. Once crossed, the full stamp value of ₹96 lakh becomes the consideration; ₹88 lakh is only where the gate stood.

options.text: ₹92 lakh for the first sale; ₹96 lakh for the second
options.why: The first sale's stamp value of ₹100 lakh sits within 110 per cent of ₹92 lakh (₹101.2 lakh), so the tolerance protects the actual price. The second sale's ₹96 lakh exceeds 110 per cent of ₹80 lakh (₹88 lakh), so the deeming replaces the consideration in full — not merely the excess.

options.text: ₹92 lakh and ₹80 lakh — actual consideration governs capital gains
options.misconception: ignores the deeming provision entirely
options.why: Section 50C exists because understated property prices are the oldest trick in the book. Outside the tolerance, the stamp value is the consideration whether or not more money moved.

items.scenario: An individual sells a plot for ₹92 lakh. The stamp duty authority values it at ₹100 lakh for registration. In a second sale the same year, another plot fetches ₹80 lakh against a stamp value of ₹96 lakh.

items.stem: What is the consequence in the firm's computation?

options.text: The full ₹20 lakh is disallowed until the default is made good
options.misconception: applies the old full-disallowance rule or the non-resident clause
options.why: Hundred per cent disallowance is the pre-2014 history of this clause and remains the rule for payments abroad under 40(a)(i). For residents, Parliament softened it to thirty.

options.text: ₹6 lakh is disallowed permanently as the price of the default
options.misconception: reads a timing disallowance as a forfeiture
options.why: The clause's second limb restores the amount in the payment year. The cost of default is deferral and interest under the TDS chapter, not permanent loss.

options.text: ₹6 lakh is disallowed this year, and returns as a deduction in the year the TDS is paid
options.why: Section 40(a)(ia) disallows thirty per cent of the sum on which tax went undeducted, and the disallowance is temporary — the year the tax is finally deposited, the thirty per cent comes back. Genuineness of the expense never enters this section's arithmetic.

options.text: Nothing is disallowed, since the expense is genuine and evidenced
options.misconception: treats genuineness as answering a withholding default
options.why: The section polices deduction of tax, not the truth of the expense. The most genuine payment in the books still loses thirty per cent for the default.

items.scenario: A firm pays ₹20 lakh as contract charges to a resident contractor during the year and deducts no tax at source. The books are otherwise clean and the expense is genuine and fully evidenced.

items.stem: How much 54EC exemption does she actually get?

options.text: ₹65 lakh — the whole land gain, since she invested more than that
options.misconception: accepts the asset gate but misses the monetary cap
options.why: Right asset, right window, but the section counts only fifty lakh of the investment. The remaining ₹15 lakh of gain is taxed at the long-term rate.

options.text: ₹1.35 crore — the full amount invested within six months
options.misconception: reads the six-month window as the only condition
options.why: Timing is necessary, not sufficient. The asset-class gate and the fifty-lakh cap operate on top of it, and here they cut the claim by more than half.

options.text: ₹1 crore — fifty lakh against each of the two gains
options.misconception: applies the cap per asset instead of per financial year
options.why: The fifty-lakh ceiling is on investment in the financial year, not per transfer — and the share gain was never eligible, whatever the cap.

options.text: ₹50 lakh, against the land gain only
options.why: Two gates close most of the claim: 54EC covers only gains from land or building, so the share gain is out entirely, and the investment that counts is capped at fifty lakh in a financial year. Of the ₹65 lakh land gain, ₹50 lakh is exempt and the rest is taxed.

items.scenario: An individual sells listed shares in June, realising a long-term gain of ₹70 lakh, and a plot of land in July, realising a long-term gain of ₹65 lakh. In September she invests ₹1.35 crore in NHAI-class 54EC bonds and claims exemption for both gains in full.

items.stem: What does opting into 115BAA actually cost the company?

options.text: All three go — the incentives are surrendered, and with MAT inapplicable the MAT credit lapses
options.why: The concessional rate is bought by giving up the specified incentives, unabsorbed additional depreciation and profit-linked deductions among them. MAT not applying sounds like relief but also means the accumulated credit has nothing to set against — which is why companies with large credits often wait before opting.

options.text: Only a timing cost — the option can be dropped in a lean year and retaken later
options.misconception: treats an irrevocable option as an annual election
options.why: Once exercised, the option applies to that year and all subsequent years. Walking out in a lean year is exactly the flexibility the section withholds.

options.text: The deductions go, but the MAT credit survives to offset the new liability
options.misconception: keeps a credit born of a levy the company has left
options.why: MAT credit exists to smooth MAT paid against regular tax. Under 115BAA there is no MAT at all, and the credit cannot cross into a regime that never charges it.

options.text: Nothing — the lower rate and the incentives run together
options.misconception: prices the option at zero
options.why: Parliament's bargain is rate for incentives. A company keeping both would make the regular regime pointless for everyone.

items.scenario: A manufacturing company weighing the 115BAA option has ₹12 crore of unabsorbed additional depreciation, sizeable MAT credit carried forward, and a claim under a profit-linked deduction. The CFO believes the company can opt in, enjoy twenty-two per cent, and still use all three.

items.stem: What survives the change in ownership?

options.text: Neither — every carried-forward claim dies with the change in control
options.misconception: sweeps depreciation into a section that never mentions it
options.why: Section 79 speaks of "loss". Unabsorbed depreciation merges into the next year's depreciation under its own section and survives ownership changes untouched.

options.text: Both, provided the new owners continue the same line of business
options.misconception: imports the old business-continuity idea into a shareholding test
options.why: Continuity of business matters in other places; section 79's test is continuity of voting power. Running the identical trade with new owners fails it just the same.

options.text: Only the ₹4 crore of unabsorbed depreciation — section 79 kills the business loss
options.why: With 70 per cent changing hands, the 51 per cent continuity test fails and the business loss cannot be carried forward and set off. Unabsorbed depreciation travels under section 32(2), not section 79, and courts have consistently kept it outside the shareholding test — which is why acquirers price the two very differently.

options.text: Both — losses belong to the company, and the company has not changed
options.misconception: stops at separate legal personality
options.why: Separate personality is exactly what section 79 overrides for closely held companies. The section exists because buying a shell for its losses is trading in tax attributes, and Parliament closed that market.

items.scenario: A closely held trading company has ₹10 crore of carried-forward business loss and ₹4 crore of unabsorbed depreciation. During the year, promoters holding 70 per cent sell their entire stake to a new investor group. The new owners plan to set both amounts off against this year's profits.

items.stem: Who is right?

options.text: The adviser — a treaty overrides domestic law without further formality
options.misconception: quotes the override while skipping the statutory condition on it
options.why: The override itself flows through section 90, and Parliament wrote the TRC condition into the same section. The gate and the door come as a set.

options.text: Neither — the company must always pay the higher of the two rates
options.misconception: inverts the beneficial-provision rule
options.why: Section 90(2) says the treaty applies to the extent it is more beneficial. Higher-of-the -two is the one reading the section forbids.

options.text: The adviser, provided the company files an Indian return declaring residence in Singapore
options.misconception: substitutes self-declaration for the other state's certificate
options.why: The certificate must come from the government of the residence country — that is the point of it. Form 10F supplements a TRC; nothing the taxpayer signs replaces one.

options.text: The officer — section 90(4) makes the TRC a condition for claiming any treaty benefit
options.why: The beneficial-treaty rule in section 90(2) is real, but subsection (4) hangs a key on the door: a certificate of residence from the other government. Without it the company cannot invoke the treaty at all, and the Act's rate applies until the certificate is obtained.

items.scenario: A Singapore company earns fees from India that the treaty taxes at 10 per cent but the Act taxes at a higher rate. It has no tax residency certificate. Its adviser says the treaty rate applies automatically because treaties override the Act; the tax officer says treaty benefit is barred without the certificate.

items.stem: Can the addition under section 68 stand?

options.text: Yes, but taxed at normal slab rates with business losses set off
options.misconception: adds the income but forgets 115BBE's special regime
options.why: Section 115BBE exists to make unexplained money expensive: sixty per cent plus surcharge, and no deduction or loss set-off. Slab treatment would make an addition under section 68 cheaper than declaring the income honestly.

options.text: No, because money received by cheque can never be a cash credit
options.misconception: confuses the credit's mode with its explanation
options.why: Section 68 speaks of any sum credited; the cheque is merely how it travelled. Unexplained money does not launder itself by passing through one bank account.

options.text: Yes — for closely held share capital, the resident investor's own source must also satisfy the officer
options.why: The proviso to section 68 makes the source of the source part of the company's burden for share application money from residents. A banking trail that begins with unexplained cash explains nothing; the addition stands and 115BBE prices it at sixty per cent plus surcharge, with no losses set off against it.

options.text: No — identity, genuineness and creditworthiness were all evidenced
options.misconception: applies the classic three-limb test without the share-capital proviso
options.why: The three limbs remain the law for ordinary credits. For closely held companies' share capital, Parliament added the fourth question, and the cash deposit is where this explanation dies.

items.scenario: A closely held company shows ₹2 crore of fresh share capital from a resident investor. Asked to explain, it produces the investor's confirmation, PAN and bank statement showing the cheque — but the investor's account received ₹2 crore in cash days before investing, and he offers no explanation of where that came from. The company argues its own burden ended with identity, genuineness and the banking channel.

items.stem: How does the clubbing fall in year two?

options.text: Nothing clubs — the gift was genuine and she is assessed on her own deposits
options.misconception: treats a genuine gift as adequate consideration
options.why: Genuineness was never the issue; consideration is. Love and affection make a gift real and still leave it without adequate consideration, which is the very case the section taxes to the transferor.

options.text: Both amounts club with the husband — everything traces back to his gift
options.misconception: follows the money forever instead of following the asset
options.why: The section stops at income from the transferred asset. Income on accumulated income is one step beyond its words, and the settled reading leaves it with the transferee.

options.text: Both amounts are the wife's, but the husband loses ₹30 lakh from his capital
options.misconception: imagines clubbing ends once the transfer is complete
options.why: The transfer is complete in property law; tax law keeps the income tethered to the transferor for as long as the marriage and the asset both subsist.

options.text: The ₹2.4 lakh on the gifted money clubs with the husband; the ₹18,000 on the reinvested interest is the wife's
options.why: Section 64(1)(iv) clubs income arising from the transferred asset — the ₹30 lakh — so its interest belongs to the husband year after year. The first year's interest, once earned, is the wife's own money; what it earns in turn is income from her asset, outside the clubbing.

items.scenario: A husband gifts his wife ₹30 lakh, which she puts in a fixed deposit earning ₹2.4 lakh interest in year one. She reinvests that interest in a second deposit, which itself earns ₹18,000 in year two. In year two, whose income is what?

items.stem: What does section 44AE actually presume for the year?

options.text: The same rates, but skipping the five workshop months
options.misconception: reads "per month" as per operating month
options.why: The words are months of ownership, and the scheme's bargain is bluntness. An assessee wanting his idle months recognised must leave the presumption, keep books and be audited.

options.text: ₹16,000 a month for each heavy vehicle and ₹7,500 for each light one, for all twelve months of ownership
options.why: The presumption runs on ownership, not operation: 16MT × ₹1,000 = ₹16,000 per heavy vehicle per month or part, ₹7,500 per light vehicle, for every month the vehicle was owned. The workshop months count in full — the section trades exactness for simplicity, in both directions.

options.text: ₹7,500 per vehicle across the fleet, heavy or light
options.misconception: misses the separate tonnage rate for heavy vehicles
options.why: The 2018 amendment split the rates: heavy goods vehicles earn the presumption by the ton. Flat-rating a 16MT lorry understates each heavy vehicle by more than half.

options.text: Nothing — six lorries make him ineligible, since the limit is five
options.misconception: shrinks the ten-carriage ceiling
options.why: Eligibility runs to ten goods carriages at any time during the year. Six is comfortably inside.

items.scenario: A transporter owned six lorries all year — two heavy vehicles of 16MT gross weight each and four light ones. One heavy vehicle stood in the workshop for five months after an accident. He computes presumptive income counting only the months each vehicle actually ran.

items.stem: Does GAAR reach this borrowing?

options.text: Yes — a tax benefit above three crore whose purpose test is met is automatically impermissible
options.misconception: collapses the two-limb test into the threshold
options.why: The three-crore line in Rule 10U is a floor below which GAAR is not invoked, not a trigger above which it applies. Above it, the tainted-element limb still has to be proved.

options.text: No — a real loan on arm's-length terms carries no tainted element, and choosing the tax-efficient route is permissible planning
options.why: GAAR needs both limbs: the main-purpose tax benefit and a tainted element. Genuine borrowing at market terms from a real lender, deployed in the business, misuses nothing and lacks no commercial substance. The Act itself makes interest deductible; using a provision as intended is planning, not avoidance, whatever the amount saved.

options.text: No, because GAAR applies only to cross-border arrangements
options.misconception: confines a general rule to international transactions
options.why: The chapter reaches any arrangement, domestic or foreign. This borrowing escapes on the merits — the missing tainted element — not on geography.

options.text: Yes, because the company admits tax drove the choice of debt over equity
options.misconception: makes motive alone sufficient
options.why: Every rational taxpayer weighs tax; section 96 demands more — dealings not at arm's length, misuse of provisions, absence of substance, or abnormal means. An ordinary loan exhibits none.

items.scenario: To fund expansion, a company chooses to borrow rather than issue equity because interest is deductible and dividends are not, saving ₹20 crore of tax over the loan's life. The assessing officer invokes GAAR: the financing was chosen mainly for the tax benefit, which exceeds three crore rupees.

items.stem: Is CUP the most appropriate method here?

options.text: No method applies — a transaction with no comparables is outside transfer pricing
options.misconception: reads absence of a comparable price as absence of an arm's length price
options.why: The methods exist to approximate arm's length outcomes precisely where direct prices are missing. Escaping the regime for want of comparables would exempt every captive arrangement — the core of what the regime polices.

options.text: Yes, because captive sales to a parent can never be tested by profit-based methods
options.misconception: excludes profit methods from exactly the situation they were designed for
options.why: A captive routine supplier is where transactional net margin thrives — its comparables are independent companies with similar functions, not identical products.

options.text: No — with no true comparable, a net margin method fits a routine manufacturer better than a heavily adjusted CUP
options.why: CUP's directness depends entirely on comparability; when adjustments do the real work, the method's precision is an illusion. Rule 10B asks for the most appropriate method, not the most direct-sounding — and a routine, intangible-free manufacturer is the textbook case for testing net margins against comparable companies.

options.text: Yes — the law ranks CUP first, so it applies whenever any comparison can be constructed
options.misconception: imports a hierarchy the Indian rules never adopted
