options.why: Section 92C lists methods without ranking them. The selection standard is appropriateness to the transaction and data; a constructed comparison fails that test exactly when the adjustments dominate.

items.scenario: An Indian subsidiary manufactures components sold only to its foreign parent; nothing identical trades between independents, and the subsidiary performs routine functions with no unique intangibles. The transfer pricing officer insists on the comparable uncontrolled price method as "the most direct", using a broadly similar product's price with heavy adjustments.

items.stem: What does the company actually pay, and what happens to the difference?

options.text: ₹6 crore — tax follows total income as computed under the Act
options.misconception: computes tax as if MAT did not exist
options.why: MAT exists because companies with healthy book profits and skilful deductions were paying near zero. The book-profit floor is precisely for this fact pattern.

options.text: ₹6 crore now, with ₹9 crore payable only if book profits persist three years
options.misconception: invents an averaging test the section does not contain
options.why: The comparison is annual and unconditional: each year stands alone, higher of the two numbers, no waiting period.

options.text: About ₹15 crore — fifteen per cent of book profit — with the ₹9 crore excess carried as MAT credit for up to fifteen years
options.why: Section 115JB compares regular tax with fifteen per cent of book profit and collects the higher. The extra ₹9 crore is not lost: it rides forward as credit, usable in years when regular tax exceeds MAT, for fifteen assessment years — a prepayment, provided the company stays in the MAT regime long enough to use it.

options.text: ₹15 crore, gone for good — MAT is a penalty for excessive deductions
options.misconception: reads a timing levy as a punishment
options.why: The credit mechanism is the section's other half. MAT accelerates tax; over the cycle the credit hands the acceleration back against future regular liability.

items.scenario: A company under the regular regime reports book profit of ₹100 crore but, thanks to accelerated depreciation and deductions, total income of just ₹20 crore. Regular tax on ₹20 crore comes to about ₹6 crore. The CFO budgets ₹6 crore for the year's tax.

items.stem: How does section 270A actually apply to the two additions?

options.text: No penalty on either if the company pays the tax and interest demanded
options.misconception: stretches 270AA immunity over misreporting
options.why: Payment-and-no-appeal immunity exists for under-reporting cases. The provision expressly withholds it where the penalty arises from misreporting — the bogus bills stay exposed.

options.text: Fifty per cent on both, since both were disclosed somewhere in the books
options.misconception: lets book entries of fake bills count as disclosure
options.why: Recording a false invoice is not disclosing a fact; it is the false entry itself — the statute's own example of misreporting. Disclosure saves the debatable claim, not the fabricated one.

options.text: The disclosed debatable claim may escape penalty entirely; the bogus bills draw two hundred per cent
options.why: A claim made with full disclosure and a bona fide explanation sits in the section's carve-outs from under-reported income — losing a debatable point is not under-reporting. False entries are named misreporting, and misreporting is priced at two hundred per cent with no 270AA immunity available.

options.text: Two hundred per cent on both — every addition sustained is misreporting
options.misconception: erases the section's central two-tier design
options.why: The section splits honest-but-wrong from dishonest, at fifty and two hundred per cent, with carve-outs before either. Flattening it to the top rate restores the arbitrariness the old penalty regime was replaced to end.

items.scenario: Two additions survive a company's assessment: ₹1 crore disallowed because the officer read a genuinely debatable provision differently, with the company's claim fully disclosed in the return's notes; and ₹60 lakh of purchases that proved to be bogus bills from a non-existent vendor. The officer proposes two hundred per cent penalty on the tax on both.

items.stem: Can the revision stand?

options.text: No — after real enquiry, a possible view is not erroneous, and prejudice alone cannot carry a revision
options.why: Section 263 needs error and prejudice together. The officer asked, received, weighed and reasoned; that his conclusion favoured the assessee makes it prejudicial in the Commissioner's eyes, but a plausible view after enquiry is not error. Revision on preference would make every assessment provisional.

options.text: Yes — any order that collects less tax than it might is prejudicial, which suffices
options.misconception: reads one condition where the section writes two
options.why: Prejudice without error covers half the section's text. Both limbs are conditions, and the enquiry on record defeats the first.

options.text: Yes, because share premium acceptance is inherently a high-risk error
options.misconception: substitutes the issue's risk profile for the order's actual defect
options.why: Risk explains why enquiry was needed; the record shows it happened. Section 263 reviews what the officer did, not how dangerous the topic sounds.

options.text: No, because the Commissioner can never revise a completed assessment
options.misconception: denies the power instead of its limits
options.why: The power is real and regularly used — above all where the officer made no enquiry at all. This order survives on its record, not on any immunity.

items.scenario: An assessing officer examined a large share premium during assessment — issued a questionnaire, received valuation reports and investor confirmations, discussed them in the order — and accepted the premium. The Commissioner, reviewing later, would have added it, and invokes section 263 on the ground that the acceptance cost the revenue tax.

items.stem: What does section 94B actually do to the ₹40 crore?

options.text: All ₹40 crore deducts if the loan's interest rate is proven arm's length
options.misconception: answers a thin-cap section with a transfer pricing defence
options.why: Section 94B assumes the rate is fine and attacks the quantum of debt instead. Arm's length pricing answers 92C; the EBITDA cap applies on top of it.

options.text: Nothing deducts — interest to related non-residents above one crore is disallowed outright
options.misconception: turns the threshold into a cliff
options.why: One crore is the gate below which the section ignores you, not a line beyond which everything falls. Past the gate, the EBITDA formula does the limiting.

options.text: ₹30 crore deducts this year; ₹10 crore carries forward up to eight years; TDS runs on the full ₹40 crore regardless
options.why: The cap is thirty per cent of EBITDA — ₹30 crore — and the excess is not lost but parked, deductible within the cap in the next eight years. The section only limits the payer's deduction; the interest is still paid, still the non-resident's income, and still bears withholding in full.

options.text: ₹30 crore deducts and TDS applies only to that deductible portion
options.misconception: lets the payer's cap shrink the payee's income
options.why: Withholding follows the payment, not the deduction. The disallowed ₹10 crore is still interest paid to a non-resident, taxable in its hands and withheld on accordingly.

items.scenario: An Indian subsidiary pays ₹40 crore interest to its foreign parent. Its EBITDA is ₹100 crore. The CFO fears the entire ₹40 crore is lost as a deduction; the tax head counters that at least the section leaves TDS obligations lighter on the disallowed part.

items.stem: Does SEP catch the platform?

options.text: No, because digital services can never have an Indian business connection
options.misconception: right answer, mistaken ground
options.why: Domestically, SEP creates exactly that business connection — thresholds crossed, the hook holds. What saves the platform is the treaty override, not any gap in section 9.

options.text: Yes, because streaming into India constitutes a virtual permanent establishment
options.misconception: invents a PE category the treaty does not contain
options.why: PE under the treaty means fixed places, dependent agents and the like. Virtual presence concepts live in domestic law and multilateral proposals, not in the operative treaty text.

options.text: No — the treaty's permanent establishment article governs a treaty resident, and SEP cannot override it
options.why: Section 90(2) lets the taxpayer take the treaty where more beneficial, and the treaty taxes business profits only through a permanent establishment — which needs more than users and revenue. SEP rewrote the domestic definition of business connection, not the treaty; its practical reach is non-treaty jurisdictions, and this platform is not one.

options.text: Yes — SEP was enacted precisely to tax digital businesses like this one
options.misconception: reads the purpose while skipping the treaty ceiling
options.why: The purpose is real and the domestic hook now exists — but a treaty resident claims the treaty, and business profits without a PE stay untaxed here until the treaty itself changes.

items.scenario: A US-based streaming platform with no office, server or staff in India earns large subscription revenue from Indian users, crossing the significant economic presence thresholds. The platform is entitled to the India-US tax treaty. The assessing officer taxes its profits, holding that the SEP amendment overrides treaties as later domestic law.

items.stem: Where do you stand under Clause 8?

options.text: Not guilty — he communicated, and the outgoing auditor raised no objection
options.misconception: reads the clause as requiring communication in any form
options.why: Form is the substance here. A telephone call leaves nothing to show what was asked or answered, which is why the clause specifies writing.

options.text: Guilty, because the fee dispute meant he needed the outgoing auditor's consent
options.misconception: converts communication into permission
options.why: No consent is ever required — an outgoing auditor cannot veto a successor. Unpaid fees are a fact to weigh, not a bar. The failure is only the missing writing.

options.text: Guilty — the communication must be in writing, and a phone call is not that
options.why: The clause's words are "without first communicating with him in writing". The conversation happened and even produced no objection, but the safeguard the clause builds — a record that the incoming auditor asked and what he was told — exists only on paper. Oral communication, however cordial, is the misconduct.

options.text: Not guilty if he now sends a letter confirming the earlier call
options.misconception: backdates a safeguard that must come before acceptance
options.why: The clause says "first" — the writing must precede acceptance. A confirming letter after the appointment records the breach; it does not repair it.

items.scenario: A company removes its auditor and approaches you. You telephone the outgoing auditor, who says he has no objection but warns you the client disputes his fees. You accept the audit the next day, and a month later the outgoing auditor complains to the Institute that you never wrote to him.

items.stem: What may you tell the competitor client, and what must you give the tax officer?

options.text: Tell the competitor only what it could eventually learn from public filings
options.misconception: discloses early and calls it harmless
options.why: A pending negotiation is not public, and its value lies in the timing. What might become public later is still confidential now, and now is when you would be telling it.

options.text: Both — a firm owes each client the benefit of everything the firm knows
options.misconception: treats the firm's knowledge as a pooled asset of its clients
options.why: The information belongs to the engagement it came from. Pooling it is the precise disclosure the clause forbids, and would end professional confidence between auditor and client.

options.text: Nothing to the competitor; the summoned papers to the officer — legal compulsion is the exception, another client's interest is not
options.why: Clause 1 permits disclosure only with the client's consent or where law requires it. A statutory summons is the law requiring it. The competitor's commercial appetite is nothing at all — serving two clients does not merge their entitlement to what you learned from each.

options.text: Neither — auditor confidentiality is absolute, like privilege, and beats the summons
options.misconception: promotes a professional duty into a legal privilege
options.why: The clause itself carves out disclosure required by law. Defying a valid summons is not loyalty; it is contempt with a confidentiality label.

items.scenario: During an audit you discover your client is negotiating to buy a supplier. Another client of your firm competes with that supplier and would dearly want to know. Separately, an income-tax summons under section 131 requires you to produce the client's working papers.

items.stem: Does the disclosure save the engagement?

options.text: No — the clause bars the opinion itself where the firm or any partner has substantial interest, and disclosure is no cure
options.why: Clause 4 reaches "he, his firm, or a partner in his firm". One partner's 30 per cent poisons every signature the firm can produce, and the clause prohibits expressing the opinion — a prominent confession of the conflict still expresses it. Independence questions of this kind are answered by declining.

options.text: No, but the firm may accept if the partner undertakes to sell the shares within the year
options.misconception: audits first, becomes independent later
options.why: Independence is tested when the opinion is given. A promise to divest afterwards means the opinion was expressed while the interest stood — which is the whole offence.

options.text: Yes, provided the interested partner takes no part in the audit work
options.misconception: builds an information wall the clause does not recognise
options.why: The prohibition follows the interest, not the staffing chart. The firm profits from the fee and the partner from the company; no allocation of files changes either.

options.text: Yes — transparency lets the reader discount the opinion appropriately
options.misconception: substitutes disclosure for independence
options.why: Disclosure manages many things; this clause is not one of them. An opinion from an interested firm is worthless even when labelled, because the reader cannot un-know the auditor wanted a particular answer.

items.scenario: A two-partner firm is offered the audit of a private company in which one partner holds 30 per cent of the shares. The other partner proposes to sign the report personally, disclosing the shareholding prominently in the audit report so readers can weigh it.

items.stem: Is he guilty under Clause 7?

options.text: Yes — certifying without examination is gross negligence, and honesty is no defence to it
options.why: Clause 7 punishes the absence of due diligence, not the presence of dishonesty. A certificate tells the world the certifier verified; signing on the manager's say-so means he verified nothing. Good faith and a small fee measure his intentions, not his diligence.

options.text: No — reliance on management representations is an accepted audit technique
options.misconception: stretches a corroborating tool into a substitute for evidence
options.why: Representations support evidence; they never replace it. Where a certificate rests on nothing but the interested party's own statement, the technique has become the abdication.

options.text: No — without fraudulent intent there can be no professional misconduct
options.misconception: imports a mens rea requirement the clause deliberately omits
options.why: The Second Schedule separates dishonesty offences from negligence offences precisely so that careless certification is punishable on its own. Clause 7 is the negligence limb.

options.text: Yes, but only because the figures proved wrong — accurate figures would have cleared him
options.misconception: judges diligence by outcome
options.why: The breach was complete when he signed unverified. Figures that happened to be right would have been luck, and luck is not diligence.

items.scenario: A chartered accountant certifies the circulation figures of a newspaper for an advertising body, relying entirely on a statement prepared by the newspaper's manager, without checking the print orders, newsprint consumption, or dispatch records. The figures turn out inflated. He argues he acted honestly and charged a modest fee.

items.stem: Which engagements does Clause 11 permit?

options.text: None — a member in practice can hold no position in any company or business
options.misconception: erases the proviso and the permission routes
options.why: The clause's own proviso protects the plain board seat, and the Council's general permissions cover more. Absolute prohibition is the one reading the text itself contradicts.

options.text: Only the second — the trading partnership needs Council permission, and the auditor link poisons the third
options.why: Active business alongside practice is what the clause gates behind Council permission, and a working partnership in trade does not enjoy any general permission. A directorship simpliciter is saved by the proviso — but the proviso itself withdraws the saving where the member or any partner audits the company, which sinks the third.

options.text: All three — what a member does outside office hours is his own affair
options.misconception: reads professional exclusivity as a working-hours rule
options.why: The clause regulates occupation, not timetable. Divided commercial interests compromise independence at any hour, which is why permission is the Council's to give.

options.text: The second and third — directorships are always within the proviso
options.misconception: stops reading the proviso before its exception
options.why: The proviso saves directorship simpliciter "unless he or any of his partners is interested in such company as an auditor". The third scenario is that exception in terms.

items.scenario: A practising chartered accountant (1) joins his family's textile trading business as a working partner, without asking the Institute; (2) accepts an ordinary directorship in a listed company his firm does not audit; and (3) is offered a directorship in a company where his partner is the auditor.

items.stem: Is the CA guilty under Clause 10?

options.text: Yes, but only if the client account shortfall exceeded a reasonable float
options.misconception: invents a de minimis buffer the clause does not offer
options.why: The clause has no tolerance band. Separate account, intended use, reasonable time — each is absolute, and the salaries payment breached the second outright.

options.text: No — the tax was paid on time and the client lost nothing
options.misconception: measures the offence by the ending
options.why: The clause protects the arrangement, not just the outcome. A trustee who borrows the trust fund and wins is still a trustee who borrowed the trust fund.

options.text: No, because money handed voluntarily to a professional becomes his to manage
options.misconception: converts custody into ownership
options.why: The money was received for a stated purpose — that is custody. Fees belong to the firm; the client's tax money never did.

options.text: Yes, twice over — the money never entered a separate client account, and it was used for foreign purposes meanwhile
options.why: Money received to be expended for the client must sit in a separate banking account until spent as intended. The office account was the wrong pocket from day one, and paying salaries from it was use for a purpose never intended. Restoration and the punctual June deposit mitigate; they do not undo either limb.

items.scenario: A client hands a practising CA ₹12 lakh in March to deposit toward the client's advance tax in June. The CA parks the sum in the firm's office account, uses part of it through April to pay office salaries, restores the full amount in May, and deposits the tax on time in June. No fee remains unpaid and the client suffers no loss.

items.stem: How much revenue does the manufacturer recognise for the year ended 31 March 2026?

options.text: Revenue for the 60 per cent the agent has sold to end customers
options.why: Control of consigned goods does not pass on despatch — the agent can return them and holds them for the manufacturer. Control passes when the agent sells to a customer, so only those units have satisfied a performance obligation under Ind AS 115.

options.text: Revenue spread evenly over the consignment period
options.misconception: converts a point-in-time obligation into an over-time one without meeting any criterion
options.why: Over-time recognition needs one of the Ind AS 115 criteria — the customer consuming the benefit as the entity performs, or the entity creating an asset the customer controls. A consignment of finished goods meets none of them.

options.text: Revenue for the full despatch, since the goods have left the premises
options.misconception: treats despatch as sale, the recognition trigger Ind AS 115 replaced
options.why: Despatch moves the goods, not control. The agent has no obligation to pay for unsold units and can return them, so the manufacturer still controls them.

options.text: No revenue until the agent remits the money
options.misconception: uses receipt of cash as the recognition trigger
options.why: Collection is a separate matter from recognition. Once control of a unit has passed to an end customer, the obligation is satisfied whether or not the agent has remitted.

items.scenario: A manufacturer despatches goods to a consignment agent on 28 March 2026. The agent holds the goods, can return any unsold units, and sells to end customers on the manufacturer's behalf. By 31 March the agent has sold 60 per cent of the units to customers.

items.stem: Which inventory cost formula does Ind AS 2 not permit?

options.text: Specific identification
options.misconception: forgets the formula required for non-interchangeable items
options.why: Specific identification is not merely permitted — it is required where items are not ordinarily interchangeable, such as goods segregated for a specific project.

options.text: LIFO
options.why: Ind AS 2 allows specific identification for non-interchangeable items, and FIFO or weighted average for the rest. LIFO is expressly not an option — in a rising price environment it books the newest, dearest cost first and leaves inventory at stale values.

options.text: Weighted average
options.misconception: assumes averaging is imprecise and therefore barred
options.why: Weighted average is the other permitted formula for interchangeable items.

options.text: FIFO
options.misconception: confuses the permitted default with the prohibited formula
options.why: FIFO is one of the two formulas permitted for interchangeable items.

items.stem: Does the company control the investee under Ind AS 110?

options.text: No, but the investee is a joint venture
options.misconception: mislabels one-sided board control as joint control
options.why: Joint control requires unanimous consent of the sharing parties over relevant activities. A right to appoint four of seven directors is unilateral, not shared.

options.text: No, the 45 per cent holding gives significant influence and equity accounting
options.misconception: stops at the shareholding percentage and applies the associate test
options.why: Significant influence is the fallback when control is absent. Here the board rights give actual power, so the investee is a subsidiary and is consolidated.

options.text: No, because control requires holding more than half the voting power
options.misconception: equates control with majority shareholding
options.why: Majority voting power is one route to power, not the definition of it. Ind AS 110 was written precisely to catch control held through other means.

options.text: Yes — it has power through the board rights, variable returns, and the link between them
options.why: All three elements of control are present. Power does not have to come from a majority of shares; a contractual right to appoint the majority of the board directs the relevant activities just as effectively.

items.scenario: A company holds 45 per cent of the voting shares of an investee. A shareholders' agreement gives it the contractual right to appoint four of the seven directors, and its returns vary with the investee's performance.

items.stem: What does Ind AS 109 require instead?

options.text: An allowance once a receivable is more than 90 days overdue
options.misconception: imports the banking overdue norms into financial reporting
options.why: Ninety days is a prudential banking classification, not an Ind AS measurement rule. There is a rebuttable presumption of default at 90 days past due, but the allowance exists long before that.

options.text: A 12-month expected credit loss allowance unless credit risk has increased significantly
options.misconception: applies the general staging model where the simplified approach governs
options.why: The two-stage general model applies to loans and debt investments. Trade receivables take the simplified approach, which is lifetime losses without a staging test.

options.text: A lifetime expected credit loss allowance on trade receivables from initial recognition
options.why: Ind AS 109 replaced the incurred-loss model with expected credit losses, recognised before any default. For trade receivables the simplified approach removes the staging debate entirely — the allowance is always lifetime expected losses.

options.text: The company's policy is compliant, since losses should not be anticipated
options.misconception: defends the incurred-loss model the standard replaced
options.why: Waiting for the loss event is exactly what Ind AS 109 abolished. Expected losses are an estimate of the future, made from the first day the receivable exists.

items.scenario: A company recognises a loss allowance on trade receivables only when a customer has actually defaulted, on the ground that anything earlier would be providing for losses that have not happened.

items.stem: Where does the ₹8 crore gain go under Ind AS 103?

options.text: Other comprehensive income, accumulated in capital reserve
options.why: This is the Indian carve-out. IFRS 3 takes a bargain purchase gain to profit or loss; Ind AS 103 routes it through other comprehensive income into capital reserve, keeping a purchase discount out of earnings.

options.text: Reduced from the values of the assets acquired
options.misconception: treats the gain as a measurement error to be spread over assets
options.why: Reassessment happens first, and this scenario says it already has. Once the measurements stand, the difference is a recognised gain, not an allocation.

options.text: Deferred and amortised to profit or loss over five years
options.misconception: invents an amortisation treatment the standard does not contain
options.why: Nothing in Ind AS 103 spreads a bargain purchase gain over time. It is recognised at once, in other comprehensive income.

options.text: Profit or loss immediately
options.misconception: applies the IFRS 3 treatment where the Indian carve-out differs
options.why: Correct under IFRS 3, and the classic trap in an Ind AS paper. The carve-out exists precisely because recognising acquisition-day gains in earnings was thought unsuitable.

items.scenario: A company acquires a business for ₹70 crore when the fair value of identifiable net assets acquired is ₹78 crore. After reassessing the identification and measurement, the ₹8 crore difference remains.

items.stem: How is revenue recognised on the two contracts?

options.text: Both at a point in time, on completion of each project
options.misconception: defaults everything to completion without testing the over-time criteria
options.why: The factory meets two routes into over-time recognition. Deferring it all to completion would misstate every year the construction spans.

options.text: Both over time, because construction contracts are always percentage-of-completion
options.misconception: carries the old AS 7 reflex into a standard that tests criteria, not contract type
options.why: There is no contract-type rule any more. Each contract is tested against the para 35 criteria, and the flats fail them — alternative use exists and payment rights do not.

options.text: The flats over time, since forty units means performance is continuous
options.misconception: reads continuous physical work as continuous transfer of control
options.why: Continuous effort is not the test — continuous transfer of control is. Buyers of the flats control nothing until handover, however steadily the builder works.

options.text: The factory over time; the flats at a point in time on handover
options.why: The factory sits on the customer's land — the customer controls the asset as it is built — and there is an enforceable right to payment for work to date, so the over-time criteria are met. The flats have an alternative use to the builder and carry no right to payment before handover, so control passes only then.

items.scenario: A builder constructs a customised factory on the customer's own land. The contract entitles the builder to payment for work completed to date, including a reasonable margin, if the customer terminates. A separate contract in the same year is for 40 identical flats built on the builder's land, saleable to anyone, with payment only on handover.

items.stem: Is a provision recognised at 31 March 2026?

options.text: Yes, as a contingent liability measured at ₹18 crore
options.misconception: recognises a contingent liability instead of disclosing it
options.why: Contingent liabilities are never recognised on the balance sheet; they are disclosed. Recognition and disclosure are different acts, and this scenario earns neither a provision nor, before any obligation exists, a disclosure.

options.text: Yes, because the decision is formal, detailed and reliably costed
options.misconception: treats an internal decision as the obligating event
options.why: Formality and a reliable estimate satisfy other conditions, but the first condition — a present obligation — fails. An unannounced plan binds nobody, not even the company.

options.text: No — without announcement or commencement there is no constructive obligation yet
options.why: A provision needs a present obligation from a past event. A board decision alone creates none: the company can still change its mind. The obligating event arrives only when the plan is announced to those affected or implementation begins, creating a valid expectation.

options.text: No, but the ₹18 crore must be set aside as a reserve out of profits
options.misconception: substitutes an appropriation of profit for a liability test
options.why: Reserves are appropriations decided by the company; provisions are liabilities decided by the standard's criteria. Failing the liability test does not create an appropriation requirement.

items.scenario: In March 2026 a company's board resolves to close a loss-making division next year. The plan is detailed and costed at ₹18 crore, but nothing has been announced to anyone affected by 31 March.

items.stem: How is the ₹8 crore accounted for?

options.text: Deferred as a prepaid expense and spread over five years
options.misconception: parks a component of PPE in prepayments
options.why: Spreading over five years is the right rhythm but the wrong home. The cost belongs in the vessel's carrying amount as a component with its own depreciation, not in current assets.

options.text: Charged to profit or loss, since an inspection is maintenance
options.misconception: files a capitalisable overhaul under routine repairs
options.why: Day-to-day servicing is expensed. A five-yearly dry-docking required for the licence is not servicing — it purchases five more years of operation, which is an asset.

options.text: Capitalised, but nothing derecognised because the old inspection was never recognised separately
options.misconception: lets poor componentisation at purchase block the derecognition
options.why: The standard anticipates exactly this and directs an estimate — the cost of the new inspection is the indication of what the old one was. Skipping derecognition would carry two inspections in one carrying amount.

options.text: Capitalised into the vessel, with the ₹1.5 crore remnant of the old inspection derecognised
options.why: A major inspection that is a condition of operating is a component in its own right. The new cost enters the carrying amount and is depreciated to the next dry-docking; the previous inspection's remnant leaves, and Ind AS 16 says this holds even where that cost was never separately identified at acquisition.

items.scenario: A shipping company must dry-dock each vessel every five years as a condition of its licence. This year's dry-docking of one vessel costs ₹8 crore. The previous dry-docking, done by the seller before the vessel was purchased, was never identified as a separate component; its estimated remaining carrying amount is ₹1.5 crore.

items.stem: How are the two items translated at the year end?

options.text: The receivable moves to ₹86, with the gain deferred until the customer actually pays
options.misconception: holds unrealised exchange gains out of income
options.why: Ind AS 21 recognises exchange differences on monetary items in profit or loss in the period they arise. Realisation is not the trigger; the rate movement is.

options.text: The receivable moves to ₹86 with a ₹8 lakh gain in profit or loss; the inventory stays at ₹82
options.why: The receivable is a monetary item — a right to receive currency — so it takes the closing rate and its difference goes to profit or loss. Inventory is non-monetary at historical cost, frozen at the transaction-date rate, subject only to its own NRV test.

options.text: Both move to ₹86, since both arose in dollars
options.misconception: translates everything foreign at closing rate
options.why: The currency of origin is not the test; the monetary character is. Restating inventory for exchange movements would revalue an asset the standard keeps at cost.

options.text: Both stay at ₹82, the rate at which they were recorded
options.misconception: freezes monetary items at the transaction rate
options.why: A dollar claim is worth what dollars are worth today. Leaving the receivable at ₹82 hides a real ₹8 lakh of value the reporting date has already delivered.

items.scenario: At 31 March a company holds a $200,000 trade receivable booked at ₹82, and inventory imported during the year for $100,000 also booked at ₹82. The closing rate is ₹86.

items.stem: Can the internally built brand be recognised?

options.text: No — internally generated brands are expressly barred from recognition
options.why: Ind AS 38 bars internally generated brands, mastheads and customer lists because their cost cannot be told apart from the cost of growing the business as a whole. The rivals' brands sit on balance sheets because they were bought — a transaction gives them a cost.

options.text: Yes, at fair value determined by an independent brand valuer
options.misconception: substitutes valuation for the prohibited recognition
options.why: A valuer can price what the standard will not recognise. Fair value is a measurement basis, and measurement never arises for an asset barred at the recognition step.

options.text: No, but the ₹12 crore can be carried as deferred marketing expenditure
options.misconception: parks a barred asset under a different label
options.why: Deferred expenditure with no recognisable asset behind it is the same asset in a different coat. The spending is expense in the year it is incurred.

options.text: Yes, at the ₹12 crore actually spent, since the cost is reliably measured
options.misconception: treats measurable spending as satisfying recognition
options.why: The bar is not about measurement difficulty alone; it is absolute for these items. The standard refuses the asset however tidy the cost records are.

items.scenario: A consumer company spends ₹12 crore during the year building its flagship brand through design, promotion and market position, and its finance team proposes recognising the brand as an intangible asset, pointing to rival companies whose acquired brands sit on their balance sheets.

items.stem: Which segments must be reported separately?

options.text: Only the first two, since only they cross ten per cent
options.misconception: stops at the thresholds and misses the 75 per cent floor
options.why: The thresholds select; the floor then checks coverage. Passing the first test with 72 per cent coverage is precisely the case the second test exists to catch.

options.text: The first two on the thresholds, plus one more until reported segments cover 75 per cent
options.why: Crossing any ten per cent test makes the first two reportable, but para 15 adds a floor — reportable segments must carry at least 75 per cent of external revenue. At 72 per cent the entity keeps adding segments, threshold or not, until the floor is met.

options.text: Only the first, since it alone dominates the entity's results
options.misconception: reports the dominant segment and discards the tests entirely
options.why: Dominance is not the criterion — the ten per cent tests are, and the second segment crosses them. One-segment reporting would fail both the thresholds and the floor.

options.text: All four, because segments identified internally must all be reported
options.misconception: equates operating segments with reportable ones
options.why: Identification and reportability are different steps. Small segments can be aggregated or folded into an all-other column once the floor is satisfied.

items.scenario: A company has four operating segments. Segment revenues including inter-segment sales are ₹700, ₹150, ₹90 and ₹60 crore against a combined ₹1,000 crore. Only the first two cross any ten per cent test. External revenue of the first two together is 72 per cent of the entity's external revenue.

items.stem: How is the loan classified at 31 March?

options.text: Non-current, since the bank never actually demanded repayment
options.misconception: waits for the demand instead of testing the right
options.why: The test is the existence of the lender's right, not its exercise. A loan the bank could call today is current even if the bank stays friendly.

options.text: Split — current until the waiver date, non-current for the rest of the year
options.misconception: prorates a classification that is binary at one date
options.why: Classification speaks as at the reporting date, one date and one answer. There is no part-year presentation of the same liability.

options.text: Current — the waiver came after the reporting date, when the right to defer did not exist
options.why: Classification is tested on conditions existing at the reporting date. On 31 March the bank could demand repayment, so no right to defer settlement existed; the April waiver is a non-adjusting later event, disclosed rather than reclassified.

options.text: Non-current — the waiver arrived before the accounts were approved and restores the schedule
options.misconception: lets an approval-date event rewrite a reporting-date condition
options.why: The approval date matters for what is disclosed, not for what existed. At the year end the company stood exposed to demand, and the statements report the year end.

items.scenario: A company breaches a debt-equity covenant on its ₹120 crore term loan as at 31 March, making the loan repayable on demand. On 20 April, before the accounts are approved, the bank issues a formal waiver and confirms the original 2030 repayment schedule stands.

items.stem: How does Ind AS 7 classify the two flows for this company?

options.text: Interest paid as financing; interest received as investing
options.why: The Indian carve-out removed the IFRS options — for an entity that is not a financial institution, interest paid belongs to financing and interest received to investing, full stop. The accountant's rule is real IFRS and wrong Ind AS.

options.text: Both as operating, since IAS 7 permits it and Ind AS follows IFRS
options.misconception: assumes convergence means identity
options.why: Ind AS converges with carve-outs, and this is a named one. The options were removed precisely to make Indian cash flow statements comparable to each other.

options.text: Both as financing, since both concern borrowing and lending money
options.misconception: nets the two sides of treasury into one classification
options.why: Paying for capital and earning on deposits are different activities. The statement's whole purpose is keeping those directions apart.

options.text: The classification is the entity's accounting policy choice, applied consistently
options.misconception: preserves the choice the carve-out abolished
options.why: Consistency was IFRS's condition on a choice that Ind AS does not offer. For non-financial entities there is one answer, not a policy.

items.scenario: A manufacturing company paid ₹18 crore of interest on term loans and received ₹2 crore of interest on surplus deposits. Its accountant, trained on IFRS materials, classifies both as operating cash flows, noting that IAS 7 permits it.

items.stem: Which leases can stay off the balance sheet?

options.text: The warehouse and the laptops — nine months is under twelve
options.misconception: counts the months and misses the purchase-option bar
options.why: A lease with a purchase option is excluded from the short-term exemption by definition — the option signals the asset may never come back, which is not a short-term arrangement in substance.

options.text: Only the laptops — the warehouse's purchase option defeats the short-term exemption, and three years is simply long
options.why: The short-term election is barred where a purchase option exists, whatever the term's length, so the warehouse comes on. Three years of office space is outside every exemption. The laptops ride the low-value election, which is available asset by asset.

options.text: All three, by electing the exemptions across the portfolio
options.misconception: stretches two narrow elections into a general escape
options.why: The elections cover only what their conditions cover. Ind AS 116 exists because keeping ordinary leases off balance sheets is the outcome standard-setters buried.

options.text: None — Ind AS 116 abolished off-balance-sheet leases entirely
options.misconception: overcorrects past both stated exemptions
options.why: The two elections are in the standard's own text. The laptops are the case they were written for.

items.scenario: A company signs three agreements — a nine-month lease of a warehouse with an option to buy it at the term's end, a three-year lease of office space, and one-year leases of forty laptops of modest value. The CFO wants every one of them kept off the balance sheet.

items.stem: Is the impairment correct?

options.text: No impairment now, but the ₹15 crore excess of value in use must be written up as a gain
options.misconception: turns an impairment test into a revaluation
options.why: Ind AS 36 only writes down. Headroom above carrying amount is simply the absence of impairment; writing assets up is a different policy under a different standard.

options.text: No — recoverable amount is ₹85 crore, above carrying amount, so there is no impairment
options.why: Recoverable amount takes the higher of the two measures, and value in use at ₹85 crore beats fair value less costs of disposal at ₹70 crore. The entity is not obliged to sell; an asset worth more in use than on the block recovers its carrying amount by being used.

options.text: Yes — an asset cannot be carried above what it would fetch in the market
options.misconception: treats fair value as a ceiling on carrying amount
options.why: That ceiling belongs to assets held for sale. For assets held for use, Ind AS 36 lets value in use answer, precisely because a business often earns more from a plant than a buyer would pay for it.

options.text: Yes, but the loss is ₹5 crore, impairing down to the average of the two measures
options.misconception: splits the difference instead of taking the higher
options.why: Nothing in the standard averages the two. The comparison is carrying amount against the higher measure, and ₹80 crore against ₹85 crore needs no write-down at all.

items.scenario: A plant is carried at ₹80 crore. A broker would pay ₹70 crore for it net of costs, and the discounted cash flows from continuing to run it come to ₹85 crore. The accountant books a ₹10 crore impairment loss, reasoning that the market has spoken and the plant cannot be sold for its carrying amount.

items.stem: Which balances are retranslated at ₹84?

options.text: The receivable and the advance — both arose from cash actually paid or receivable
options.misconception: tests where the balance came from instead of how it settles
options.why: The advance began as cash but ends as goods. Settlement in something other than a fixed amount of currency is what makes it non-monetary, however cash-flavoured its origin.

options.text: All three — every foreign currency balance is restated at closing
options.misconception: retranslates by currency instead of by monetary character
options.why: Para 23 splits the balance sheet by nature, not by currency. Restating inventory and advances manufactures exchange differences on items that will never turn into dollars.

options.text: None, holding all items at ₹80 until realised, with differences booked on settlement
options.misconception: defers monetary retranslation to settlement
options.why: For monetary items the standard books the difference each reporting date, realised or not. Waiting for settlement understates a ₹8 crore gain the year-end position already holds.

options.text: Only the receivable — the inventory and the goods-advance are non-monetary and stay at ₹80
options.why: The receivable is a right to receive fixed currency units — monetary, closing rate, gain to profit or loss. Inventory is a thing, not a claim to currency. The advance, because it will be settled by delivery of goods rather than refund of cash, carries no right to currency units and stays frozen at the rate it was paid.

items.scenario: At year-end an Indian company holds three dollar balances from when the dollar was ₹80: a $2 million trade receivable, inventory that cost $1 million, and a $0.5 million advance paid to a supplier against future delivery of goods. The closing rate is ₹84.

items.stem: Which of the three actually adjust the 31 March statements?

options.text: Only the bankruptcy — the fire and the dividend are disclosed, not adjusted
options.why: A customer's collapse weeks after year-end normally evidences a debt already bad at the reporting date — an adjusting event. The fire is a condition born in April, so it belongs to next year's numbers, disclosed if material. The dividend has its own rule: declared after the period, it is no liability at 31 March.

options.text: The bankruptcy and the dividend, since both concern amounts as at year-end
options.misconception: treats the dividend as accruing to the year it relates to
options.why: A dividend "for" a year is still created by its declaration. Ind AS 10 says expressly that a post-period declaration is not a liability at the reporting date.

options.text: All three — anything known before approval of the statements is adjusted
options.misconception: replaces the condition-at-the-reporting-date test with a knowledge test
options.why: Approval only fixes the window in which events are considered. Inside that window the question is always which period's conditions the event evidences.

options.text: None — the reporting period closed on 31 March and later events are next year's story
options.misconception: shuts the window that adjusting events exist to keep open
options.why: Some April knowledge is precisely about March: the bankruptcy tells you what the receivable was truly worth on the last day of the year. Ignoring it states an asset the entity already knew was bad.

items.scenario: A company's year ends 31 March. In April, before the statements are approved: (1) a customer owing ₹3 crore at year-end goes bankrupt; (2) a fire destroys a warehouse; (3) the board declares a final dividend of ₹5 crore. The accountant adjusts for all three, reasoning that all are known before approval.

items.stem: What is wrong with the CFO's presentation?

options.text: Only the timing — once the board resolves to sell, classification follows
options.misconception: mistakes intention for commitment
options.why: The criteria demand a plan in motion: buyer search begun, marketing under way, sale expected within a year. A resolution aimed at a better market someday is hope, not a programme.

options.text: Everything — the criteria are not met, and even when met the measurement never writes the asset up
options.why: A board resolution without an active programme, active marketing, or a within-a-year expectation fails the highly-probable test — an intent to sell in a distant future is the standard's own disqualifier. And classification measures at the lower of carrying amount and fair value less costs to sell; it is a write-down mechanism, never a gain.

options.text: Nothing, provided the fair value came from an independent valuer
options.misconception: cures a classification failure with valuation quality
options.why: The valuer answers what the factory is worth, not whether it qualifies. And the measurement rule would still cap the carrying amount at the lower of the two figures.

options.text: Only the uplift — classify as held for sale but keep it at carrying amount
options.misconception: fixes the measurement while leaving the wrong classification standing
options.why: Held-for-sale presentation tells readers recovery will come by sale within the year. For a producing factory with no buyer search, that message is false however it is measured.

items.scenario: In February the board resolves to sell a factory and expects a good price sometime in the next two or three years once the property market improves. No broker is appointed and the plant keeps producing. The CFO wants the factory shown as held for sale at 31 March at fair value, which is above carrying amount, booking the uplift.

items.stem: Which restatement is wrong?

options.text: The inventory method — valuation approaches may never change once chosen
options.misconception: freezes policy instead of regulating how it changes
options.why: Policies may change when a standard requires it or the new policy gives more relevant, reliable information. The regulation is the retrospective mechanics, not a bar on changing at all.

options.text: Both — no change of any kind may touch prior periods without a court order
options.misconception: confuses restatement under Ind AS 8 with reopening accounts under the Companies Act
options.why: Retrospective application under Ind AS 8 restates comparative columns in the current statements; it does not reopen adopted accounts. Policy changes and error corrections do this as a matter of course.

options.text: The useful life — an estimate change works prospectively, so the comparatives stay
options.why: A useful life is an estimate, and para 36 spreads its revision over the current and future periods; the past stays as reported because it reflected the best estimate of its own day. The inventory change is closer to how existing policy is applied to new information — and where policy and estimate blur, the standard's own tiebreak says treat it as an estimate too.

options.text: Neither — comparability demands both years on the new basis
options.misconception: promotes comparability over the standard's split
options.why: Restating history for every new estimate would mean re-opening accounts each time knowledge improved. The standard buys stability by confining estimates to the future.

items.scenario: During the year a company (1) moves from writing down slow inventory by fixed percentages to an item-wise net realisable value assessment, and (2) revises the useful life of its plant from 15 years to 10 after a technology shift. The accountant restates prior-year comparatives for both, to keep the years comparable.

items.stem: Where does interest capitalisation actually run?

options.text: On all three — interest on borrowed money is a cost of whatever the money bought
options.misconception: capitalises by traceability instead of by qualification
options.why: Tracing shows which asset the money funded; qualification decides whether time-cost belongs in that asset. For assets ready at once, interest is a financing expense, full stop.

options.text: On nothing — borrowing costs are always period expenses
options.misconception: states the alternative treatment Ind AS 23 abolished
options.why: For qualifying assets, capitalisation is mandatory under para 8, not a choice. The expense-everything policy died with the standard's revision.

options.text: Only on the refinery while construction is active — not the stock, not the idle months
options.why: The refinery is the textbook qualifying asset: it necessarily takes a substantial period to become ready. Trading stock ready in weeks never qualifies. And para-level suspension rules stop capitalisation during extended periods of paused development, so the leisurely eight months carry their interest to expense.

options.text: On the refinery throughout, halt included, since the loan kept costing interest
options.misconception: lets the loan's clock override the asset's activity
options.why: Interest indeed accrued through the halt — as an expense. Capitalisation follows active development; an asset not being worked on is not being made ready, and its cost should not quietly grow.

items.scenario: A company borrows to fund three things: a refinery taking three years to build; a consignment of trading stock bought and sold within weeks; and the refinery again during an eight-month halt when work stopped for a redesign the company undertook at leisure. The CFO capitalises interest on all three.

items.stem: What does Ind AS 40 permit?

options.text: Cost less depreciation on the balance sheet, with the ₹150 crore fair value disclosed in the notes
options.why: The Indian carve-out deleted the fair value model: investment property is carried at cost, and fair value's role is disclosure. The CFO's treatment is correct IFRS and wrong Ind AS — the ₹60 crore uplift never touches profit or loss while the tower is held.

options.text: Fair value carrying, since rental property is effectively a financial investment
options.misconception: reasons from economic substance past the standard's text
options.why: Whatever the economics, the notified standard prescribes cost. Substance arguments choose between treatments the law offers; they do not create a third.

options.text: A free choice between cost and fair value models, applied consistently
options.misconception: states IAS 40's option as Indian law
options.why: The choice is precisely what MCA removed on notification. In India the model is cost, for everyone, which keeps unrealised property gains out of distributable profits.

options.text: Fair value through other comprehensive income, like revalued PPE
options.misconception: borrows Ind AS 16's revaluation route for a standard that lacks it
options.why: The revaluation model belongs to owner-occupied property under Ind AS 16. Ind AS 40 offers no revaluation route at all — cost is the only game.

citation.ref: measurement after recognition (cost model; fair value model not permitted)

items.scenario: A company holds an office tower purely for rental income. Its valuer reports fair value ₹150 crore against carrying cost ₹90 crore. The CFO, trained on IFRS, wants the tower carried at ₹150 crore with the ₹60 crore gain in profit or loss, noting that IAS 40 allows exactly this.

items.stem: Where does each holding actually sit in the hierarchy?

options.text: Levels 1, 2 and 2 — a recognised valuation technique lifts the startup out of Level 3
options.misconception: ranks the technique rather than what feeds it
options.why: DCF is a fine technique fed here by unobservable projections, and the level follows the lowest significant input. Technique sophistication cannot launder inputs upward.

options.text: Levels 1, 2 and 3 respectively — the hierarchy grades the inputs, not the documentation
options.why: The exchange quote for identical shares is the definition of Level 1. Similar-bond prices are observable but not identical-item quotes — Level 2. Management's own projections are unobservable inputs, and their significance drags the DCF to Level 3. Quality of paperwork never enters the ranking.

options.text: Levels 2, 2 and 3 — closing prices need adjustment for size before use
options.misconception: adjusts a Level 1 price the standard says to use as-is
options.why: Para 76's whole point is the unadjusted quoted price for identical items in an active market. Blockage-style adjustments to Level 1 prices are specifically not made.

options.text: All Level 1 — each value is reliable and independently reviewable
options.misconception: grades reliability of process instead of observability of inputs
options.why: The hierarchy tells readers how much market and how much management is in each number. A beautifully documented Level 3 is still built from unobservable inputs.

items.scenario: A company fair-values three holdings: listed shares priced off the exchange's closing quote; a corporate bond priced from quoted prices of similar bonds adjusted for credit spread; and an unlisted startup stake valued by a discounted cash flow built on management's own projections. The CFO labels all three Level 1, since each valuation is documented and professionally prepared.

items.stem: What moves in the expense calculation, and what does not?

options.text: Neither moves — grant-date figures of ₹40 and 90,000 both lock in
options.misconception: freezes the estimate along with the measurement
options.why: Only the fair value locks. The number expected to satisfy service conditions is an estimate, revised until vesting so the final expense reflects options actually earned.

options.text: Both move — expense should track what the options are worth now
options.misconception: applies liability-style remeasurement to an equity award
options.why: Remeasurement to current value is the cash-settled rule, because cash-settled awards are liabilities. Equity awards fix value once; that asymmetry is the standard's central design choice.

options.text: The count moves to 75,000; the ₹40 grant-date value never moves
options.why: Equity-settled awards lock their unit value at grant date — the employees were paid in options worth ₹40 when granted, and the market's later verdict on the shares is the holders' affair, not a remeasurement trigger. Service-condition estimates are the part that trues up, so the falling headcount flows through each period.

options.text: The value drops to ₹12 but the count stays at 90,000 for consistency
options.misconception: inverts the standard on both limbs at once
options.why: This updates the one thing the standard fixes and fixes the one thing it updates. The share price fall changes nothing; the attrition changes the charge.

items.scenario: A company grants 1,00,000 options to employees, fair value ₹40 each at grant, vesting after three years' service. By year two the share price has fallen sharply and the options' fair value is ₹12; attrition has also cut expected vesting from 90,000 to 75,000 options. The CFO wants the expense recomputed on ₹12 to reflect reality.

items.stem: How does the ₹17 crore actually land?

options.text: ₹8 crore in profit or loss; the ₹9 crore loss in OCI immediately, never to be recycled
options.why: Service cost and net interest belong to profit or loss; remeasurements go to other comprehensive income in full, in the period they arise, and para 122 forbids reclassifying them later. The corridor and spreading devices of the old standards are gone — the loss is recognised at once, only not in the operating result.

options.text: All ₹17 crore in profit or loss — a cost is a cost wherever it comes from
options.misconception: ignores the standard's mandated split
options.why: The split is the standard's design: actuarial swings driven by discount rates would drown the operating story. OCI recognises them fully without letting them whipsaw profit.

options.text: The loss parks in OCI this year and recycles to profit or loss as the plan pays out
options.misconception: assumes OCI items always recycle eventually
options.why: Some OCI items recycle; remeasurements are expressly not among them. They may move within equity, but profit or loss never sees them.

options.text: ₹8 crore now, with the ₹9 crore spread over remaining service life
options.misconception: applies the abolished corridor-and-spread approach
options.why: Deferral mechanisms let funded status hide off balance sheet for years. Ind AS 19 killed them; the balance sheet now carries the full deficit as it stands.

items.scenario: A company's gratuity plan produces this year: current service cost ₹6 crore, net interest cost ₹2 crore, and an actuarial loss of ₹9 crore after bond yields fell. The CFO, horrified at a ₹17 crore charge to profit, proposes spreading the actuarial loss over the employees' remaining service years, recalling that approach from older standards.

items.stem: Is the twenty per cent rule being applied correctly?

options.text: Yes — below twenty per cent, associate accounting is unavailable as a matter of law
options.misconception: hardens a presumption into a threshold
options.why: The standard says presumed, unless clearly demonstrated otherwise — in both directions. A bright line would invite structuring holdings at 19.9 per cent, which the rebuttable form exists to prevent.

options.text: No — the presumption is rebuttable, and board seats plus technical dependence demonstrate influence at 15 per cent
options.why: Twenty per cent is a presumption in both directions, and para 6 lists exactly these evidences — representation on the board, essential technical information, material transactions. Two of five board seats participating in policy decisions is influence in operation, whatever the shareholding. The stake is an associate, equity accounted.

options.text: Yes, unless the company acquires five more per cent during the year
options.misconception: waits for arithmetic to answer a question about power
options.why: Influence is assessed on all facts now, not on a future purchase. The extra five per cent would change nothing the board seats have not already established.

options.text: No — the board seats and dependence show control, so full consolidation applies
options.misconception: overshoots influence into control
options.why: Control means power to direct the relevant activities; two seats of five and a technology contract let the company participate, not decide. Between passive investment and control lies exactly the ground the associate standard covers.

items.scenario: A company holds 15 per cent of a supplier's voting power, but has two seats on its five-member board, supplies the technology the supplier's plant runs on, and is its largest customer. The accountant carries the stake as a plain financial investment, citing the twenty per cent rule.

items.stem: Does the deferred tax asset belong on this balance sheet?

options.text: Yes in full — the losses exist and the law permits carrying them forward
options.misconception: confuses the tax attribute with the accounting asset
options.why: The carry-forward right is necessary but not sufficient. The asset is the future tax saving, and a saving requires future profit to save against — the very thing three loss years cast doubt on.

options.text: Never — loss-making companies are barred from deferred tax assets outright
options.misconception: hardens a high evidence bar into a prohibition
options.why: The standard sets a stricter test, not a ban. Sufficient taxable temporary differences alone can carry recognition, and genuine turnaround evidence can too.

options.text: Not on this evidence — a loss history demands convincing evidence beyond another optimistic budget
options.why: Para 35 treats the existence of recent losses as evidence that future profit may not come. Against that, the standard asks for taxable temporary differences or convincing other evidence — and a budget of the same species as the two that failed convinces nobody. A verifiable turnaround — a signed long-term contract, a loss-making division actually closed — could support recognition, in part or full.

options.text: Yes, because prudence favours recognising every available asset
options.misconception: points prudence in the wrong direction
options.why: Prudence restrains asset recognition; it never compels it. Booking a doubtful asset overstates equity — the opposite of caution.

items.scenario: A company has lost money for three straight years and carries ₹80 crore of unused tax losses. Its budget projects a return to profit next year, as the previous two budgets also did. The CFO books a full deferred tax asset, arguing the losses are real, the law allows their carry-forward, and the budget is board-approved.

items.stem: Which instruments qualify for amortised cost?

options.text: The government bond and the debenture — sovereign and near-sovereign credit passes
options.misconception: mistakes credit quality for cash flow character
options.why: SPPI examines what the cash flows are, not how safe they are. A risky bond with plain interest passes; a safe note with an equity kicker fails.

options.text: The two bonds — identical instruments must carry identical measurement
options.misconception: classifies the instrument and ignores the portfolio
options.why: The business model test is assessed at portfolio level, so the same ISIN can sit at amortised cost in treasury and fair value on the trading desk. Context is half the classification.

options.text: Only the government bond — the debenture fails the cash flow test, the trading-desk bond fails the business model test
options.why: Para 4.1.2 demands both conditions. The plain bond held to collect passes both. The equity-linked debenture's cash flows are not solely principal and interest, however firmly it is held. The trading desk's bond has perfect cash flows inside a sell-driven business model — one pass, one fail, and one fail is enough.

options.text: All three — intention to hold to maturity is what amortised cost rewards
options.misconception: revives the old held-to-maturity single test
options.why: Ind AS 109 replaced intention with two objective tests. An instrument can be held forever and still owe its returns to a share price, which no effective interest method can unwind.

items.scenario: A treasury holds three instruments to maturity, with no intention of selling any: a plain government bond paying fixed interest; a debenture whose return is 2 per cent plus half the issuer's share price appreciation; and a corporate bond identical to the first but sitting in the trading desk's portfolio, where positions turn over weekly.

items.stem: As auditor, what do you require before the report is signed?

options.text: A written representation from the CFO that the banks have been informed separately
options.misconception: routes a reporting defect into a representation
options.why: Whom the bankers heard from privately has no bearing on what the statements must say to every reader. And a representation is never sufficient evidence on its own, least of all about a disclosure that is visibly missing.

options.text: Disclosure of the material uncertainty in the notes to the financial statements themselves
options.why: Ind AS 1 puts the disclosure duty on the financial statements when management is aware of material uncertainties over going concern. The directors' report is not audited to the same standard and is not where SA 570's dedicated section can point. Without the note the statements are misstated, and the opinion — not just a paragraph — is what changes.

options.text: Nothing further, since the auditor's own going concern section will inform readers
options.misconception: uses the auditor's report to carry management's disclosure duty
options.why: The auditor's section draws attention to the note; it does not replace it. Where the note is absent, the statements are wrong and the response is a modified opinion, not a louder auditor's paragraph.

options.text: A more detailed description in the directors' report, cross-referenced from the audit report
options.misconception: accepts other-information disclosure as a substitute for the note
options.why: The directors' report is other information. A cross-reference from the audit report cannot cure an omission inside the statements — it would advertise the very gap it papers over.

items.scenario: A company has defaulted on its term loans and its net current liabilities are ₹80 crore. The CFO agrees a material uncertainty exists but proposes to describe it in the directors' report only, keeping the financial statements clean "so the bankers do not panic". The audit is in final review.

items.stem: What does section 188 require for this contract?

options.text: No approval, because buying fabric is the company's ordinary course of business
options.misconception: applies half the exemption and drops the arm's length half
options.why: The exemption needs both limbs: ordinary course and arm's length. An 8 per cent premium concedes the second limb, and one failed limb brings the section fully into play.

options.text: Only disclosure in the board's report, since the amount is below ₹50 crore
options.misconception: substitutes a disclosure threshold for the approval requirement
options.why: Thresholds decide when shareholders must approve on top of the board — they never reduce the requirement to disclosure alone. The board resolution is the floor, not the ceiling.

options.text: Approval of the Registrar of Companies before execution
options.misconception: sends a governance decision to the regulator
options.why: Section 188 keeps the decision inside the company — board, and shareholders where thresholds require. The Registrar receives filings; he does not approve contracts.

options.text: Board approval by resolution, with the interested director not participating
options.why: The counterparty is a related party and the pricing is not arm's length, so the ordinary- course-and-arm's-length exemption is unavailable. Section 188 then requires a board resolution — with shareholder approval as well if the prescribed thresholds are crossed — and the interested director stays out of the discussion and the vote.

items.scenario: A public company proposes to buy fabric worth ₹12 crore annually from a partnership in which a director's son is a partner, at prices about 8 per cent above the market, citing assured quality. The purchase committee asks what approvals the contract needs.

items.stem: Can the auditor accept this fee arrangement?

options.text: Yes, because fee structure is a private contract between auditor and client
options.misconception: places the engagement contract above the professional schedules
options.why: The Chartered Accountants Act sits over every engagement letter a member signs. A contract cannot authorise what the First Schedule defines as misconduct.

options.text: Yes, if the arrangement is disclosed to shareholders in the general meeting
options.misconception: treats disclosure as curing a prohibited arrangement
options.why: Disclosure cures conflicts that are permissible to hold. This one is prohibited outright; telling the shareholders about it only documents the misconduct.

options.text: No — fees contingent on results or based on a percentage of profits are prohibited
options.why: An auditor paid a share of the profit he certifies holds a stake in the number under audit. The First Schedule makes such fees professional misconduct, outside the narrow exceptions the Council has prescribed for specific engagements — statutory audit is not among them.

options.text: No, unless the percentage is capped at a maximum absolute amount
options.misconception: believes a ceiling converts a contingent fee into a fixed one
options.why: A capped percentage still rises and falls with the profits below the cap — the stake in the certified number remains. The defect is the linkage, not the size.

items.scenario: A client offers its statutory auditor a fee of 2 per cent of audited net profits, arguing it aligns the auditor's diligence with the company's success and is common for consultants.

items.stem: What does section 143(12) require of you?

options.text: Qualify the audit opinion and treat that as the report
options.misconception: treats the audit report to members as the fraud report to the Government
options.why: The opinion speaks to the financial statements; the 143(12) report is a separate filing to a different addressee with its own form and timeline. One cannot stand in for the other.

options.text: Report to the Central Government, routing it through the board or audit committee for their reply within the prescribed time
options.why: The fraud is by an employee against the company and crosses the one crore threshold, so the report goes to the Central Government in the prescribed manner — the board or audit committee gets the prescribed window to respond, and their comments travel with the report. Handling it quietly is not among the options the section leaves open.

options.text: Resign from the engagement to avoid association with the fraud
options.misconception: substitutes exit for the statutory duty
options.why: Resignation does not discharge section 143(12), and a resigning auditor still carries reporting duties. The Act wants the fraud reported, not the auditor gone.

options.text: Report it to the audit committee only, since internal fraud is a governance matter
options.misconception: applies the below-threshold route to an above-threshold fraud
options.why: Audit-committee-only reporting is the route for frauds under one crore. At ₹1.8 crore the section escalates the duty to the Central Government, and the committee cannot absorb it.

items.scenario: During the audit of a listed company you find that a purchase manager, colluding with a vendor, has siphoned ₹1.8 crore through inflated invoices over two years. Management asks you to note it internally and let the audit committee handle it quietly.

items.stem: Does section 135 apply?

options.text: Yes — the thresholds are alternatives, and the profit test is crossed
options.why: Any one of the three gates opens the section, and ₹6.2 crore of net profit is past the ₹5 crore gate. The committee, the policy and the 2 per cent of three-year average net profits all follow, however modest the balance sheet looks beside the other thresholds.

options.text: No, because CSR obligations attach only to listed companies
options.misconception: confuses CSR applicability with listing status
options.why: Section 135 never mentions listing. A private limited company past any threshold is as bound as a listed one.

options.text: Yes, but spending is optional so long as the board explains the shortfall
options.misconception: carries the old comply-or-explain regime past its amendment
options.why: Explain-only died with the 2021 amendments. Unspent money now transfers to an ongoing project account or a specified fund on a statutory clock, with penalties behind it.

options.text: No, because two of the three thresholds are not met
options.misconception: reads the alternative thresholds as cumulative
options.why: Requiring all three would confine CSR to giants. The section says net worth OR turnover OR profit, and one is enough.

items.scenario: A company has net worth ₹120 crore and turnover ₹800 crore, but its net profit for the immediately preceding year was ₹6.2 crore. The CFO argues CSR does not apply because the company is nowhere near the net worth or turnover thresholds.

items.stem: How do the two opinions in your report come out?

options.text: Unmodified on the financial statements; adverse on internal financial controls
options.why: Section 143(3)(i) makes controls a separate opinion answering a separate question. A material weakness draws an adverse controls opinion even where extended substantive work let the statements themselves be proved true and fair.

options.text: Unmodified on both, because the statements were ultimately proved right
options.misconception: lets the financial statement outcome absolve the controls
options.why: The controls opinion reports the state of the controls, not the state of the numbers. A material weakness that existed at the year end is reported whether or not it did damage.

options.text: The control failures go only in a management letter, not the audit report
options.misconception: demotes a statutory reporting duty to a private communication
options.why: The management letter supplements; it cannot substitute. Section 143(3)(i) puts the controls opinion in the report to members by force of statute.

options.text: Both must be qualified, since a control failure infects the statements
options.misconception: chains the two opinions together
options.why: The opinions can and do diverge. Broken controls raise the risk of misstatement; they do not prove one occurred, and here the substantive work proved otherwise.

items.scenario: Finalising a listed company's audit, you conclude the financial statements are true and fair, but testing showed the purchase-to-pay controls failed repeatedly and a material weakness exists at the year end.

items.stem: Which of the four falls foul of Clause 6?

options.text: The tender response, because concurrent audit was never offered to this firm personally
options.misconception: treats responding to an open invitation as uninvited approach
options.why: A tender is an invitation to everyone qualified. Answering an invitation is the opposite of soliciting; the mischief is approaching those who never asked.

options.text: The letter to the other firm, since work must come from clients directly
options.misconception: bars the one channel the clause expressly keeps open
options.why: Securing work from another chartered accountant in practice is a stated exception — professional sub-engagement is how overflow and specialisation have always moved.

options.text: All four, since each is an attempt to obtain professional work
options.misconception: reads the bar as covering every pursuit of work
options.why: The clause was never a vow of passivity. Its carve-outs exist precisely so that open, invited competition — tenders, empanelment, professional-to-professional requests — stays lawful.

options.text: Only the brochure mailing to the two hundred companies
