options.why: Unsolicited circulars to prospective clients are the textbook form of solicitation the clause bars. The other three are its stated exceptions — responding to tenders, applying against announced empanelments, and seeking work from another chartered accountant in practice.

items.scenario: A firm of chartered accountants does four things in one quarter — mails brochures about its audit expertise to two hundred companies chosen from the registrar's records, responds to a public tender floated by a state bank for concurrent audit, applies against a public empanelment notice of a government corporation, and writes to another CA firm offering to take its overflow tax work.

items.stem: Does the proposed committee comply?

options.text: Yes, provided the committee's recommendations are ratified by the full board
options.misconception: cures defective composition with board ratification
options.why: Ratification cannot rebuild the committee. The statute regulates who deliberates, not just what emerges; a wrongly composed committee stays wrongly composed however its output is later blessed.

options.text: No, because the CFO's relative can never sit on any board committee
options.misconception: invents a blanket relative disqualification
options.why: Relationship to an officer affects independence classification, not committee membership as such. The defect is arithmetic — the independents lack a majority — not the presence of one related non-executive.

options.text: Yes — four exceeds the minimum of three, and independents are represented
options.misconception: checks the headcount and skips the majority condition
options.why: Representation is not the test; majority is. The minimum of three and the independent majority are separate conditions, and the second one fails here.

options.text: No — independent directors must form the majority, and two of four is not one
options.why: Section 177 requires a minimum of three directors with independents in the majority. Two of four fails the majority test, and a committee chaired by the managing director invites exactly the management dominance the composition rules exist to prevent.

items.scenario: A listed company proposes an audit committee of four directors — two independent, the managing director, and the CFO's brother as a non-executive director, chaired by the managing director. The company secretary certifies the composition complies with section 177.

items.stem: Does CARO 2020 apply to this company's audit?

options.text: No, since two of the three financial limits are within bounds
options.misconception: reads the cumulative exemption conditions as majority-satisfied
options.why: The exemption is conjunctive. Meeting two limits while breaking the third is simply breaking the conditions — the order does not average them.

options.text: Yes, but only the fraud and statutory dues clauses apply to private companies
options.misconception: invents a partial CARO for private companies
options.why: CARO has no reduced edition. Once applicable, the whole order applies; applicability is the only company-level question.

options.text: Yes — the revenue of ₹14 crore crosses the ten crore limit, and one breach is enough
options.why: The private-company exemption needs every limit honoured together — capital and reserves, borrowings, and revenue. Revenue at ₹14 crore breaks the ten crore ceiling, so the order applies with all its reporting clauses, whatever the other two figures say.

options.text: No, because CARO never applies to private companies
options.misconception: turns a conditional exemption into a blanket one
options.why: Private companies are exempt only inside the size limits. Beyond them, a private company answers every CARO clause a public one does.

items.scenario: A private limited company, not a holding or subsidiary of a public company, has paid-up capital and reserves of ₹80 lakh, bank borrowings that peaked at ₹95 lakh during the year, and revenue of ₹14 crore. Its auditor treats CARO 2020 as inapplicable since capital and borrowings are within a crore each.

items.stem: What is the most the company can distribute from current profits?

options.text: ₹28 crore, by adding the securities premium to distributable profit
options.misconception: treats securities premium as a free reserve
options.why: Premium is shareholders' capital contribution, usable only for the purposes section 52 lists. Distribution as dividend is not among them.

options.text: ₹3 crore — after depreciation and after setting off the carried-forward loss
options.why: Section 123 charges depreciation first (₹10 minus ₹3) and then requires previous losses and unabsorbed depreciation to be set off (₹7 minus ₹4), leaving ₹3 crore of distributable profit. The premium and revaluation balances watch from the sidelines.

options.text: ₹7 crore — depreciation must be provided, but old losses concern the balance sheet, not dividends
options.misconception: provides depreciation and skips the loss set-off
options.why: The set-off is a statutory pre-condition, not a presentation nicety. Paying dividends across an unabsorbed loss distributes capital dressed as income.

options.text: ₹18 crore, by drawing on the revaluation surplus
options.misconception: distributes an unrealised book write-up
options.why: A revaluation surplus is an accounting remeasurement, not realised profit. Dividending it hands out money the company never earned and may never see.

items.scenario: A company has current-year profit of ₹10 crore before providing ₹3 crore of depreciation, a brought-forward business loss of ₹4 crore, a securities premium of ₹25 crore, and a revaluation surplus of ₹15 crore. The board wants the largest lawful dividend.

items.stem: Can either proposal stand?

options.text: Neither — the cooling-off blocks any reappointment for five years, and the partner-linked firm is equally barred
options.why: Ten years is the ceiling, and the five-year cooling-off admits no short extensions — two years inside a barred window is barred. The fallback fails on the same section's own words: a firm with common partners as at the appointment date stands in the retiring firm's shoes.

options.text: The linked firm works, because it is a distinct legal entity
options.misconception: hides continuity behind a fresh registration
options.why: The statute anticipated the manoeuvre and named it: common partners carry the disqualification across the entity line.

options.text: The two-year extension works, since it is shorter than a term
options.misconception: reads the bar as prohibiting only full terms
options.why: The section bars appointment as auditor during the cooling-off, for any length. Slicing the term thin does not slip it through.

options.text: Both work if the audit committee certifies the firm's independence
options.misconception: lets a committee certify around a statutory bar
options.why: Independence certification supplements eligibility; it cannot manufacture it. A candidate the statute disqualifies stays disqualified with the finest certificate attached.

items.scenario: An audit firm completes its second five-year term at a listed company. The shareholders, pleased with its work, propose reappointing it for two more years only, arguing a short extension is not a fresh five-year term. As fallback they suggest a different firm in which three partners of the retiring firm hold a majority.

items.stem: Which of the CFO's three grounds survives section 138?

options.text: The first — private companies are outside internal audit requirements
options.misconception: reads section 138 as a public-company provision
options.why: The rule names private companies with their own thresholds. Two hundred crore of turnover is one of them, and this company is past it.

options.text: The third — the internal auditor must be a practising chartered accountant
options.misconception: narrows the section's deliberately wide eligibility
options.why: The provision expressly allows a cost accountant or such other professional as the board decides, and the rule adds that the appointee may be an employee. Parliament left the choice to the board.

options.text: None — the turnover line is crossed, in-house review is not internal audit, and the board may appoint a qualified employee
options.why: A private company past two hundred crore of turnover is squarely covered. A management team reviewing its own controls is self-review, not the independent function the section contemplates — but the section is generous on who: a chartered accountant, cost accountant or other professional, employee included, as the board decides.

options.text: The second — a documented monthly management review satisfies the requirement
options.misconception: accepts self-review as the audit of self
options.why: The reviewers report to the very management whose controls they review. Internal audit exists to stand outside that loop, reporting toward the audit committee.

items.scenario: A private company had turnover of ₹230 crore in the preceding year and no borrowings. The CFO resists appointing an internal auditor on three grounds — the company is private, its own accounts team reviews controls monthly, and in any case only chartered accountants can be internal auditors, which would mean hiring outside.

items.stem: Is the company covered, and can unspent CSR sit in the balance sheet?

options.text: Covered — the profit test alone triggers section 135 — and unspent amounts must move to the statutory accounts, not sit in the balance sheet
options.why: The three thresholds are alternatives; net profit of ₹9 crore against the five-crore line is enough on its own. Since the 2019 amendments, unspent money has mandated destinations — an unspent-CSR account within thirty days for ongoing projects, a Schedule VII fund within six months otherwise. A general reserve is neither.

options.text: Covered, but spending remains comply-or-explain, so unspent amounts need only a board explanation
options.misconception: states the pre-2019 regime as current law
options.why: Explanation alone was the original design. The amendments kept the explanation and added teeth — mandatory transfer of unspent amounts on a statutory clock, with penalties behind it.

options.text: Not covered — CSR needs at least two of the three thresholds crossed
options.misconception: reads "or" as "and"
options.why: The section strings its thresholds with "or". One gate open is enough, and the profit gate is open by four crore.

options.text: Covered, and the obligation is two per cent of the preceding year's ₹9 crore profit
options.misconception: computes on one year instead of the three-year average
options.why: Eligibility reads one year; the spend reads three. Two per cent applies to the average net profits of the three immediately preceding financial years, which smooths a lumpy profit like this one.

items.scenario: A company with turnover of ₹800 crore and net worth of ₹300 crore earned net profit of ₹9 crore in the immediately preceding year. Its CFO argues CSR does not apply since neither the net worth nor the turnover threshold is crossed. The board separately proposes that if CSR does apply, any unspent amount can be carried in the general balance sheet for later use.

items.stem: Which alternatives does section 149 permit?

options.text: The third — a gap of any length resets the two-term count
options.misconception: reads the cooling-off as a courtesy interval rather than a three-year statutory bar
options.why: The reset needs the full three years. A shorter gap leaves him inside the exclusion period, and any association during it is itself prohibited.

options.text: The first, with shareholders' special resolution blessing the third term
options.misconception: lets a resolution extend a statutory maximum
options.why: The special resolution is how a second term is granted. No resolution reaches past two consecutive terms; the statute's ceiling binds the shareholders too.

options.text: None of the three — ten years is the ceiling, and the three-year cooling-off bars any association, consultancy included
options.why: Two consecutive terms exhaust the independent-director route, and section 149(11)'s cooling-off is not merely a pause before reappointment — during those three years he may not be appointed in or associated with the company in any other capacity. The consultancy and the one-year gap both walk into that bar.

options.text: The second — the consultancy is a different capacity outside section 149
options.misconception: routes around the bar through a side door the section explicitly closed
options.why: The subsection's words reach appointment in the company "in any other capacity". A paid consultancy is also precisely the pecuniary relationship that destroyed independence while he served.

items.scenario: A listed company's independent director completes two consecutive five-year terms. The board, valuing his experience, proposes three alternatives: reappoint him for a third term as independent director; appoint him immediately as a paid consultant to the company; or bring him back as an independent director after one year's gap.

items.stem: How many section 186 requirements does the proposal break?

options.text: Three — the limit needs a special resolution, board approval must be unanimous, and the rate is below the statutory floor
options.why: ₹140 crore exceeds both limbs of the limit — sixty per cent of ₹200 crore is ₹120 crore — so shareholders must pass a special resolution first. The board sanction must carry the consent of all directors present, which two dissents defeat. And no loan may be priced below the government-security yield for the matching tenor; a group discount is exactly what the floor exists to stop.

options.text: One — only the shareholder resolution is missing; boards act by majority and price freely
options.misconception: applies ordinary board-majority rules to a section that demands unanimity
options.why: Section 186(5) requires the consent of all directors present at the meeting for these decisions — a deliberate departure from majority rule — and subsection (7) fixes the interest floor.

options.text: Two — resolution and unanimity fail, but interest is a commercial matter for the board
options.misconception: concedes the process points while missing the pricing floor
options.why: Subsection (7) writes the minimum into the statute: not lower than the prevailing yield on government securities closest to the loan's tenor. Commercial freedom starts above that line, not below it.

options.text: None — lending to a group company is exempt from section 186
options.misconception: stretches the wholly-owned-subsidiary carve-outs over the whole group
options.why: The exemptions cover specific cases such as loans to wholly owned subsidiaries. A group company generally is just another body corporate, and every limb of the section applies.

items.scenario: A company with paid-up capital plus free reserves of ₹200 crore (free reserves portion ₹90 crore) has existing inter-corporate loans of ₹100 crore. The board wants to lend a further ₹40 crore to a group company at an interest rate below the prevailing government-security yield, approving it by majority vote at a board meeting with two directors dissenting.

items.stem: Which advances can lawfully be made?

options.text: All three, if shareholders approve each by special resolution
options.misconception: reads the whole section as resolution-curable
options.why: The special resolution route exists only for the entities in which directors are interested. For the director personally, the prohibition has no key — that is the section's core.

options.text: The first and third — loans to individuals are personnel matters outside company law
options.misconception: exempts exactly the person the section names first
options.why: "Any loan to any of its directors" is the opening prohibition. The individual director is not the exception; he is the addressee.

options.text: The second with a special resolution, and the third under the employee-scheme exception — never the first
options.why: The direct loan to a director sits in section 185's absolute bar; no resolution reaches it. The interested private company is in the conditional ring — special resolution plus use in the borrower's principal business activities. The managing director's housing loan rides the exception for schemes extended to all employees.

options.text: None — section 185 bans anything that benefits a director directly or indirectly
options.misconception: inflates the bar over the section's own exceptions
options.why: The 2017 rewrite deliberately split the section into a bar, a conditional window and exceptions. Reading it as a wall outlaws employee welfare schemes Parliament expressly saved.

items.scenario: A public company's board considers three advances: ₹50 lakh to a director to buy a house; ₹2 crore to a private company in which the same director holds 40 per cent, for that company's working capital; and ₹30 lakh to the managing director under a housing-loan scheme the company extends to all employees.

items.stem: What happens to the section 9 application?

options.text: It fails — the rejection letter is a pre-existing dispute, and section 9 cannot decide whose case is right
options.why: The dispute predates the demand notice by six months in writing, which is exactly what the dispute defence requires. The adjudicating authority only asks whether a plausible dispute existed before the notice — not who would win it — because the Code rescues failing companies rather than collecting contested bills. The supplier's forum is a civil suit or arbitration.

options.text: It succeeds — the undisputed two-thirds alone exceeds the threshold
options.misconception: severs the debt to salvage the application
options.why: A genuine dispute touching the claimed operational debt bars the application; the tribunal does not carve the invoice into clean and contested slices to keep the petition alive.

options.text: It succeeds if the supplier proves the goods were not defective
options.misconception: turns the admission stage into the trial
options.why: Proof of quality is a trial, with evidence and cross-examination — everything the summary admission under the Code is built not to be. Plausibility of the dispute ends the enquiry.

options.text: It fails only if the buyer had also filed a suit before the notice
options.misconception: demands litigation where the Code asks only for a dispute
options.why: The definition covers a dispute including a suit or arbitration — the correspondence raising a real quality claim is enough. Requiring a filed suit would reward the fastest court fee, not the true state of accounts.

items.scenario: A supplier is owed ₹3 crore for goods delivered. Six months before any insolvency step, the buyer had written rejecting a third of the goods as defective and withholding payment. The supplier now serves a section 8 demand notice and, on non-payment, files under section 9, arguing the defect claim is an afterthought to dodge insolvency.

items.stem: Which section 203 breaches are running?

options.text: None — the search is genuine and the CEO's roles are both disclosed
options.misconception: substitutes good faith and disclosure for statutory limits
options.why: The six-month line and the one-company rule are bright lines. Diligent interviewing past the deadline is still a default, disclosed dual office still a dual office.

options.text: Only the CFO vacancy — CEOs are not key managerial personnel
options.misconception: drops the CEO from the definition
options.why: Section 2(51) lists the chief executive officer among KMP expressly. The whole-time restrictions ride on that definition.

options.text: Two — the CFO vacancy passed its six-month limit in July, and a whole-time KMP cannot hold office in an unrelated company
options.why: The board's window to fill a KMP vacancy is six months from the date it arose; September is past it, and an informal stand-in is not an appointment. The one-company rule for whole-time KMP allows only a subsidiary as the second seat — an unrelated company fails it, and part-time labels do not undo the office.

options.text: Only the CEO's dual role — vacancies may stay open until the right candidate appears
options.misconception: reads the six-month limit as aspirational
options.why: The section commands the board to fill the vacancy within six months, with penalties behind it. Candidate quality is why the window is six months, not why it is open-ended.

items.scenario: A listed company's CFO resigns in January. In September, the board is still interviewing, with the finance controller handling the work informally. Meanwhile the company's CEO also serves as CEO of an unrelated private company, describing both as part-time engagements.

items.stem: Is the group barred?

options.text: No — any single shareholder may always petition against oppression
options.misconception: erases the standing requirement altogether
options.why: Open standing would hand every disgruntled member a Tribunal lever against the company. The thresholds filter; the waiver handles the exceptions.

options.text: Yes — thresholds are jurisdictional and the Tribunal cannot relax them
options.misconception: reads the section without its waiver proviso
options.why: The proviso to section 244(1) exists precisely so a meritorious minority is not silenced by arithmetic. Waiver is discretionary, but the power is in the text.

options.text: Not necessarily — the tests are alternatives with a waiver besides; 80 falls short of each, but the Tribunal can waive on merits
options.why: Section 244 offers the least demanding of its routes: one hundred members, one-tenth of members (600 here), or one-tenth of capital. The group misses all three — but the proviso lets the Tribunal waive the requirement for a case worth hearing, and adding 20 consenting members would cure standing outright. The objection opens a door; it does not close the case.

options.text: Yes, unless the group first acquires two more per cent of capital
options.misconception: fixes on the capital route as if it were the only one
options.why: Ten per cent of capital is one of three alternative routes, and the cheapest fix here is twenty more consenting members — or persuading the Tribunal to waive numbers entirely.

items.scenario: A company has 6,000 members. A group of 80 members holding 8 per cent of the issued capital wants to petition against the promoters for oppression. The promoters' counsel objects: fewer than one hundred members, less than ten per cent of capital — no standing, end of matter.

items.stem: What stops the proposal?

options.text: Nothing — the amount is within the board's ten per cent power
options.misconception: clears the quantum test and stops reading
options.why: Section 68 stacks its conditions; each stands independently. The cooling period exists so buy-backs are considered capital events, not a running price-support tool.

options.text: The absence of a special resolution, required for every buy-back
options.misconception: erases the board-only route
options.why: Up to ten per cent of paid-up equity plus free reserves, the board's resolution suffices — that carve-out is the provision's whole convenience. The defect here is timing, not authority.

options.text: The size — buy-backs are capped at ten per cent of paid-up capital alone
options.misconception: shrinks the base to bare capital
options.why: Both the ten and twenty-five per cent ceilings measure against capital plus free reserves. On ₹400 crore, the board route alone reaches ₹40 crore.

options.text: The one-year cooling period since the last buy-back — the arithmetic is within the board's limit, but the calendar is not
options.why: Ten per cent of ₹400 crore is ₹40 crore, so ₹38 crore sits inside the board-resolution route. What the proposal cannot survive is the bar on a fresh buy-back within one year of the preceding one's completion — a limit that applies whichever organ approves. Wait four months, and the same resolution works.

items.scenario: A company with paid-up equity of ₹100 crore and free reserves of ₹300 crore completed a buy-back eight months ago. The board now proposes, by board resolution alone, a fresh buy-back of ₹38 crore, noting it is under ten per cent of capital plus reserves and therefore within the board's own power.

items.stem: Can the company take the ₹7.2 lakh input tax credit?

options.text: No, and the goods must also be returned to the supplier
options.misconception: attaches a consequence to the goods when the defect is in the tax chain
options.why: The purchase itself is untouched — the goods are the company's. What fails is the credit; the company's remedy against the supplier is contractual, not a return of goods.

options.text: Yes — a valid invoice and receipt of goods complete the recipient's obligations
options.misconception: treats the recipient-side conditions as the whole test
options.why: That was the intuition under the old regime and it is the specific thing section 16(2)(c) rejects. The credit is of tax paid, and no tax was paid.

options.text: No — payment of the tax to the Government by the supplier is itself a condition
options.why: Section 16(2)(c) makes the supplier's actual payment a condition of the recipient's credit. Invoice, receipt and GSTR-2B appearance satisfy three conditions of five; all of them must hold together, and the missing one defeats the claim.

options.text: Yes, provisionally, reversible if the supplier stays in default for six months
options.misconception: recalls the provisional-credit mechanism that no longer exists
options.why: Provisional credit was removed from the law. Credit now follows GSTR-2B and the satisfied conditions, with no provisional window to occupy.

items.scenario: A company buys raw material worth ₹40 lakh plus ₹7.2 lakh GST, holds a valid tax invoice, has received the goods, and the invoice appears in its GSTR-2B. It then learns the supplier collected the tax but never deposited it with the Government.

items.stem: What is the GST position on these fees?

options.text: The company pays under reverse charge by debiting its input tax credit
options.misconception: discharges a reverse-charge liability through the credit ledger
options.why: Reverse charge must be paid through the cash ledger. The credit ledger can pay output tax on the company's own supplies, not the tax it owes as a recipient.

options.text: The company pays the GST under reverse charge, in cash
options.why: Legal services from an advocate to a business entity are notified under section 9(3), so the liability sits on the recipient. Reverse charge liability is discharged in cash — the company may then take credit of it, but cannot pay it out of credit.

options.text: The advocate should have charged GST on the bill
options.misconception: applies forward charge to a notified reverse-charge supply
options.why: For notified services the supplier neither charges nor collects. A bill without GST is the correct bill here; the tax travels on the company's own liability.

options.text: No GST arises, because legal services are exempt
options.misconception: stretches the small-recipient exemption to every recipient
options.why: The exemption covers advocates serving individuals and small business entities below the registration threshold. A ₹300 crore company is squarely outside it.

items.scenario: A manufacturing company with ₹300 crore turnover engages a senior advocate for a High Court matter and pays fees of ₹5 lakh. The advocate's bill shows no GST.

items.stem: Is registration required?

options.text: Yes, because every supplier of services must register from the first rupee
options.misconception: erases the threshold entirely for services
options.why: First-rupee registration applies to specific cases — inter-State taxable supply, e-commerce, reverse-charge recipients — not to services as a class.

options.text: No, not until turnover reaches ₹1.5 crore
options.misconception: mistakes the composition ceiling for the registration threshold
options.why: ₹1.5 crore is the composition scheme's eligibility ceiling — a choice available after registration, not a limit before it.

options.text: No, not until turnover reaches ₹40 lakh
options.misconception: applies the goods-only threshold to a service provider
options.why: The ₹40 lakh limit belongs to suppliers exclusively of goods in eligible States. One rupee of service supply keeps the ₹20 lakh limit in charge.

options.text: Yes — the services threshold of ₹20 lakh is crossed
options.why: A supplier of services takes the ₹20 lakh aggregate turnover limit, and ₹25 lakh is past it. Registration follows, with tax on supplies from the effective date.

items.scenario: A management consultant in Madhya Pradesh, supplying only services within the State, reaches aggregate turnover of ₹25 lakh during the year and asks whether registration is now compulsory.

items.stem: Can he make this supply while remaining in the scheme?

options.text: Yes, because his turnover is within the ₹1.5 crore ceiling
options.misconception: treats the turnover ceiling as the only eligibility condition
options.why: The ceiling is one condition of several. The inter-State bar is separate, and breaching it disqualifies regardless of how modest the turnover is.

options.text: No — inter-State outward supply ends composition eligibility
options.why: Section 10(2) bars a composition taxpayer from inter-State outward supplies. Shipping to Maharashtra means leaving the scheme and paying tax as a regular taxpayer, with the compliance that follows.

options.text: Yes, paying IGST on this order at the composition rate
options.misconception: extends the composition rate across State lines
options.why: There is no composition IGST. The scheme is a local-trade bargain, and the levy it charges exists only for intra-State supply.

options.text: Yes, if the Maharashtra buyer arranges his own transport from Indore
options.misconception: locates the supply by who carries the goods
options.why: Place of supply follows the movement's termination for delivery, not who pays the transporter. Goods bound for Maharashtra make an inter-State supply either way.

items.scenario: A composition dealer in Indore, selling hardware with turnover of ₹90 lakh, receives a large order from a buyer in Maharashtra and intends to supply it under the composition scheme.

items.stem: Which of these amounts is not added in arriving at the assessable value?

options.text: The selling commission of $2,000
options.misconception: excludes all commissions instead of only the buying commission
options.why: Selling commission is paid for the seller's benefit and is expressly added. The carve-out is for buying commission alone.

options.text: None of them — all payments connected with the import are added
options.misconception: adds everything rather than testing each payment against the rule
options.why: The rule works addition by addition, and buying commission is its stated exception. Adding everything overstates the value and the duty with it.

options.text: The buying commission of $1,500
options.why: Rule 10(1)(a) adds commissions and brokerage except buying commission. The importer's own agent works for the buyer, and paying him is part of the cost of buying, not part of the price of the goods.

options.text: The freight of $3,000
options.misconception: leaves transport out of a value that is built to the place of importation
options.why: Cost of transport to the place of importation is a Rule 10(2) addition. Assessable value is the landed value, and freight is part of landing the goods.

items.scenario: An importer's invoice shows goods at $50,000, selling commission of $2,000 paid to the exporter's agent, buying commission of $1,500 paid to the importer's own agent abroad, and freight of $3,000 to the Indian port.

items.stem: Can the credit still be taken?

options.text: No, because credit must be taken in the same month as the invoice
options.misconception: shrinks the statutory window to the invoice month
options.why: The law allows credit any time up to the section 16(4) date — often twenty months from an early-year invoice. The failure here is missing a generous window, not a same-month rule.

options.text: Yes, because the annual return for 2025-26 has not yet been filed
options.misconception: reads the two limbs as alternatives that each keep the window open
options.why: The section takes the EARLIER of the two dates. An unfiled annual return cannot extend the November cut-off; it can only close the window sooner.

options.text: No — the window closed on 30 November 2026
options.why: The invoice belongs to financial year 2025-26, so section 16(4) shuts the credit at the thirtieth of November following that year's end. Discovery in December is discovery too late, however eligible the credit was on its merits.

options.text: Yes, at any time within four years, as with other indirect tax refunds
options.misconception: imports a limitation period from refund law into the credit provision
options.why: Refund limitation under section 54 is a different clock for a different claim. Credit has its own guillotine in section 16(4), and it is measured in months, not years.

items.scenario: During a December 2026 review, a company discovers an unclaimed input tax credit of ₹6 lakh on a supplier invoice dated 14 February 2026. All section 16(2) conditions are satisfied and the annual return for 2025-26 has not yet been filed.

items.stem: What is the place of supply, and which tax applies?

options.text: Madhya Pradesh, because the buyer arranged the transport himself
options.misconception: lets who carries the goods decide the place of supply
options.why: Movement "whether by the supplier or the recipient" is within the same rule. The statute cares about the destination of the movement, not about whose truck it is.

options.text: Madhya Pradesh — an intra-State supply, since delivery was taken at the factory gate
options.misconception: fixes the place of supply where possession changed hands rather than where movement ends
options.why: Handing over at the gate is how the movement begins, not where it terminates. The section looks at where the goods are going for delivery to the recipient, which is Ahmedabad.

options.text: Gujarat, but as an intra-State supply of Gujarat attracting CGST and SGST
options.misconception: gets the place right and then misreads what inter-State means
options.why: Inter-State or intra-State compares the supplier's location with the place of supply. Supplier in Madhya Pradesh, place of supply Gujarat — that is inter-State, and IGST is the levy.

options.text: Gujarat — an inter-State supply attracting IGST
options.why: The supply involves movement of goods, and the movement terminates for delivery at the Ahmedabad plant. Section 10(1)(a) fixes the place of supply there, and Madhya Pradesh to Gujarat is inter-State, so IGST applies.

items.scenario: A dealer in Bhopal sells machinery to a buyer registered in Gujarat. The buyer sends its own truck, takes delivery at the Bhopal factory gate, and carries the machinery to its Ahmedabad plant.

items.stem: Who pays GST in March on the advance?

options.text: Neither, because no invoice has been issued by either
options.misconception: makes the invoice the sole trigger for both goods and services
options.why: For services the payment reaches back as a trigger on its own. The software company's liability arises in March with or without an invoice.

options.text: Both, since money received against a taxable supply is taxable when received
options.misconception: applies the services rule across the goods-services line
options.why: That was the position for goods only briefly. The notification removed advances on goods from the net after the compliance burden proved unworkable, and the asymmetry is now the tested point.

options.text: Only the manufacturer, since goods are tangible and the machine is identifiable
options.misconception: reverses the asymmetry
options.why: The rule runs the other way. Tangibility has nothing to do with it — the notification names goods as the excused side.

options.text: Only the software company — advances for services are taxable on receipt; for goods they are not
options.why: Time of supply for services reaches the earlier of invoice and payment, catching the advance in March. For goods, Notification 66/2017 confined the liability to invoice issue, so the manufacturer pays in May with the invoice.

items.scenario: On 20 March a machine manufacturer receives a ₹10 lakh advance against a machine to be delivered in May, and a software company receives a ₹10 lakh advance against an implementation project starting in May. Both are regular taxpayers.

items.stem: Which discount reduces the value of supply for GST?

options.text: The 2 per cent scheme discount, provided the dealer reverses the proportionate credit
options.why: It was agreed before the supplies, is linkable to specific invoices, and the recipient's credit reversal completes section 15(3)(b). The tax follows the price the parties had genuinely agreed all along.

options.text: Both, since both are genuine discounts actually passed on
options.misconception: treats commercial genuineness as the statutory test
options.why: Genuineness is necessary but the section demands prior agreement and invoice linkage. The goodwill discount was born after the supplies and fails at the first condition.

options.text: Neither, because post-supply discounts never reduce taxable value
options.misconception: reads the pre-supply agreement condition as banning all later discounts
options.why: The section exists precisely to allow post-supply discounts that were pre-agreed. What it shuts out is the discount invented after the event.

options.text: The goodwill discount, since it is unconditional and unilateral
options.misconception: rewards the discount with fewer strings as the cleaner deduction
options.why: Unconditional generosity is exactly what the section will not net off. The strings — prior agreement, linkage, reversal — are the qualification, not the disqualification.

items.scenario: A distributor agreement signed in April promises a 2 per cent year-end discount on all purchases if the dealer crosses ₹5 crore. The dealer crosses it, and the distributor issues a credit note for ₹10 lakh plus tax, linked invoice-wise. Separately, the distributor gives another dealer an unplanned ₹4 lakh goodwill discount for staying loyal in a hard year.

items.stem: On what amount does the section 50 interest run?

options.text: On the full ₹20 lakh of the liability
options.misconception: charges interest on the gross liability the way the section originally read
options.why: Gross-liability interest was the original position, litigated hard and then rewritten retrospectively. Answers citing the old position are answering a repealed law.

options.text: On nothing, since the liability was fully discharged at filing
options.misconception: treats the eventual payment as erasing the delay
options.why: The tax was due with the period's return, not four months later. Discharge ends the clock; it does not unwind it.

options.text: On the ₹14 lakh met from credit, since credit was applied late
options.misconception: inverts the proviso and charges the credit portion
options.why: The proviso protects exactly that portion. Credit sitting in the ledger was already tax paid once; charging interest on it would tax the delay twice.

options.text: On the ₹6 lakh paid through the cash ledger
options.why: The proviso to section 50(1) confines interest, where the return is filed late, to the portion discharged through the electronic cash ledger. The ₹14 lakh met by credit was the Government's money in the system all along, and Parliament amended the section retrospectively to say so.

items.scenario: A taxpayer files a GSTR-3B four months late. The tax liability of ₹20 lakh for the period was covered ₹14 lakh by input tax credit and ₹6 lakh by cash, both applied on the day of the late filing.

items.stem: What is the position in August 2026?

options.text: Neither, because goods sent for job work are not supplies at all
options.misconception: remembers the concession and forgets its condition
options.why: The tax-free movement is conditional on timely return. Break the condition and the law rewrites history — the despatch becomes a taxable supply from day one.

options.text: The fabric is deemed supplied in June 2026, when the year expired
options.misconception: dates the deemed supply at the breach instead of the despatch
options.why: The deeming is retrospective to the date the goods went out. That is what makes the interest bite — fourteen months of it here, not two.

options.text: The fabric is deemed supplied on 1 June 2025, with tax and interest; the dies have time until June 2028
options.why: Inputs get one year, and the fabric's year ran out in June 2026 — the deeming reaches back to the day of despatch, so interest runs from 2025, not from the breach. Capital goods get three years, so the dies are safely out until 2028.

options.text: Both are deemed supplied, since neither returned within one year
options.misconception: applies the inputs window to capital goods
options.why: The section keeps two clocks. Dies are capital goods on a three-year clock, and treating them on the one-year clock manufactures a liability that does not exist.

items.scenario: A manufacturer sent dies worth ₹30 lakh (capital goods) and fabric worth ₹12 lakh (inputs) to a job worker on 1 June 2025 without payment of tax. The fabric is still with the job worker in August 2026; the dies are expected back in 2027.

items.stem: Is the colleague right?

options.text: Yes, unless the exporter pays IGST on exports first and reclaims it
options.misconception: makes the pay-and-refund route the only lawful one
options.why: Paying IGST and claiming it back is one of two routes. The LUT route reaches the same destination without routing ₹18 lakh through the Government and back.

options.text: Partly — credit survives but can only offset future domestic output tax, never refund
options.misconception: allows the credit but denies the refund that makes exporting viable
options.why: An exporter with no domestic sales would accumulate credit forever. Refund of unutilised credit on zero-rated supplies is the section's whole mechanism.

options.text: No — zero-rating keeps the credit alive, and the unutilised ₹18 lakh is refundable
options.why: Zero-rated is a different legal creature from exempt. Section 16 of the IGST Act preserves credit on inputs feeding zero-rated supplies, and the LUT route exists precisely so the exporter can skip charging tax yet recover the input side as a refund.

options.text: Yes — supplies on which no tax is charged are exempt, and exempt supplies block credit
options.misconception: collapses zero-rated into exempt
options.why: For exempt supplies the credit dies; for zero-rated it survives by express provision. The zero on the invoice looks identical and works oppositely, which is why the paper tests it.

items.scenario: An exporter of garments buys inputs carrying ₹18 lakh of GST and exports the entire output under a letter of undertaking, charging no tax on the export invoices. A colleague warns that selling without charging tax makes the supplies exempt, killing the input credit.

items.stem: Was an e-way bill required?

options.text: Yes — the bill attaches to movement of goods above fifty thousand rupees, sale or no sale
options.why: Rule 138 is triggered by causing movement of a consignment worth more than ₹50,000, and a branch transfer moves goods as surely as a sale does. The delivery challan takes the place of the invoice; the e-way bill is needed either way.

options.text: No, because both godowns belong to the same legal entity
options.misconception: treats intra-entity movement as outside the rule
options.why: The rule asks what is moving and how much it is worth, not who owns each end of the journey. Same-entity transfers above the limit are squarely inside it.

options.text: Yes, but only if the goods cross the State border
options.misconception: confines the requirement to inter-State movement
options.why: Intra-State movement carries the requirement too, though States may set higher limits for it. Indore to Bhopal is within one State and still within the rule.

options.text: No, because an e-way bill accompanies a tax invoice, and none exists here
options.misconception: ties the bill to the invoice instead of the movement
options.why: Movements without invoices travel on delivery challans, and the rule expressly covers reasons other than supply. The paperwork changes; the bill does not.

items.scenario: A registered dealer sends goods worth ₹3.2 lakh from its Indore godown to its own Bhopal branch, a stock transfer with no sale and no payment. The despatch clerk skips the e-way bill on the ground that nothing has been sold.

items.stem: What does release under section 129 cost him?

options.text: Nothing beyond a ₹10,000 general penalty, since no tax was evaded
options.misconception: imports the no-evasion leniency into a strict transit provision
options.why: Section 129 is deliberately indifferent to intent. The absent e-way bill is the offence, and courts have upheld the harshness because transit checks are where evasion hides.

options.text: A bond for the goods' value, with the penalty argued later in adjudication
options.misconception: offers the security route available to a non-owner as the owner's escape
options.why: Security in lieu is a route the section provides, but the release price stays the same penalty. The bond defers payment; it does not reduce what unlocks the truck.

options.text: A penalty of ₹3.6 lakh — two hundred per cent of the tax payable
options.why: Where the owner comes forward, section 129(1)(a) prices release at 200 per cent of the tax payable on the goods. The invoice showing tax charged does not soften it — the section punishes the movement's non-compliance, not evasion of the levy.

options.text: The ₹1.8 lakh tax plus a modest general penalty
options.misconception: applies the pre-amendment tax-plus-penalty formula
options.why: The section was rewritten to a pure penalty of 200 per cent. Answers built on the old tax-plus-100-per-cent split describe a provision that no longer exists.

items.scenario: A truck carrying taxable goods worth ₹10 lakh (tax ₹1.8 lakh) is intercepted without a valid e-way bill. The consignor owns up, produces the invoice showing tax fully charged, and argues that since the tax is on the invoice and will be paid with the return, only a token fine can apply.

items.stem: What is the GST position on the two transactions?

options.text: Neither is taxable, since GST requires consideration
options.misconception: treats consideration as indispensable to supply
options.why: Consideration is the general rule and Schedule I is the list of exceptions to it. The van is the textbook case — credit was enjoyed on the way in, so the way out is taxed.

options.text: The van is a deemed supply and taxable; the hampers stay outside as gifts within fifty thousand
options.why: Permanent disposal of a business asset that carried credit is Schedule I's first entry — consideration is irrelevant once the credit was taken. Employee gifts have their own carve-out and ₹4,000 sits well inside the fifty-thousand-per-employee-per-year line.

options.text: The van escapes because it went to a charity; the hampers are taxable perquisites
options.misconception: imports an income-tax charity instinct and a perquisite label into GST
options.why: GST has no donee-based relief here — the recipient's character does not undo Schedule I. And perquisite is an income-tax word; for GST the hampers are simply gifts under the fifty-thousand line.

options.text: Both are taxable, since both are supplies without consideration by a business
options.misconception: sweeps the employee-gift carve-out into the deeming
options.why: Gifts up to fifty thousand rupees a year per employee are expressly kept out. Taxing the hampers taxes what the proviso protects.

items.scenario: A company gives away an old delivery van, on which it had claimed input tax credit, free to a charitable school. The accountant books no GST since nothing was received in return. The same month, the company gifts each of its forty employees a festival hamper worth ₹4,000.

items.stem: How do these two sales sit under GST?

options.text: The building is taxable because it was sold by a developer in the course of business
options.misconception: lets the seller's trade override the completion certificate
options.why: Business character brings a transaction into GST only if it is a supply. A completed building with its certificate is out by schedule, developer or not — the tax belongs to under-construction sales.

options.text: Both are exempt supplies, and count toward aggregate turnover
options.misconception: confuses non-supplies with exempt supplies
options.why: Exempt supplies are supplies that a notification relieves; Schedule III transactions never become supplies in the first place. The difference shows up exactly where the accountant worried — turnover computations.

options.text: The land escapes but the building attracts GST at the works contract rate
options.misconception: taxes a completed sale as if construction services were still being supplied
options.why: Works contract rates belong to construction underway for a buyer. After completion and certification there is no service left to tax; what changes hands is immovable property.

options.text: Neither is a supply at all — Schedule III keeps land and completed buildings outside GST
options.why: Sale of land, and of a building after its completion certificate, are Schedule III entries — treated as neither goods nor services. They are not exempt supplies; they are non-supplies, which is why they also stay out of aggregate turnover.

items.scenario: A developer sells a completed office building with its occupancy certificate in hand for ₹48 crore, and separately sells a plot of land for ₹12 crore. His new accountant worries that these sales, being high-value, will attract GST and swell aggregate turnover past every threshold.

items.stem: Is the refund claim within time?

options.text: Yes — where tax was paid under a demand later set aside, the relevant date is the judgment's date
options.why: Section 54's two years run from the relevant date, and the definition assigns judgment-driven refunds the date of the judgment. The clock the department is reading — the payment date — belongs to a different ground of claim.

options.text: No — two years from payment is absolute, and equity cannot extend limitation
options.misconception: reads one relevant date as the only relevant date
options.why: The rigour of the limitation is real, but the statute itself moves the starting line by ground of claim. No equity is needed; the definition does the work.

options.text: Yes, because limitation never applies to tax collected without authority
options.misconception: right result, lawless route
options.why: Even unconstitutional levies travel through the refund machinery with its windows. The claim succeeds here because the statutory clock starts at the judgment, not because clocks stop for good causes.

options.text: No, unless the company had paid the tax under protest in 2024
options.misconception: imports the old excise protest requirement into GST
options.why: Payment under protest shaped refunds under the old law. Section 54's relevant-date definition replaced that scaffolding; the judgment date governs with or without a protest letter.

items.scenario: In August 2026 a company wins its writ petition: tax of ₹40 lakh it paid in March 2024 under a demand is held to have been collected without authority. The department resists the refund, arguing the two-year window from the March 2024 payment closed in March 2026.

items.stem: Is the adviser right?

options.text: No — the consultancy can use the ordinary one per cent traders' rate instead
options.misconception: puts the right taxpayer into the wrong scheme
options.why: The ordinary scheme's rates belong to manufacturers, traders and restaurants. A pure service provider enters through 10(2A) and pays that scheme's six per cent, not the traders' one.

options.text: Yes for this year, since eligibility needs current-year turnover below fifty lakh first
options.misconception: tests eligibility on the running year instead of the preceding one
options.why: The gate reads the preceding financial year — ₹42 lakh, inside the line. The current year's growth ends the scheme prospectively when it crosses, never retrospectively.

options.text: Yes — composition remains closed to every service except restaurants
options.misconception: states the pre-2019 law as current
options.why: True until section 10(2A) arrived, and stale ever since. The scheme the adviser denies is sitting in the section he cited.

options.text: No — section 10(2A) gives pure service providers their own scheme at six per cent within fifty lakh
options.why: The adviser's rule described the original section 10. The 2019 insertion built a parallel scheme for exactly this taxpayer — services, preceding-year turnover within fifty lakh, six per cent on turnover, with the same stay-local discipline.

items.scenario: An interior design consultancy with preceding-year turnover of ₹42 lakh wants a simple flat levy instead of regular GST compliance. Its adviser rules out composition entirely, saying the scheme is for traders and restaurants, never for service providers.

items.stem: On which vehicles is the credit good?

options.text: All three — each vehicle is used in the course of business
options.misconception: lets section 16's general test override section 17's specific block
options.why: Business use is the entry condition, and section 17(5) then blocks listed items notwithstanding it. The sedan is genuinely for business and still loses its credit.

options.text: The bus and the van — only the sedan's credit is blocked
options.why: The block in section 17(5)(a) reaches motor vehicles for transporting persons with seating up to thirteen, and the sedan fits none of the three saving uses. The bus escapes on capacity — above thirteen seats — and the van escapes because it transports goods, a category the block never covered.

options.text: None — credit on motor vehicles is blocked for everyone except vehicle dealers
options.misconception: remembers the block without its capacity and goods carve-outs
options.why: The block was drawn narrowly on purpose: passenger vehicles up to thirteen seats. Buses and goods carriages are ordinary creditable business assets.

options.text: The sedan and the bus, since both carry persons; the van fails as it carries no people
options.misconception: inverts the block — reads it as favouring passenger transport
options.why: Carrying persons in a small vehicle is what triggers the block, not what saves from it. The van's goods-carrying character is exactly why its credit flows.

items.scenario: A consulting firm buys three vehicles in a year: a five-seater sedan for partners' travel, a twenty-seater bus to shuttle staff, and a delivery van for moving office equipment between branches. It claims input tax credit on all three.

items.stem: What is the time of supply for each part of the consideration?

options.text: 10 May for everything — liability arises when full payment is received
options.misconception: waits for the last rupee
options.why: Earlier of the events, not latest. Waiting for final payment would let parties schedule their own tax periods, the exact discretion the section removes.

options.text: 25 March for the advance; 20 April for the balance
options.why: The invoice is timely, so the rule is the earlier of invoice and payment, applied to the extent of each amount. The advance's payment date beats the invoice, pulling 40 per cent into March — the earlier tax period. For the balance the invoice of 20 April beats the May payment.

options.text: 5 April for everything — tax follows completion of the service
options.misconception: replaces the statutory comparators with the completion date
options.why: Completion enters the rule only when the invoice misses its thirty-day window. With a timely invoice, the statute reads invoice against payment and never asks when the work finished.

options.text: 20 April for everything, since one invoice covers the whole supply
options.misconception: lets the invoice absorb an advance received earlier
options.why: The provision applies to the extent the invoice or payment covers the supply. Money received in March is taxable by reference to March; the invoice cannot pull it forward into April.

items.scenario: A service is completed on 5 April. The client pays an advance of 40 per cent on 25 March, before completion. The invoice is issued on 20 April, within the thirty-day limit, and the balance is paid on 10 May.

items.stem: What does the company actually get?

options.text: ₹39.2 lakh, but only if the re-export happens within six months of import
options.misconception: shrinks the two-year window
options.why: Section 74 allows two years from payment of duty, extendable on sufficient cause. Fourteen months is comfortably inside.

options.text: The full ₹40 lakh, since the machine was never used in India
options.misconception: rounds ninety-eight up to a hundred
options.why: The statute keeps two per cent even for unused goods — the cost of the round trip through customs. Only the tapering rates for used goods fall below that.

options.text: Nothing — drawback requires the goods to have been used in manufacturing exports
options.misconception: knows only section 75 and reads it as the whole of drawback
options.why: That manufacturing route is real but parallel. Section 74 exists for the simpler case — the goods go back out as themselves — and asks only identity and the time window.

options.text: ₹39.2 lakh — ninety-eight per cent under section 74, since the same goods left within two years
options.why: Re-export of the imported goods themselves, identified as such and inside the two-year window, is exactly section 74's case, and the unused-goods rate is ninety-eight per cent. The department's objection describes section 75, which is the drawback for inputs consumed in manufacture — a different section for a different exporter.

items.scenario: A company imports a specialised machine paying ₹40 lakh in duty. The buyer's project is cancelled, and fourteen months later the identical machine, unused and identified by the customs authorities as the imported one, is shipped back to the seller. The company claims the whole ₹40 lakh back; the department offers nothing, saying drawback belongs to manufacturer-exporters.

items.stem: Where is the place of supply, and why?

options.text: Maharashtra — services are supplied from where the supplier works
options.misconception: taxes the origin instead of the destination
options.why: GST is a destination tax; the supplier's location matters for identifying the levy, not the place of supply. Where the architect sits is the one place the section never picks.

options.text: Goa — services directly relating to immovable property are supplied where the property is
options.why: Section 12(3) carves property-linked services out of the default: an architect's design for a specific site takes the site's location. The building in Goa anchors the supply, and the recipient's Karnataka registration never enters the analysis.

options.text: Karnataka — the registered recipient's location governs services between registered persons
options.misconception: applies the general rule over the specific carve-out
options.why: Section 12(2)'s default yields wherever a specific sub-section speaks. Property-linked services have their own rule precisely because the consumption happens at the site.

options.text: The firm may choose any of the three states if it discloses the choice on the invoice
options.misconception: makes place of supply elective
options.why: Place of supply is fixed by statute so that the consuming state gets the revenue. An election on the invoice would let suppliers route tax to convenient states.

items.scenario: An architect registered in Maharashtra designs a hotel to be built in Goa for a client registered in Karnataka. The firm bills IGST with place of supply Karnataka, using the default rule that services go where the registered recipient is.

items.stem: How does GST actually treat the contract?

options.text: As one supply of services for the whole ₹10 crore — Schedule II deems the entire works contract a service
options.why: The composite construction contract on immovable property is a works contract, and Schedule II declares it a supply of services in its entirety. One classification, one rate for the whole consideration. The VAT-era vivisection of a single contract is the precise mischief the deeming ended.

options.text: As a supply of goods, since materials dominate the contract value
options.misconception: classifies by the larger component instead of by the deeming
options.why: Dominance tests decide unlisted composite supplies. Works contracts never reach that test — the schedule has already answered, and it answered services regardless of the ratio.

options.text: The split is right — goods are goods and services are services, whatever the contract says
options.misconception: carries the pre-GST split into a regime that abolished it
options.why: Under the old twin levies the split was compulsory; under GST the deeming makes it wrong. The embedded steel is not sold as steel — it disappears into an immovable whole.

options.text: Whichever classification yields less tax, at the contractor's option
options.misconception: converts a statutory deeming into a planning choice
options.why: Schedule II exists to remove exactly this election. Classification is fixed by law so that identical contracts cannot be taxed differently by drafting.

items.scenario: A contractor builds a factory for ₹10 crore, of which ₹6 crore is steel, cement and machinery embedded in the works and ₹4 crore is labour and services. Its accountant splits the invoice — charging goods rates of GST on ₹6 crore and service rates on ₹4 crore — the way the firm did under VAT and service tax.

items.stem: Is the officer's approach correct?

options.text: No — the relationship displaces the price only if it influenced the price, which the importer may disprove
options.why: Section 14 accepts the price actually paid unless the relationship influenced it, and the valuation rules give the importer the chance to show the price approximates arm's-length benchmarks — a discount explicable by volumes or reduced marketing costs can survive. Rejection needs examination, not the mere existence of the relationship.

options.text: Yes — related-party prices are automatically substituted with the catalogue price
options.misconception: converts a rebuttable concern into an automatic rejection
options.why: Automatic substitution would tax corporate structure rather than value. The rules order an examination of the circumstances of sale first, and accept the price where the relationship did not move it.

options.text: No, because customs must always accept the invoice as conclusive
options.misconception: swings to the opposite absolute
options.why: The declared price is the starting point, not scripture. Where the relationship did influence it, the rules walk down the substitute methods — identical goods, similar goods, and onward.

options.text: Yes, unless the parent certifies in writing that the price is fair
options.misconception: lets the interested party certify its own valuation
options.why: A self-serving certificate from the seller proves nothing. What counts is evidence — test values, comparable sales, cost build-ups — examined under the valuation rules.

items.scenario: An Indian subsidiary imports components from its foreign parent at a price 8 per cent below the parent's catalogue price to independent distributors. The customs officer rejects the declared value outright, holding that a price between related persons can never be the transaction value.

items.stem: What is the correct value of supply?

options.text: ₹10.35 lakh — the subsidy is included but interest never is
options.misconception: right on the subsidy, wrong on delayed-payment interest
options.why: Clause (d) names interest, late fee and penalty for delayed payment of consideration as part of value. It is taxed when received, but it is taxed.

options.text: ₹10 lakh — everything beyond the price of the machine is a separate matter
options.misconception: reads value as bare price
options.why: The subsection exists to stop exactly this unbundling. Packing and levies are the cost of delivering the supply, and the statute plants them in its value.

options.text: ₹11.05 lakh at the outset — packing, the levy and the subsidy come in — plus the ₹8,000 interest when received
options.why: Section 15(2) sweeps in incidental expenses charged by the supplier, taxes other than GST, and price-linked subsidies from non-Government sources — the state board is a Government body, but the item to test is its character; a board subsidy directly linked to price from other than Central or State Government enters the value. Interest for delayed payment joins the value when it materialises.

options.text: ₹10.20 lakh — only the packing, since the supplier itself rendered it
options.misconception: admits one inclusion and drops the rest of the list
options.why: The subsection is a list, not an example. The municipal levy and the price-linked subsidy stand on the same statutory footing as the packing.

items.scenario: A machine is sold for ₹10 lakh. The invoice adds ₹20,000 packing, ₹15,000 municipal levy the supplier must pay on the sale, and the buyer later pays ₹8,000 interest for settling two months late. A state agricultural board also pays the supplier a ₹50,000 subsidy tied to each machine's price. The accountant charges GST on ₹10 lakh alone.

items.stem: Which supply is actually an export of services?

options.text: Neither, because software services are consumed where they are written
options.misconception: invents an origin rule for services
options.why: Place of supply for such services follows the recipient's location. The German client's supply lands outside India and qualifies; the branch supply fails on identity, not on geography.

options.text: Both — each crosses the border and brings in foreign exchange
options.misconception: tests exports by geography and currency alone
options.why: Those are two conditions of five. The merely-establishments clause was written for precisely the branch case, where money moves inside one legal person.

options.text: Only the German one — the Dubai branch is the same person, and a supply to yourself fails the export definition
options.why: Section 2(6)'s fifth condition excludes supplies between establishments of the same person treated as distinct persons. The branch is the company; convertible currency and a foreign address cannot make a transaction with oneself an export. The German supply ticks all five conditions.

options.text: Both, provided the Dubai branch is separately registered in the UAE
options.misconception: lets foreign registration split one legal person
options.why: Registration abroad changes the branch's local compliance, not its identity. The Indian Act's definition looks at whether supplier and recipient are one person, and they are.

items.scenario: An Indian software company provides development services to its own branch in Dubai, which pays in dirhams through banking channels. Separately it serves an unrelated German client, paid in euros. The company treats both as zero-rated exports and claims refunds.

items.stem: Does the tax reduction survive scrutiny?

options.text: Yes, if the buyer certifies it has reversed the corresponding input credit
options.misconception: lets reversal on one side reopen a closed window on the other
options.why: The buyer's reversal is a condition of the mechanism working inside the window, not a key to it afterwards. Past the date, the section offers no route back.

options.text: No, and even the commercial credit note is barred after November
options.misconception: extends the tax deadline to the price itself
options.why: Parties may adjust prices between themselves forever; that is contract, not tax. What expires in November is only the right to take GST back from the government.

options.text: No — the window for a January 2026 (FY 2025-26) supply closed on 30 November 2026
options.why: Section 34(2) lets the credit note reduce tax only up to the thirtieth of November following the financial year of the supply. A December 2026 note for an FY 2025-26 supply is out of time: the goods may come back and the price may be refunded, but the tax adjustment is barred — a commercial credit note is all that remains.

options.text: Yes — returns within one year of supply always carry their tax back
options.misconception: invents a rolling one-year window
options.why: The clock is anchored to the financial year's end, not the invoice date. A supply made in March gets eight months; one made in April gets nearly twenty — the statute accepts that unevenness for the sake of closing years.

items.scenario: In January 2026 a wholesaler supplied goods with ₹18 lakh GST. In December 2026 the buyer returns a third of the goods. The wholesaler issues a GST credit note for ₹6 lakh of tax and reduces its output liability in the December 2026 return.

items.stem: How much of the ₹29.8 lakh is actually creditable?

options.text: All ₹29.8 lakh — every tax on a business input is creditable under GST
options.misconception: sweeps basic customs duty into a credit system it never joined
options.why: BCD is a customs levy proper, protecting the border, with no credit mechanism. Only the IGST component crosses into the input tax ledger.

options.text: The ₹19.8 lakh IGST — collected by customs but creditable as input tax; only the ₹10 lakh BCD is cost
options.why: The proviso to section 5(1) routes the tax on imported goods through customs machinery for collection, but what is collected is IGST — input tax in the importer's hands, creditable against output liability like any other. Basic customs duty stays outside the credit chain and lands in cost.

options.text: The IGST, but only half now and half next year, as for capital goods under the old law
options.misconception: applies CENVAT's instalment rule to GST
options.why: The fifty-per-cent-per-year split for capital goods died with CENVAT. GST credits capital goods IGST in full in the year of receipt.

options.text: Nothing — duties paid at the port never enter the GST credit stream
options.misconception: classifies the tax by its collector instead of its character
options.why: The collection point is administrative convenience. The levy's character is IGST on an inter-State supply, and the credit provisions treat it exactly so.

items.scenario: A registered manufacturer imports machinery: assessable value ₹1 crore, basic customs duty ₹10 lakh, IGST ₹19.8 lakh charged at the port. Its accountant books the entire ₹29.8 lakh as cost, saying taxes collected by customs are customs duties, and no customs duty is ever creditable under GST.

items.stem: What does GST make of the two internal flows?

options.text: Neither — a person cannot make a supply to himself under any tax law
options.misconception: argues from general law against a specific statutory fiction
options.why: The fiction of distinct persons was enacted to override exactly this intuition. Without it, consuming States would lose the tax on everything routed through another State's warehouse.

options.text: Both, but only when the depot actually sells the stock onward
options.misconception: defers the internal supply to the external sale
options.why: The transfer is itself the taxable event, at its own time of supply. The depot's later sale is a second supply with its own tax — two events, two levies, credit linking them.

options.text: The goods yes, the services no — offices only assist, they do not supply
options.misconception: taxes what moves in trucks and misses what moves between offices
options.why: Services between distinct persons sit in the same Schedule I entry. A head office keeping the group's books renders a service the branches would otherwise buy.

options.text: Both are taxable supplies between distinct persons — the stock transfer and the head office services alike
options.why: Each State registration is a distinct person, and Schedule I taxes supplies between them without consideration. The stock transfer bears IGST on its rule-based value, and the head office's centralised services to branches are supplies too. Credit at the receiving end typically neutralises the cash cost — but the compliance is not optional.

items.scenario: A company's Maharashtra factory sends finished stock worth ₹2 crore to its own Karnataka depot for sale there. Its Mumbai head office also handles accounting and IT for all branches. The tax head charges no GST on either, reasoning that no one can sell to themselves or invoice their own branches.

items.stem: Who bears the duty on each consignment?

options.text: Neither falls on the importer — the custodian pays for the pilfered goods, and the fire loss earns remission on proof
options.why: Section 13 lifts the importer's duty on goods pilfered between unloading and clearance and section 45 sends the bill to the custodian whose watch failed. Section 23 remits duty on goods lost or destroyed before clearance once the Assistant Commissioner is satisfied — the fire needs proving, but proven, the duty goes.

options.text: Both — importation was complete when the goods entered Indian waters
options.misconception: fixes duty at the moment of import and ignores both relieving sections
options.why: The taxable event may arise on import, but Parliament relieved exactly these casualties. Charging duty on goods the importer never received turns customs into an insurer's windfall.

options.text: The pilferage yes, the fire no — theft is the importer's commercial risk
options.misconception: reverses the two sections
options.why: Pilferage is the automatic relief — no application, duty simply not payable by the importer — because the goods sat with the custodian. It is the fire that needs a satisfaction-based remission order.

options.text: Neither, provided the importer first pays the duty and claims refunds later
options.misconception: routes statutory relief through the refund machinery
options.why: Section 13 means duty is not leviable on the importer at all, and section 23 remits before payment. Pay-first-refund-later imports the cash flow burden the sections spare.

items.scenario: Two misfortunes strike an importer at the port: one consignment is pilfered from the custodian's warehouse after unloading, before clearance; another is destroyed in a warehouse fire, also before clearance. The department demands full duty on both, saying risk passes to the importer on arrival.

items.stem: How does GST actually split the two streams?

options.text: TCS on both — the app is one platform and one compliance applies
options.misconception: runs the collection mechanism where the liability shift governs
options.why: Section 9(5) overrides for its notified services precisely because chasing thousands of drivers was impractical. Collecting TCS from a supplier the law has already displaced doubles the machinery on the wrong person.

options.text: Neither — platforms are intermediaries outside the tax net entirely
options.misconception: mistakes facilitation for invisibility
options.why: The statute built two regimes specifically for platforms. An operator with no TCS registration and no 9(5) payment is not neutral; it is non-compliant twice.

options.text: The app pays tax on both streams as the deemed supplier of everything it hosts
options.misconception: stretches 9(5) from its notified services to all commerce
options.why: The deeming covers the notified list — transport, accommodation, restaurants, housekeeping. Goods never entered it; the handicraft seller remains the taxable person, minus the TCS slice.

options.text: TCS on the handicraft sales; on the cab rides the app itself pays the tax under section 9(5), with no TCS on them
options.why: Goods sold through the platform take the section 52 route: the supplier remains liable and the operator collects a slice at source. Passenger transport is a notified 9(5) service, so the app is deemed the supplier and pays the tax itself — and since it pays as supplier, there is nothing to collect TCS on. The two regimes are exclusive by design.

items.scenario: A marketplace app hosts two businesses: a seller of handicrafts shipping goods to buyers, and a network of cab drivers carrying passengers. The app's compliance team plans to collect TCS on both streams and leave the GST liability with each supplier, treating the app as a mere platform throughout.

items.stem: Which line has its input credit wrongly reversed?

options.text: The exports — zero-rated supplies keep their input credit, unlike the other two
options.why: Zero-rating under IGST section 16 is taxability at rate zero with the credit chain deliberately intact — refundable, not reversible. The liquor is non-taxable and the vegetables exempt; input credit attributable to those two does reverse. Calling all three tax-free treats the one favoured category as if it were the penalised ones.

options.text: The vegetables — nil-rated goods are taxable supplies, so their credit stays
options.misconception: reads nil-rated as outside exemption
options.why: Nil-rated is taxable at zero per cent, but the exempt-supply definition sweeps nil-rated in for credit purposes. The credit attributable to them reverses like any exempt supply's.

options.text: None — no tax on the output always means no credit on the inputs
options.misconception: states the exemption rule as if it were universal
options.why: That symmetry is exactly what zero-rating suspends. Exports carry no tax and full credit — the design that keeps Indian goods competitive abroad.

options.text: The liquor — outside GST means GST rules cannot touch its credit
options.misconception: hopes non-taxability shields the inputs too
options.why: The inputs bore GST even though the output escapes it, and the exempt-supply definition includes non-taxable supplies precisely so their input credit reverses. Outside the levy is inside the reversal.

items.scenario: A distillery-cum-exporter reviews three revenue lines: liquor for human consumption sold in India; fresh vegetables (nil-rated) traded domestically; and packaged spices exported to Dubai. The accountant lumps all three as "tax-free sales" and reverses input credit proportionately across them all.

items.stem: What level of assurance does an audit conducted in accordance with the Standards on Auditing obtain?

options.text: Reasonable assurance, which is a high but not absolute level of assurance
